posts.title: Go-around: power first, flaps in stages
posts.headline: Raise all the flaps at once just above the runway and a Cessna 172 can settle back onto it. Power goes in first, then the flaps come up in stages.
posts.alt: Seen from behind at dusk, a Cessna 172 flies low over the airfield, with a second Cessna 172 on the runway ahead of it.
posts.related_text: A go-around is a normal maneuver, used when approach and landing parameters deviate from expectations or when it is hazardous to continue (AFH ch 9). The go-around is not inherently dangerous; it becomes dangerous only when delayed unduly or executed improperly. Delay normally stems from landing expectancy, the belief that the approach is sure to end in a safe landing, and from pride, the mistaken belief that going around is an admission of failure (AFH ch 9). In the Cessna 172P the balked landing checklist is: throttle full open; carburetor heat cold; wing flaps 20 degrees (immediately); climb speed 55 KIAS; wing flaps 10 degrees until obstacles are cleared; retract after reaching a safe altitude and 60 KIAS (172P POH 4-10; 4-3: Balked Landing, Maximum Power, Flaps 20 degrees, 55 KIAS). Power is the pilot's first concern: full power is applied smoothly, without hesitation, and carburetor heat is turned off to obtain maximum power. The 172P POH reduces the flap setting to 20 degrees immediately after full power is applied (AFH ch 9; 172P POH 4-20). The sudden addition of power tends to raise the nose and causes left yaw. Allowing the nose to rise too early could result in an unrecoverable stall at low altitude, so the pilot anticipates considerable forward elevator pressure to hold the nose level or in a safe climb attitude and applies right rudder pressure. Once the airspeed and climb attitude are set the pilot rough trims, and finer trim follows when conditions have stabilized (AFH ch 9). The 172P's carburetor heat is a knob on the instrument panel, pulled out for heat and pushed full in for none. The before-landing checklist sets it ON, full heat before reducing power, and the descent checklist calls for full heat as required to prevent carburetor icing. Full carburetor heat at full throttle costs approximately 75 to 150 RPM, and the balked landing checklist puts it to COLD (172P POH 4-9, 4-10, 4-11, 7-19). After the descent has been stopped, the landing flaps are partially retracted. It is wise to retract the flaps intermittently in small increments to allow time for the airplane to accelerate progressively as they are raised; a sudden and complete retraction of the flaps could cause a loss of lift resulting in the airplane settling into the ground (AFH ch 9). At 2,400 lb, power off and wings level, at either the most forward or the most rearward CG, the 172P stalls at about 33 KIAS with 30 degrees of flap, about 35 to 37 KIAS with 10 degrees and about 44 KIAS with the flaps up (KIAS values are approximate). Altitude loss during a stall recovery may be as much as 230 feet (172P POH Figure 5-3). Ground effect's apparent cushion of air is borrowed performance, repaid when the airplane climbs out of the ground effect area; an attempt to climb prematurely may leave the airplane unable to climb or even maintain altitude at full power. The pilot should resist any impulse to pitch up for a climb if airspeed is insufficient (AFH ch 9). In an extremely low go-around the airplane may settle onto the runway and bounce. This is not particularly dangerous provided the airplane is kept straight and a constant, safe pitch attitude is maintained; with power applied it attains a safe flying speed rapidly (AFH ch 9). The 172P flap switch lever moves in a slotted panel with mechanical stops at the 10 and 20 degree positions, and a scale and pointer on the left side of the lever indicate flap travel in degrees. Full flaps are 30 degrees (172P POH 7-10, 2-4). The newer, fuel-injected 172S has no carburetor heat step in its balked landing checklist, climbs at 60 KIAS and retracts the flaps after reaching a safe altitude and 65 KIAS, so pilots fly their own airplane's checklist (172S POH 4-17).

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Traffic on the runway, wind shear, a bigger airplane's wake or an unstable approach can each call for a go-around. You give up the landing and climb away. Cessna's checklist calls it a balked landing. A go-around is a normal maneuver. It only turns dangerous when it starts late or is flown wrong.

In a Cessna 172P go-around, power goes in first. Push the throttle full open, smoothly and without hesitation. The carb heat knob goes full in, to cold, so no heated air reaches the carburetor. Hold the nose with forward pressure and add right rudder.
Then bring the flaps up to 20 degrees and climb at 55 knots. Next comes 10 degrees until you're clear of obstacles, then all the way up at a safe height and 60 knots.

article.heading: Power first, then hold the nose
paragraphs: Move the throttle smoothly, because a sudden shove can make some engines falter. Leave it full open. The 172P's go-around climb is flown at maximum power.
Carb heat was on for the approach, to keep ice out of the carburetor. Full heat at full throttle costs about 75 to 150 RPM, power you need now.
The sudden power tends to raise the nose and swing it left. This close to the ground, letting the nose rise too early could cause a stall you can't recover from.

So expect considerable forward pressure on the yoke to hold the nose level or in a safe climb attitude. You were trimmed for a slow approach, so the push is firm. Add right rudder to keep it straight.
Trim takes that pressure off the yoke. Once the speed and climb are set, give it a rough setting, then fine-tune it once things settle.

figure.caption: Power is the first step. With it in, the flaps come to 20 degrees and the airplane climbs at 55 knots.
figure.alt: A Cessna 172 climbs straight away, wings level, against the dusk sky, under three lit step boxes reading Power, Flaps 20 and 55 KT.

article.heading: Flaps up in stages, and why
paragraphs: Flaps let the wing fly slower. Below its stall speed an airplane can't keep flying, and that speed is not fixed. Raise the flaps and it goes up, from about 33 knots with full flaps to about 44 with none.

Raise them all at once, just above the runway, and the sudden loss of lift can settle the airplane into the ground. Raised a little at a time, they give the airplane time to accelerate as each stage comes up.
Just above the runway, a stall leaves no room. In a 172P, recovering from one can cost as much as 230 feet.
The flap lever helps you stop at each stage. It has mechanical stops at 10 and 20 degrees.
A newer, fuel-injected 172S has no carb heat step and climbs at 60 knots. It raises the last flaps at a safe height and 65 knots. Fly your own airplane's checklist.

table.caption: A 172P's stall speed at 2,400 pounds, power off, wings level, between its forward and rearward balance limits

figure.caption: With every flap up, the stall speed jumps from about 33 knots to 44, and the airplane sinks toward the 172 on the runway.
figure.alt: Seen low from behind at dusk, a Cessna 172 flies low over the airfield near a second Cessna 172 on the runway, under the label Stall speed and the numbers 33 to 44 KT.

article.heading: Four go-around mistakes to avoid
paragraphs: Add the power before you touch the flaps. Raise them all with the throttle at idle and the nose pulled up, and the airplane sinks instead of climbing.
Go around as soon as you need to. A late go-around usually comes from landing expectancy, the belief that the landing will work out, or from pride. Going around is never a failure.

Let the speed build before you pitch up. Near the ground the wing makes less drag, which is called ground effect. It can feel like a cushion of air, but that help is borrowed. Climb out of it too soon and you may be unable to climb or even hold altitude at full power.
In a very low go-around the airplane may settle onto the runway and bounce. Keep it straight and hold the pitch steady, rather than pulling the nose up. The power soon gives you a safe flying speed.

figure.caption: The wrong move, the flap lever pushed from full flaps straight to UP in one sweep.
figure.alt: A finger pushes a Cessna 172's flap lever up to the UP stop, while the flap pointer still reads FULL.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. What comes first when you decide to go around in a 172P?
2. Why can a 172P settle into the ground if all its flaps come up at once?
3. What speed do you climb at with flaps 20, and when do the last flaps come up?
4. Why does the carb heat go to cold in a go-around?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Full power, smoothly and without hesitation, with the carb heat to cold.
2. Its stall speed jumps from about 33 knots to 44, and the loss of lift can settle it before the speed builds.
3. Climb at 55 knots, set 10 degrees until clear of obstacles, and raise the rest at a safe height and 60 knots.
4. Full carb heat at full throttle costs about 75 to 150 RPM, power you need for the climb.

posts.title: The leans: why a slow bank feels level
posts.headline: In clouds, a slow bank can feel level, and the quick fix can feel like a bank the other way. Pilots call it the leans.
posts.alt: From the cockpit in clouds, the attitude indicator shows a left bank. Light blue REAL marks follow the bank while red YOU FEEL marks stay level.
posts.related_text: The leans is the most common illusion during flight; it follows a sudden return to level flight after a gradual, prolonged turn the pilot did not notice (PHAK ch 17). A rotational acceleration of 2 degrees per second or lower is below the detection threshold of the semicircular canals (PHAK ch 17). A bank entered too slowly does not set the fluid in the roll canal moving; an abrupt correction does, creating the illusion of a bank the other way (IFH ch 3). The disoriented pilot may roll back into the original bank or, holding level flight, feel compelled to lean (IFH ch 3; AIM 8-1-5). The pilot needs to believe what the flight instruments show about the airplane's attitude regardless of what the natural senses tell (AFH ch 18).

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 17

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: In clouds, a wing can drop so slowly that you never feel the bank. When you spot it and roll level quickly, your inner ear feels only that quick roll. So level feels like a bank the other way.

Believe the attitude indicator, the instrument that shows your bank and pitch, over your body. Cross-check it with the heading indicator and the turn coordinator, which shows when you are turning. Level the wings smoothly on the attitude indicator and keep believing it.

article.heading: How your inner ear feels a roll
paragraphs: Each inner ear holds three semicircular canals, small fluid-filled tubes set at roughly right angles, one each for roll, pitch and yaw. In a small bulge of each canal sits the cupula, a soft gel flap with fine sensory hairs reaching into it.
When the airplane starts to roll, the roll canal turns with your head while the fluid lags behind. That lag bends the cupula and its hairs, and your brain reads the bend as a roll.

figure.caption: The canal turns faster than its fluid, so the fluid pushes the cupula and its hairs the other way.
figure.alt: A cutaway of the roll canal during a quick roll, showing lagging fluid bending the pink cupula over.

article.heading: Why a slow bank feels level
paragraphs: A roll that builds gently, at about 2 degrees per second or less, is too faint for your canals to sense. Roll that slowly and the fluid keeps pace with its canal, so the cupula stays upright and you feel level.
At half a degree a second, a bank reaches 30 degrees in a minute, and you feel none of it. Your seat gives no warning either, because a coordinated turn still presses you straight down into it.
Clouds are not the only place this happens. A dark night over water or empty land can hide the horizon just as well.

figure.caption: The white lines in the middle show the bank angle building, under 2 degrees a second. The fluid keeps pace, so the cupula stays upright.
figure.alt: The roll canal cutaway under the words UNDER ~2°/SEC, with an upright cupula and center lines showing bank angle.

article.heading: Why a quick rollout feels like a bank
paragraphs: Sooner or later you spot the bank, on the attitude indicator or in a heading that keeps creeping. If you roll level quickly, that roll sets the fluid moving, so your ear feels it.
Your brain never felt the roll in, so it counts only the roll out. After a slow bank to the left, level now feels like a bank to the right. The false bank lasts until the illusion fades.
A long, steady turn sets the same trap. In the canal that senses the turn, friction drags the fluid up to the canal's speed in about 15 to 20 seconds. Then the turn stops feeling like one.
A level airplane that feels banked is the leans, the most common illusion in flight. To feel upright, you lean toward the old bank in your seat.

figure.caption: After a quick roll out of a left bank, the wings are level, but your inner ear reports a right bank.
figure.alt: A Cessna 172 flying wings level at dusk, with a light blue line marked REAL lying level and a red dashed line tipping down to the right.

article.heading: Three mistakes the leans sets up
paragraphs: Keep the wings level once the attitude indicator shows them level. Rolling back into the old bank feels like the fix, but it is the danger. In that bank the tilted lift lets the nose drop, and the airplane loses altitude. Pulling back then only tightens a steepening descent, the graveyard spiral. Reduce power if the speed builds, level the wings, then raise the nose smoothly.

Keep cross-checking the heading indicator and the turn coordinator while the urge to lean passes. A steady heading and a turn coordinator showing no turn, with its ball centered, confirm the wings are level.
Make small, smooth corrections in clouds. Large, sudden attitude changes set the fluid moving and invite disorientation and loss of control.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Which do you trust when you feel perfectly level in clouds but the attitude indicator shows a left bank?
2. What should your hands do when, seconds after a brisk roll back to level, you feel banked to the right?
3. What has changed inside your ear when a long, steady turn no longer feels like a turn?
4. Back in level flight after a long left turn, why do you catch yourself leaning hard to the left in your seat?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Trust the instruments, not your body. A heading that keeps changing and a turn coordinator showing a turn confirm a bank that crept in too slowly to feel.
2. Hold the wings level on the attitude indicator and leave them there. The right bank you feel is only fluid moving in your roll canal, set off by that quick roll.
3. The fluid caught up with the canal walls. With nothing bending the hairs, your brain stopped getting a signal of a turn.
4. Your ear is reporting a false bank to the right, set off when you rolled out of the left turn. Leaning left is your body reaching for what feels upright.

posts.title: How a turboprop works, compared with your 172's engine
posts.headline: Your 172 does its four engine jobs in turns, about 80 fires a second at cruise. A turboprop does all four at once, with one steady flame.
posts.alt: The see-through nose of a TBM 930 in flight above the clouds, with its turboprop engine glowing inside and the labels No mixture knob and No magnetos.
posts.related_text: Both engines do the same four jobs: intake, compression, combustion and exhaust (suck, squeeze, burn and blow). In a reciprocating engine all four take place in the same combustion chamber, so each must have the chamber to itself in turn, and in a four-cylinder engine each cylinder operates on a different stroke; a gas turbine engine has a separate section for each job and performs all of them simultaneously without interruption, four continuous and constant events (AMT ch 1 p 1-36, p 1-58; PHAK ch 7 p 7-4). The Cessna 172P's O-320-D2J is a horizontally-opposed, four-cylinder, direct-drive engine of 160 BHP at 2,700 rpm with a fixed-pitch propeller (172P POH p 1-3). On the intake stroke the piston moves away from the cylinder head (in toward the crankshaft in a flat engine, whose cylinder heads sit outboard) and draws in the fuel-air mixture; on compression it moves back toward the head and squeezes it; the spark ignites it and the expanding gas forces the piston back in, the power stroke; on exhaust it moves out again and pushes the burned gases out (PHAK ch 7 p 7-4, Figure 7-5). Each cylinder fires once every two turns of the crankshaft (AMT ch 1 p 1-25), so the four fire twice a turn (computed: 4 / 2 = 2). Engine ignition is provided by two engine-driven magnetos and two spark plugs in each cylinder (172P POH section 7), and the pilot leans the mixture with the mixture control (PHAK ch 7). The intake stroke begins when the intake valve opens and the fuel-air mixture is drawn in; the compression stroke begins when the intake valve closes; the exhaust stroke begins when the exhaust valve opens (PHAK ch 7 p 7-4). A fixed-pitch propeller's blade angle cannot be changed in flight (its pitch is fixed). At 2,400 rpm, a cruise setting the 172P POH's cruise table lists at every altitude from 2,000 to 12,000 feet (172P POH Fig 5-7, p 5-16), two fires a turn make 4,800 a minute, about 80 a second (computed: 2 x 2,400 = 4,800; 4,800 / 60 = 80). The TBM 930's PT6A-66D is a free-turbine, reverse-flow engine with 2 turbine sections, its combustion chamber annular, ring-shaped (PIM p 1.3.1); compressed air and fuel are mixed and sprayed into the combustion chamber by fuel nozzles, and the mixture 'is first ignited by two spark igniter plugs, then combustion continues as a result of air-fuel mixture flow' (PIM p 7.6.1): lit at start-up, it keeps burning with no spark while the fuel-air mixture flows, a continuous combustion cycle (AMT ch 1 p 1-58), though a flameout, one of the operational considerations common to all turbine engines, can still put it out (PHAK ch 7 p 7-23). The PT6A-66D is one model of the PT6A-67 series of the PT6A family (EASA TCDS IM.E.008); the PIM gives its engine type as 'Free turbine, reverse flow' (PIM p 1.3.1): it takes its air in at its rear end and lets the gas out near its front (PIM p 7.6.1, p 7.6.10), so inside the engine the air moves from back to front. In the TBM the air enters the cowling at its front lower section, under the spinner, and is driven through a duct in the engine casing before entering the engine through a protective screen (PIM p 7.6.10); the engine's own air intake is an annular casing at its rear, ahead of the accessory gearbox, which is located rearward of the engine (PIM p 7.6.1, Fig 7.6.1 item 8); so the duct carries the air back to the engine's rear end (inferred from the two places). The PT6A-66D's compressor has four axial stages, rows of spinning blades, and one centrifugal stage (PIM p 1.3.1, p 7.6.1); each consecutive pair of rotor and stator blades is a pressure stage (AMT ch 1 p 1-40), and the centrifugal wheel accelerates the air outward, perpendicular to the engine's axis (PHAK ch 7 p 7-20; AMT ch 1 p 1-38). In a reverse-flow combustor the air from the compressor enters the combustor outer case and reverses its direction as it flows into the inner liner, and again before it flows through the turbine; reverse-flow combustors are used where engine length is critical (AMT ch 1 p 1-46); in the PT6 the liner's location reduces the overall length and weight of the engine (208 POH p 7-37, the PT6A-114A, a sister engine of the same layout). In the PT6 (208 POH p 7-37, the PT6A-114A of the same layout): the compressed air passes through diffuser ducts which turn it 90 degrees in direction and is routed into the combustion chamber; the flow of air changes direction to enter the combustion chamber liner, where it reverses direction and mixes with fuel; the gases expand from the liner, reverse direction and pass to the compressor turbine; the still expanding gases pass forward to drive the power turbine. The location of the liner eliminates the need for a long shaft between the compressor and the compressor turbine, reducing the overall length and weight of the engine. With the compressor behind the chamber and the exhaust near the front, the air heads forward through the compressor (inferred from the layout). The first turbine, the gas generator (compressor) turbine, drives the compressor and the accessories (PIM p 7.6.1, Fig 7.6.1 item 11); the major part of the combustion energy is needed at the turbine stages that drive the compressor, and the remaining energy passes through the remaining turbine stages, which drive the propeller (AMT ch 1 p 1-43); in a turboprop the rest of the available energy exits the exhaust as thrust (AMT ch 1 p 1-37). The page gives no share of the energy. The two power turbines, independent from the first, drive the propeller shaft through a reduction gearbox (PIM p 7.6.1); the free turbine has only an air link from the gas generator to the power turbines, with no mechanical link from the propeller to the gas generator (AMT ch 1 p 1-54): two shafts, end to end, not joined, so only hot gas links the two turbines. The hot gases leave through two exhaust stubs, one on each side, forward on the engine cowling, just behind the propeller (PIM p 7.6.1): the engine takes its air in at its back and lets it out near its front, so the engine (not the airplane) breathes backwards. The cockpit displays both speeds separately: propeller speed in RPM (PROP RPM) and generator rotation speed in percent, Ng (PIM p 7.6.7). The PT6A-66D's reduction gearbox has 2 stages (TCDS IM.E.008 p 7); reduction gearing is necessary in turboprop engines because optimum propeller performance is achieved at much slower speeds than the engine's operating rpm (PHAK ch 7 p 7-21); the TBM's engine is rated 850 SHP at a propeller speed of 2,000 rpm (PIM p 1.3.1). No source gives the -66D's gear ratio. In the 172P the propeller bolts straight to the crankshaft: the O-320-D2J is a direct-drive engine with a fixed-pitch propeller (172P POH p 1-3), so the propeller turns at engine rpm and the tachometer is the indicator of engine power (PHAK ch 7 p 7-5). SHP, shaft horsepower, is the power delivered to the propeller shaft (850 SHP at 2000 RPM, PIM p 1.3.1). The TBM 930 has no mixture control (a hydro-mechanical fuel control unit meters the fuel, TCDS p 7) and no magnetos (two spark igniter plugs light it, the IGNITION switch normally in AUTO, PIM p 7.6.1, p 4.4.5). It has one THROTTLE with two modes, thrust and condition (PIM p 7.6.5); thrust mode modulates engine power up to max power (PIM p 7.6.5); condition mode is CUT OFF, LO-IDLE or HI-IDLE, used to start and stop the engine, and as long as the THROTTLE is in condition mode the propeller is in feather position (PIM p 7.6.6); feathered, the blades are set at 85 degrees at the 30-inch station, nearly edge-on to the passing air, against 19.5 degrees in low pitch (PIM p 1.3.1). A second lever, MAN OVRD, is a manual override used in case of an FCU or THROTTLE failure (PIM p 7.6.6). The propeller has no lever: its governor maintains rotation speed to the nominal value of 2,000 rpm (PIM p 7.6.12). No magnetos are needed because, once lit, combustion continues as a result of air-fuel mixture flow (PIM p 7.6.1); the igniters work during the start (with the IGNITION switch in AUTO, ignition is ensured whenever the STARTER switch is ON, PIM p 4.4.5, p 7.6.8), and the three-position IGNITION switch (OFF, AUTO, ON) can also run them on demand (PIM p 7.6.8). The THROTTLE is moved to the condition side by lifting the knob (PIM p 7.6.6); thrust mode modulates engine power from full reverse to max power (PIM p 7.6.5); idle is at the idle stop, and moving the THROTTLE rearward past it, past the lock using the detent, controls the power in the Beta range from idle to maximum reverse, which may only be selected with the engine running and the propeller turning (PIM p 7.6.5). The governor maintains the 2000 RPM through propeller blade pitch variation (PIM p 7.6.12). A turboprop's power output is measured by the torquemeter; torque is a twisting force applied to a shaft (PHAK ch 7 p 7-22), here the propeller shaft the power turbines drive through the reduction gearbox (PIM p 7.6.1); the TBM pilot sets TRQ, which must never exceed 100 percent (PIM p 5.8.1); engine monitoring is ensured by ITT, the interturbine temperature, read between the turbines, and oil pressure (PIM p 7.6.7, p 1.4.6); the highest temperature in any turbine engine occurs at the turbine inlet, and turbine inlet temperature is therefore usually the limiting factor in turbine engine operation (PHAK ch 7 p 7-23). In a 172 with its fixed-pitch propeller, the throttle sets the rpm and the tachometer shows the engine's power (PHAK ch 7 p 7-5). Turboprop power output is measured by the torquemeter, and torquemeters are calibrated in percentage units, foot-pounds or psi (PHAK ch 7 p 7-22, 7-23); the TBM displays engine torque in percent, TRQ (PIM p 7.6.7). Setting TRQ, three limits apply together (PIM p 5.8.1): the TRQ setting must never exceed 100 %; when setting TRQ, Ng must never exceed 104 %; and the torque must be set at or below the value of the engine operation tables for the local flight level and temperature. ITT has its own limits: takeoff 850 C, maximum climb/cruise 840 C (PIM p 2.3.1). The torque limiter on the reduction gearbox is rated to limit engine torque to 109-110 % at sea level (PIM p 7.6.11), and the engine rated 850 SHP develops a thermodynamic power of 1825 ESHP (PIM p 7.6.1): so near sea level this engine can make more than 100 % torque, and the throttle's forward stop is not a power setting (inferred from the two). The turbine inlet nozzle vanes, directly aft of the combustion chambers and immediately forward of the turbine wheel, meet the highest or hottest temperature that comes in contact with metal components in the engine, and the turbine inlet temperature must be controlled, or damage will occur to the turbine inlet vanes (AMT ch 1 p 1-46). A hot start, when the temperature exceeds its limit, is caused by too much fuel entering the combustion chamber or insufficient turbine rpm, and after one the AFM/POH or a maintenance manual gives the inspection requirements (PHAK ch 7 p 7-24); in the TBM, fuel brought in before the gas generator spins fast enough risks an overtemperature from an excessive accumulation of fuel inside the combustion chamber before ignition (PIM p 4.4.25), and its start temperature limits are counted in seconds (PIM p 2.3.1); too little rpm means the compressor moves too little air for the fuel, and the compressor's air also cools the combustion gases to a temperature the turbine can withstand (AMT ch 1 p 1-43, p 1-44). No start sequence or number is taught on the page: the airplane's own flight manual gives the start, and the page names only Ng as the speed to wait for (the starter turns only the compressor side, so propeller speed says nothing about it) and CUT OFF as the abort's first step. The air entering the combustion chamber is divided into primary air, mixed with the fuel and burned, and secondary or cooling air, which passes between the outer casing and the liner and joins the combustion gases to cool them (AMT ch 1 p 1-44). In the TBM, the start is aborted if the ITT warning lights (max ITT < 870 C for more than 20 seconds, < 1000 C for more than 5 seconds), and the abort's first step is THROTTLE CUT OFF (PIM p 4.4.25). The start ITT limits pair temperatures with seconds (< 870 C for 20 seconds max, < 1000 C for 5 seconds max, PIM p 2.3.1), so after a hot start the peak ITT and how long it lasted say which limit was passed (inferred); a hot start is when the EGT exceeds the safe limit (PHAK ch 7 p 7-24). Starting shows the two shafts at work: the starter generator drives the powerplant (PIM p 7.6.8) through the accessory gearbox on the gas generator (PIM p 7.6.1, Fig 7.6.1 items 4 and 7), so the starter turns only the gas generator, the compressor side; the power turbines are linked to it only by the gas flow (AMT ch 1 p 1-54), so only the gas flowing through the engine turns them. A turboprop engine is a turbine engine that drives a propeller through a reduction gear (PHAK ch 7 p 7-21); a turbine is a disc of blades that the expanding gases spin, converting their velocity energy to mechanical energy to drive the compressor or, through more stages, the propeller (AMT ch 1 p 1-46, p 1-54, p 1-58). The TBM 930 has one engine (PIM p 1.3.1).

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: A turboprop is a turbine engine that turns a propeller through a gearbox. A turbine is a wheel of blades that hot gas spins.

Your 172's engine does the same four jobs as a turboprop: take air in, squeeze it, burn it with fuel and push it out. The 172 does them in turns, inside each cylinder. A turboprop does all four at once, each in its own section.
In a TBM 930, a single-engine turboprop, your power gauge shows torque, the twist on the propeller shaft. You also watch the temperature between its turbines.

article.heading: Four jobs, in turns or at once
paragraphs: In each of the 172P's four cylinders, the intake valve opens and the piston moves in toward the crankshaft, drawing in fuel and air. With the valve shut, it moves back out and squeezes them. A spark lights the mixture, and the burn shoves the piston in. Then the exhaust valve opens, and the piston pushes the burned gas out.
Each cylinder fires once every two crankshaft turns, so the four fire twice a turn. At a 2,400 rpm cruise, that's about 80 fires a second.

table.caption: Where each of the four jobs happens
columns: Your 172, in each cylinder in turn
rows: The inlet at the engine's rear
The combustion chamber, whose hot gas spins the turbines
Two exhaust stubs near the front

figure.caption: Above, a 172 cylinder at its intake job, shown in blue. Below, the turboprop has blue air, amber squeezed air and red hot gas in it at the same moment.
figure.alt: A see-through 172 cylinder with its piston and a blue charge inside, above a cutaway turboprop engine with blue, amber and red flow marks along its length, with the chip Four jobs between them.

article.heading: A walk through the PT6
paragraphs: The TBM 930 flies with a Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6A-66D. It is a reverse-flow engine: air goes in at the back and leaves near the front.

Air enters the cowling low at the front, and a duct carries it back to a screen at the engine's rear. Heading forward, four rows of spinning compressor blades squeeze it, then a spinning wheel flings it outward.

The squeezed air turns into the ring-shaped combustion chamber. There it reverses and mixes with fuel from the nozzles. Two igniter plugs light it at the start, then it keeps burning as fuel and air flow in.

The hot gas reverses again to spin the compressor turbine, which drives the compressor. Then it flows forward through two power turbine wheels on their own shaft, which turn the propeller through the gearbox.

This folded path keeps the engine short and light. Only the hot gas links the two turbine shafts, a design called a free turbine. The starter spins only the compressor side, whose speed, Ng, shows in percent.

figure.caption: The PT6 cut open on its side, its rear end on the left. Blue air comes in at the back, amber squeezed air wraps around the combustion chamber, and red hot gas flows forward through the turbines.
figure.alt: A cutaway turboprop engine lying on its side, with blue flow marks at its rear end, amber marks around its combustion chamber and red marks through its turbines toward the front.

article.heading: A gearbox where your 172 has none
paragraphs: A propeller works best much slower than a turbine turns. So a gearbox at the PT6's front steps the speed down in two stages. In the TBM, the propeller turns at 2,000 rpm, and the engine is rated at 850 horsepower at the propeller shaft.
The 172P's 160-horsepower engine bolts a fixed-pitch propeller, whose blade angle never changes, straight to the crankshaft. So the tachometer, which shows engine rpm, is your power gauge.

figure.caption: Above, the round flange where a 172's propeller bolts straight to the crankshaft. Below, the PT6's power turbine shaft runs forward into its gearbox.
figure.alt: The round bolted flange of a see-through 172 engine, above the turboprop's shaft running into a geared housing.

article.heading: What changes in the cockpit
paragraphs: The TBM 930 has no mixture control: a fuel control unit measures out the fuel, so there is nothing to lean. It has no magnetos, since once lit the flame needs no spark.
The throttle sets the power. Lift its knob and it moves to a second range, CUT OFF and two idles, for starting and stopping. There the propeller stays feathered, its blades nearly edge-on to the air.
The propeller has no lever. A governor, an automatic speed control, holds its 2,000 rpm by changing the blade angle. So the torque gauge, read in percent, is the power gauge.

You also watch ITT, the interturbine temperature, read between the turbines. The vanes just ahead of the first turbine meet the hottest gas touching metal in the engine, and too much heat damages them. So temperature usually limits a turbine engine.

figure.caption: TORQUE points at the gearbox, where the twist on the propeller shaft is measured. ITT points into the hot section, where the temperature between the turbines is read.
figure.alt: A cutaway turboprop engine standing on end, with the label Torque on the gearbox at the top and the label ITT on the red-hot section below it.

article.heading: Mistakes a 172 pilot brings along
paragraphs: Set power by torque, within its limits, never by the tachometer or the throttle's stop. Keep torque at or below the flight manual's table value for your altitude and temperature, and never above 100 percent. Ng must never pass 104 percent, and ITT has its own limit. Near sea level, this engine can make more than 100 percent torque.

Wait for Ng, not propeller rpm, to reach the flight manual's minimum before you bring in fuel. Fuel too early, or too much, can cause a hot start, when the temperature passes its limit. Only part of the compressor's air burns, and the rest cools the gas. A slow compressor moves too little air for that, so ITT can pass its limit.
Watch ITT through the whole start. If it passes its start limit, abort as the flight manual sets out. In the TBM, the throttle goes to CUT OFF first.
After any hot start, note the peak ITT and how many seconds it lasted, since the start limits pair the two. The flight or maintenance manual says what to inspect.

figure.caption: With fuel in too early, the combustion chamber glows and the red ITT bar reaches its limit mark.
figure.alt: A cutaway turboprop engine with a bright red combustion chamber, the label Fuel too early below it pointing up at that section, and a tall red temperature bar above it, filled to its limit mark.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Why does fuel brought in before Ng is high enough risk a hot start?
2. What joins the compressor turbine to the power turbines in a PT6?
3. Why does a turboprop need a gearbox?
4. What do you set a TBM 930's power by, and within which limits?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. The slow compressor moves too little air to cool the burning gas, so ITT can pass its limit.
2. Only the hot gas. The two turbine shafts are not joined.
3. A propeller works best much slower than a turbine turns.
4. Torque, at or below the table value and never above 100 percent, with Ng never above 104 percent and ITT within its limit.

posts.title: VMC and the engine-out roll in a twin
posts.headline: Below a twin's minimum control speed, full rudder can no longer stop its swing toward the dead engine. Pulling the good engine's power back and lowering the nose can.
posts.alt: A see-through twin over farmland, its green rudder and the right engine's yellow thrust arrow showing, below a twin's airspeed dial labeled Airspeed with its red radial line labeled Red line, under the chip VMC, Minimum control speed.
posts.related_text: VMC is the minimum control speed: the slowest speed at which directional control can be maintained after the critical engine suddenly fails (14 CFR part 23 definition, AFH ch 13); it is typically marked with a red radial line low on most twins' airspeed indicators (AFH ch 13), a different mark from the red line at the top of the scale, which marks the never-exceed speed (PHAK ch 8); on twins with each engine rotating clockwise as viewed from the pilot's seat, the critical engine, the one whose failure most hurts directional control, is the left engine (AFH ch 13). The AFM/POH-published VMC is determined with the critical engine inoperative under conditions at or near their worst: maximum available takeoff power, the most unfavorable weight (for twins certificated under CAR 3 or early 14 CFR part 23 the weight was not specified), the most unfavorable (aft) CG, the landing gear retracted and the critical engine's propeller windmilling in the takeoff position; the one condition in the manufacturer's favor is a bank of up to 5 degrees toward the operative engine, capped to prevent an unrealistically low VMC; the results are extrapolated to a single, sea level value, and the VMC met in practice could be less or even greater than the published value, depending on conditions and pilot technique (AFH ch 13). When an engine fails, the thrust of the operating engine yaws the nose toward the inoperative engine; it is counteracted primarily with rudder on the side of the operating engine, and after rudder is applied to stop the yaw, a slight amount of aileron is used to bank the airplane toward the operative engine; attempting to correct the roll with aileron without first applying rudder increases drag and adverse yaw and further degrades directional control (AFH ch 13); adverse yaw becomes more pronounced at low airspeeds (PHAK ch 6). With one engine inoperative the climb performance is greatly reduced; the pitch attitude for VYSE, the best rate of climb speed with one engine inoperative, marked with a blue radial line on most airspeed indicators, has to be lowered from that of VY, and holding the two-engine climb attitude lets the airspeed decay (AFH ch 13; PHAK ch 8 'commonly referred to as Blue Line'). Rudder effectiveness increases with speed and falls as the airplane slows (PHAK ch 6), while the operating engine at full power keeps pulling, its thrust at a maximum at low speed (AFH ch 13); an airspeed is soon reached where full rudder travel and up to a 5 degree bank toward the operating engine can no longer counteract the asymmetrical thrust, and the airplane begins to yaw uncontrollably toward the inoperative engine (AFH ch 13). The horizontal component of lift generated by the bank toward the operating engine balances the side force from the rudder; with wings level, VMC is significantly higher than published because no horizontal component of lift helps the rudder, and loss of directional control may be experienced at speeds almost 20 knots above published VMC when the wings are held level (AFH ch 13). With one engine inoperative the centered ball is no longer the indicator of zero sideslip; rudder and ailerons used together in the proper combination give a bank of approximately 2 degrees toward the operative engine, with the ball displaced approximately one-third to one-half toward it, which gives zero sideslip, the least drag and maximum climb performance; with less than the 5 degree bank certification limit, VMC is higher than published; with the wings level and ball centered the airplane sideslips moderately toward the inoperative engine (AFH ch 13). When the nose yaws, the outside wing travels faster than the inside wing and its lift becomes greater (PHAK ch 5; AFH ch 3), so a twin yawing toward its inoperative engine rolls toward that engine (an application of that fact, stated as such). VMC increases as power is increased on the operating engine; with normally aspirated engines it is highest at takeoff power and sea level and decreases with altitude, while with turbocharged engines it stays constant up to the engine's critical altitude; VMC increases as the CG is moved aft (the moment arm of the rudder is reduced), as weight is reduced, when the landing gear is retracted (extended gear aids directional stability) and with increased drag on the inoperative engine; at its worst a windmilling propeller can produce parasite drag as great as the parasite drag of the entire airframe, and feathering stops the propeller with its blades streamlined to the relative wind and minimizes propeller drag (AFH ch 13). Stopping the yaw is critical and the airspeed must stay above VMC; the moment the pilot first recognizes an uncontrollable yaw, or experiences any symptom associated with a stall, the pilot simultaneously retards the throttle of the operating engine and lowers the pitch attitude to regain speed; if the yaw cannot be controlled with full rudder applied, reducing thrust on the operative engine is the only alternative; recovery is made at VSSE or VYSE, and only then is power increased on the operating engine, with rudder and a slight bank toward it; the AFM/POH checklist then directs the pilot to identify, verify and feather the failed engine (AFH ch 13). At the stall, the presence or introduction of a yawing moment, from rudder input or asymmetrical thrust, can initiate spin entry, and no multiengine airplane is approved for spins (AFH ch 13); the high slipstream velocity of a propeller increases the effective lift of the wing behind it (AFH ch 13), so the dead engine's wing loses that extra lift (an application, stated as such).

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapters 5, 6 and 8

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: When one engine of a twin quits, the good engine swings the nose toward the dead one. Rudder on the good engine's side holds it straight, helped by a small bank toward that engine.

The rudder's grip fades as you slow. Below VMC, the minimum control speed, even full rudder can't hold the nose, and the swing turns into a roll toward the dead engine. If the swing won't stop, reduce power on the good engine and lower the nose.

article.heading: Why one dead engine swings the nose
paragraphs: Say the left engine quits in the climb. The right engine still pulls on its side of the airplane, so the nose yaws, or swings, toward the dead engine.

You stop the yaw with rudder on the side of the good engine. The right pedal swings the rudder, pushing the tail left and the nose back right. Once the yaw has stopped, a little aileron banks the airplane toward the good engine.
On twins whose propellers both turn clockwise as seen from the cockpit, the left engine is the worse one to lose, the critical engine.

figure.caption: Left engine out. The dead left engine is red, the right engine (yellow) keeps pulling, and the nose yaws left (violet).
figure.alt: A see-through twin from above and behind under the chip Left engine out, its left engine red, a yellow thrust arrow on the right engine and a violet arrow curving left at the nose.

article.heading: Why the rudder runs out as you slow
paragraphs: VMC is the slowest speed at which you can still keep the airplane straight after the critical engine suddenly fails. Most twins mark it with a red radial line near the low-speed end of the airspeed indicator, which pilots call the red line. It is not the never-exceed red line at the high-speed end.
The rudder works by turning the air past the tail, so its force shrinks as you slow. The good engine's yaw doesn't shrink. At full power a propeller pulls hardest at low speed.
At VMC, full rudder and a small bank toward the good engine only just hold the airplane straight.

A windmilling propeller, one the airflow keeps turning after its engine quits, makes it worse. At its worst it makes as much parasite drag, the drag of a shape pushing through the air, as the whole airframe. Feathering turns the blades edge-on to the wind and cuts that drag to a minimum.
The red line is one sea-level value, set with the conditions in the table at or near their worst. On the day, the real VMC can be lower or higher.

table.caption: What the red line assumes, and why each condition raises VMC
columns: Condition when the red line is set
rows: Maximum takeoff power at sea level
The most thrust to hold against. With an engine that has no turbocharger, VMC falls as you climb.
Center of gravity at its aft limit
The rudder's lever arm is shorter
VMC rises as weight goes down. Older twins' red lines name no weight.
Lowered gear steadies the yaw, and that help is gone
Its drag on the dead side adds to the yaw

figure.caption: Slow and at full power on the good right engine, the needle sits near the red line. The rudder's push (green) depends on the airflow past the tail (cyan).
figure.alt: A see-through twin from behind and above with its left engine red, the label Full power on the right engine, cyan airflow arrows past the tail, a green arrow at the tail, an airspeed dial and a round inset labeled Rudder, from above.

article.heading: How a small bank helps the rudder
paragraphs: Bank toward the good engine and part of the wing's lift points sideways. That sideways part balances the rudder's sideways push. Without it, the rudder's push makes the airplane sideslip, moving partly sideways, toward the dead engine. That sideslip needs even more rudder, which raises VMC.

That is why the red line is set with up to 5 degrees of bank toward the good engine. Hold the wings level and VMC is much higher. In some twins you can lose control almost 20 knots above the red line.

For the best climb on one engine, fly zero sideslip, the air meeting the airplane head-on. That takes about 2 degrees of bank, with the ball in the slip indicator a third to a half out toward the good engine. That is less bank than the red line assumes, so the real VMC can rise above it.

figure.caption: The twin banked a few degrees toward the good right engine (white arrow), as the red line assumes. The green arrow is the rudder's push on the tail.
figure.alt: A see-through twin from behind with its wings tilted down to the right under the chip Red line: up to 5 degrees, a curved white arrow showing the bank and a green arrow at the tail.

article.heading: How the swing becomes a roll
paragraphs: Below VMC, the yaw toward the dead engine swings the good engine's wing forward. That wing now travels faster than the other one.
The faster wing makes more lift than the slower one, so the twin rolls toward the dead engine.
Near the stall it gets worse. A yawing moment from one engine's thrust can start a spin, and no multiengine airplane is approved for spins.

figure.caption: The nose yaws left (violet), so the right wing moves faster through the air (long cyan streaks). Its extra lift rolls the twin left.
figure.alt: A see-through twin on a dark grid with its left wing lower, a violet arrow labeled Yaw, cyan speed streaks along the right wing labeled Faster wing and a mark at the left wingtip labeled Roll.

article.heading: Four mistakes that end in the roll
paragraphs: Put in rudder first, then aileron. The mistake is lifting the low wing with aileron alone. That adds drag on that side, pulling the nose further toward the dead engine. This adverse yaw grows as you slow.
Lower the nose to hold the blue line on the airspeed indicator, VYSE, the speed for the best climb on one engine. Keep the two-engine climb attitude and the airspeed bleeds toward the red line.

Pull the good engine's power back the moment the swing won't stop, or at the first sign of a stall. The mistake is keeping full power and raising the nose to save height. Lower the nose with it and accept the height loss.
Bring the power back in only at the blue line, with rudder for the yaw it brings. Adding it while slow starts the swing again. Then fly your checklist to identify, verify and feather the dead engine.

figure.caption: The way out starts here, as the throttle comes back on the good right engine, high above the farmland.
figure.alt: A close view of a see-through twin's right engine over farmland, its propeller turning, with a gold label reading Throttle back.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Which rudder pedal do you press when your left engine quits in the climb and the nose swings left?
2. What do you do when, near the red line with full right rudder in, the nose keeps swinging left?
3. Why could holding the wings level with the ball centered after an engine failure cost you control?
4. Do a heavier weight and a forward center of gravity raise VMC or lower it?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. The right pedal, on the good engine's side.
2. Pull the right engine's power back and lower the nose.
3. With the wings level, no sideways lift helps the rudder, so VMC goes up.
4. They lower it, though too little bank can still push the real VMC above the red line.

posts.title: Crosswind landing from final to the rollout
posts.headline: A crosswind landing gets harder as you slow, right up to the moment the airplane stops.
posts.alt: A white Cessna 172 rolling down a runway at night with a wind arrow from the left, the chip Slower = more yoke, and a small panel with the yoke turned into the wind.
posts.related_text: Crosswind landings use the crab method, the wing-low (sideslip) method or a combination; the wing-low method is recommended in most cases, and on a long final one option is to crab first and smoothly transition to wing-low before the round out (AFH ch 9); the 172S manual says the wing low method gives the best control (172S POH sec 4). With the nose aligned with the runway and no correction, the airplane drifts with the crosswind; a crab is a heading toward the wind that aligns the wings-level ground track with the centerline; touching down crabbed puts a side load on the landing gear, so the crab is removed with rudder just before touchdown, and a change made too early or too late results in a side load or drift (AFH ch 9). In the wing-low method the pilot uses rudder to align the airplane with the runway and ailerons to lower the upwind wing just enough to cancel the drift; banked, the airplane tends to turn, so opposite rudder holds the heading, and the sideslip is adjusted as the crosswind changes (AFH ch 9). If the required bank is such that full opposite rudder does not prevent a turn, the wind is too strong to land safely on that runway, and the landing should be made on a more favorable runway, at that airport or an alternate (AFH ch 9); in a 172S go-around, reduce the flap setting to 20 degrees immediately after full power is applied (172S POH sec 4). The 172S's demonstrated crosswind velocity, 15 knots, is the crosswind component for which adequate control was demonstrated during certification; it is not considered limiting (172S POH sec 1), and the maximum allowable crosswind depends on pilot capability as well as aircraft limitations (172S POH sec 4). In gusty or turbulent air, fly a power-on approach slightly above the normal approach speed for more positive control; pilots often use the normal approach speed plus one-half of the wind gust factor (AFH ch 9), so a 65-knot approach with gusts 10 knots above the wind becomes 70 knots (computed); use partial flaps, the minimum flap setting the field length requires (172S POH sec 4), and retard the throttle to idle only after the main wheels touch (AFH ch 9); through gusts, adjust the correction promptly so the airplane does not drift at touchdown (AFH ch 9). In a 172S, steep slips should be avoided with flap settings greater than 20 degrees because of a slight tendency for the elevator to oscillate (172S POH sec 4). As the airplane slows in the round out the flight controls become less effective, the correction being held becomes inadequate, and the pilot gradually increases the rudder and aileron deflection; the upwind wing is kept down throughout the round out, the initial touchdown is on the upwind main wheel, and although it may appear that the upwind wingtip will strike the ground, it does not (AFH ch 9). As little as 10 degrees of cornering angle, between where a tire points and where it rolls, creates a side load equal to half the weight it supports, and a drifting touchdown's side load can roll a tricycle-gear airplane onto one main wheel, putting a wingtip or the propeller on the ground (AFH ch 9). The 172's nosewheel is steered by the rudder pedals; to prevent swerving in the direction the nosewheel is offset, the corrective rudder pressure is relaxed as the nosewheel touches down (AFH ch 9; 172S POH sec 7). On the rollout, as forward speed decreases the relative wind acts more like a crosswind and lifts the upwind wing harder, while less airflow over the ailerons makes them less effective; with more side area behind the main gear than ahead and the main wheels as a pivot, the airplane tends to weathervane into the wind; more and more aileron is applied, held fully toward the wind as the airplane comes to a stop, with directional control by rudder and nosewheel steering (AFH ch 9) and occasional braking if necessary (172S POH sec 4).
posts.credits: 3D model: “Cessna172” by KOG_THORNS (sketchfab.com), CC BY 4.0, modified.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: In a crosswind, the yoke goes into the wind to stop the drift and the rudder keeps the nose straight. As you slow in the flare, the pitch-up that ends the descent, your controls do less, so you add more of both.
The landing isn't over at touchdown. Keep turning the yoke into the wind through the rollout, the slowdown on the runway, to full at the stop.

article.heading: Crab or wing-low on final
paragraphs: Point the nose straight down the runway with no correction, and the wind drifts you sideways. One fix is a crab. Turn the nose into the wind until your track, your path over the ground, runs straight along the runway.
Touch down crabbed, though, and the wheels land at an angle and take a side load. So the crab comes out with rudder just before touchdown. Too early and you drift, too late and you land crabbed.

The wing-low method, recommended in most cases, holds the nose straight with rudder. You turn the yoke into the wind, which moves the ailerons, to lower the upwind wing just enough to stop the drift. The bank tries to turn you, so you hold opposite rudder.

The wing-low method is a sideslip, a bank held against opposite rudder. In a 172S, avoid steep slips with more than 20 degrees of flap, because the elevator can oscillate slightly. In a strong crosswind, use the least flap your runway allows.

figure.caption: With the wind from the left, the yoke is turned left to lower that wing just enough to stop the drift. Right rudder keeps the nose straight.
figure.alt: A white Cessna 172 on short final at night with one wing lowered, under the label Wing low, beside a panel with a yoke icon, bars for the left and right rudder pedals and a speed bar.

article.heading: Why you need more control as you slow
paragraphs: In the flare the airplane slows, and the controls get less effective. The correction you were holding is no longer enough, so add aileron and rudder gradually, all the way down.
Keep the upwind wing down through the flare, so the upwind main wheel touches first.

Drift at touchdown does real harm. If a tire's path runs just 10 degrees off the way it points, it takes a side load of half the weight on it. Enough of that can lift one main wheel and put a wingtip or the propeller on the runway.

figure.caption: In the flare the speed bar drops, so the inputs held on final now do less. Add more yoke and more rudder, as the labels say.
figure.alt: A white Cessna 172 in the flare over a runway at night under the labels More yoke and More rudder, beside the yoke, rudder and speed panel.

article.heading: Why the rollout still needs the yoke
paragraphs: As you slow, the headwind from your own motion shrinks. So the wind you feel swings toward the side and lifts the upwind wing harder. Less air over the ailerons makes the same yoke do less.
The airplane also tends to weathervane. The main wheels act as a pivot with more side area behind them than ahead. The wind pushes the tail around and turns the nose into it.
So keep adding aileron into the wind, holding it fully over as you stop. Steer with the pedals, which turn the nosewheel, and use a little brake if you need it.

figure.caption: As you stop with the wind from the left (cyan arrow), it tries to lift the left wing (yellow arrow). Hold the yoke full left.
figure.alt: A white Cessna 172 slowing on a runway at night under the label Yoke full left, with a cyan wind arrow from the left, a yellow arrow at the left wing and the yoke, rudder and speed panel.

article.heading: Four crosswind mistakes to avoid
paragraphs: Hold the bank right to the ground. The low wingtip looks close but won't hit, and leveling the wings lets the airplane drift as it touches down.

Go around if full opposite rudder can't stop the turn. The wind is too strong for that runway, so land on one more into the wind. In a 172S go-around with more than 20 degrees of flap, reduce the flaps to 20 degrees right after full power.
Ease the rudder as the nosewheel touches. Rudder still held for the slip steers the nosewheel the moment it takes weight, and the airplane swerves.
Fly gusty approaches a little faster. The gust factor is how many knots the gusts run above the steady wind. Unless your POH says otherwise, add half of it to your normal approach speed.

table.caption: A gusty approach in a 172S, worked out

figure.caption: Right rudder still held from the slip as the nosewheel touches swerves the airplane right. The red airplane shows where it goes.
figure.alt: A white Cessna 172 on a runway at night beside a red copy of it swerving to the side, under the label Swerve.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. With the wind from the right on short final, which wing do you lower?
2. Why does your crosswind correction run short in the flare, and what do you do about it?
3. What does it tell you when full opposite rudder can't stop the turn your bank creates?
4. With a 65-knot normal approach and the wind at 12 knots gusting 20, what speed do you fly?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. The right wing, just enough to stop the drift, with left rudder to keep the nose straight.
2. The airplane slows in the flare, so the controls do less, and you add aileron and rudder as needed to stop the drift.
3. The wind is too strong for that runway, so go around and land on one more into the wind.
4. About 69 knots, since half the 8-knot gust factor added to 65 gives 69.

posts.title: What are left-turning tendencies
posts.headline: Why a Cessna's nose swings left at full power, and what your right foot does about it.
posts.alt: A Cessna 172 on the runway seen from behind and above, with cyan corkscrew lines of the propeller's slipstream wrapping around the fuselage to the left side of the vertical fin.
posts.related_text: To the pilot, torque (the left turning tendency of the airplane) is made up of four elements: torque reaction from engine and propeller, the corkscrewing effect of the slipstream, gyroscopic action of the propeller and asymmetric loading of the propeller (P-factor) (PHAK ch 5 p 5-30). Gyroscopic action is considered more prominent in tailwheel-type aircraft and most often occurs when the tail is being raised during the takeoff roll (PHAK p 5-32). Most United States built aircraft engines rotate the propeller clockwise, as viewed from the pilot's seat (PHAK p 5-31). The high-speed rotation of the propeller gives a corkscrew or spiraling rotation to the slipstream; at high propeller speeds and low forward speed, as in takeoffs and approaches to power-on stalls, the spiral is very compact and exerts a strong sideward force on the vertical tail surface; it strikes the left side of the vertical fin and causes a yawing moment about the vertical axis; as forward speed increases the spiral elongates and becomes less effective (PHAK p 5-31 Corkscrew Effect; PHAK glossary, Spiraling slipstream). P-factor: at a high angle of attack the bite of the downward-moving blade, the right side of the propeller disc seen from the flight deck, is greater than the bite of the upward-moving blade; this moves the center of thrust to the right of the prop disc area and yaws the nose to the left; as pitch attitude is increased in the climb the center of thrust moves to the right; the unbalanced thrust reaches zero when the propeller shaft is exactly horizontal in relation to the moving air (PHAK p 5-32; AFH ch 3 Climbs). Torque reaction: as the engine parts and propeller revolve one way, an equal force tries to rotate the aircraft the other way; airborne, it acts around the longitudinal axis and tends to roll the airplane to the left (PHAK p 5-31; AFH ch 3). With the wheels on the ground during the takeoff roll, the left side is forced down, more weight is placed on the left main landing gear, which makes more ground friction, or drag, on the left tire than on the right, and a further turning moment to the left (PHAK p 5-31). The Cessna 172S engine is rated 180 BHP at 2,700 rpm (172S POH Section 1); torque in lb-ft = hp x 5,252 / rpm = 180 x 5,252 / 2,700 = 350.1, about 350 lb-ft at rated power, the same as 175 lb on the end of a 2 ft bar (175 x 2 = 350). The compensating factors are generally permanently set so that they compensate for the left-turning force at cruising speed, since most of the aircraft's operating time is at that speed (PHAK p 5-31). During glides the slipstream and P-factor effects disappear but the design compensation remains, so slight left rudder pressure is likely to be required to maintain coordinated flight (AFH ch 3 Glides). In propeller-driven airplanes at slow flight, torque, slipstream effect and P-factor may produce a strong left yaw, which requires right rudder input to maintain coordinated flight; the closer the airplane is to the 1G stall, the more right rudder pressure is required (AFH ch 5 Slow Flight). On the takeoff, the effects of engine torque and P-factor at the initial speeds tend to pull the nose to the left, and the pilot uses whatever rudder pressure is needed to correct for them; common errors are failure to anticipate the left turning tendency on initial acceleration and inadequate compensation for torque/P-factor during the initial climb, resulting in a sideslip (AFH ch 6). On the go-around the pilot applies right rudder pressure to counteract torque and P-factor (AFH ch 6). Coordinated flight is the nose yawed directly into the relative wind with the ball centered in the slip/skid indicator (AFH); with the nose yawing left uncorrected, wings level, the ball slides right and right rudder centres it. A spin occurs when at least one wing exceeds the critical angle of attack (stall) with a sideslip or yaw acting on the airplane at, or beyond, the actual stall; engine and propeller effects, including P-factor, torque, spiraling slipstream and gyroscopic precession, are among the causes of that yaw (AFH ch 5 Spins).

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Push the throttle in on a Cessna 172 and hold the controls still, and the nose swings left. Pilots call it torque, but it is really four effects of the turning propeller: the spiralling slipstream, P-factor, torque reaction and gyroscopic precession.
Together they pull hardest when the power is high and the speed is low. That is when you hold right rudder to keep the nose straight.
Gyroscopic precession matters most in a tailwheel airplane as the tail comes up on the takeoff roll. It hardly shows in a nosewheel trainer like the 172, so this page follows the other three.

article.heading: The corkscrew slipstream hits the tail
paragraphs: Seen from your seat, the propeller turns clockwise, as on most US-built airplanes. It throws its air back in a corkscrew that wraps around the fuselage and strikes the left side of the vertical fin.
That sideways push sends the tail right and the nose left.
The spiral is tightest, and pushes hardest, at high propeller speed and low forward speed, as on the takeoff roll. As the airplane speeds up, the spiral stretches out and pushes less.

figure.caption: The corkscrew of air (cyan) reaches the left side of the fin, where it builds higher pressure (amber). The amber arrow is its push on the fin, toward the airplane's right.
figure.alt: The tail of a Cessna 172 on the runway seen from behind and to the left, with cyan spiral lines around the fuselage, an amber glow on the left face of the vertical fin labelled Higher pressure, and an amber arrow pushing the fin toward the right.

article.heading: P-factor shows up in the climb
paragraphs: Raise the nose for the climb, and the propeller disc tilts up against the air.

The blade coming down on the right side, seen from the seat, now meets the air at a bigger angle. So it takes a bigger bite than the blade going up on the left, like paddling harder on the right side of a canoe.

That moves the centre of thrust to the right of the hub, and the nose yaws left. The imbalance shrinks as the nose comes down and is zero once the propeller shaft lines up exactly with the oncoming air.

figure.caption: The propeller disc seen from behind and above, nose up in the climb. The gold arrows are each blade's bite; the one on the down-going right blade is longer, and the centre of thrust (gold dot) sits right of the hub.
figure.alt: A see-through Cessna 172 seen from behind and above, its propeller disc drawn as a dashed circle with two gold forward arrows, the right one longer, and a gold dot to the right of the hub labelled Centre of thrust.

article.heading: Torque twists the airplane back
paragraphs: The engine twists the propeller one way, and the airplane gets the same twist back the other way.
At the 172S's rated 180 horsepower and 2,700 rpm, the twist is about 350 pound-feet. That is the same as a 175-pound person standing on the end of a two-foot bar.
In the air, it tries to roll the airplane left.

On the takeoff roll the wheels stop that roll, so the twist presses the left side down instead. The left main wheel carries more weight, its tyre makes more drag than the right one, and the nose turns further left.

figure.caption: On the runway, seen from behind and to the left: the white arrows are the load on each main wheel, longer on the left, and the short orange arrow is the left tyre's extra drag, pointing back toward us.
figure.alt: A Cessna 172 on the runway seen from behind and to the left, with a long white downward arrow over the left main wheel labelled Left wheel, a short one over the right main wheel, and a small orange arrow at the left tyre pointing back, labelled Extra drag.

article.heading: The built-in correction and two mistakes
paragraphs: Designers build in a correction for this left pull, set for cruise, where an airplane spends most of its time. At high power and low speed it is not enough: the takeoff, the climb, slow flight and the go-around.
The first mistake is not expecting the swing as the airplane starts to accelerate. On the runway, keep the nose on the centreline with whatever rudder it takes.

The second is too little right rudder in the climb, which leaves the airplane in a sideslip. With the wings level and the nose yawing left, the ball in the slip/skid indicator slides right, so press right rudder until it is centred. The closer to the stall, the more rudder it takes, and a stall with the nose yawing is how a spin begins, here to the left.
In a power-off glide it is the other way round. The slipstream and P-factor fade but the correction stays, so a touch of left rudder may be needed to stay coordinated.

figure.caption: In the climb over farmland, right rudder (green: the rudder's push on the tail, to the left, which swings the nose right) has brought the ball back between the two lines of the slip/skid indicator (the inset). The violet arrow is the nose's pull to the left.
figure.alt: A Cessna 172 climbing over farmland, seen from behind and above, with a violet arrow ahead pointing left, a green arrow at the tail pointing left labelled Right rudder, and a round inset of the slip/skid indicator showing a black ball centred between two lines in a curved white tube.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Climbing out with the wings level, the ball sits right of centre, so which rudder centres it?
2. Why does P-factor grow when you raise the nose for the climb?
3. On the takeoff roll the wheels stop the airplane from rolling, so how does torque reaction still turn the nose left?
4. In a power-off glide, which rudder may you need to stay coordinated?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Right rudder, pressed until the ball is back between the lines.
2. The down-going right blade meets the air at a bigger angle, so it takes a bigger bite and the thrust moves right.
3. It presses the left side down, so the left main wheel carries more weight and makes more drag than the right.
4. A touch of left rudder, because the built-in correction stays while the slipstream and P-factor fade.

posts.title: How low pressure and cold air fool your altimeter
posts.headline: Fly into lower pressure without resetting, or into cold air, and you are lower than your altimeter shows. High to low, hot to cold, look out below.
posts.alt: A Cessna 172 at night just above a snowy mountain ridge under the words So what changed? Tonight, and a green label reading 80 FT.
posts.related_text: The pressure altimeter is an aneroid barometer that measures the pressure of the atmosphere at the level where it is located and presents an altitude indication in feet, against the pressure set in its setting window (PHAK ch 8). If an aircraft is flown from a high pressure area into a low pressure area without adjusting the altimeter, the altimeter shows a constant altitude while the aircraft is actually lower than indicated: 'when flying from a high to a low, look out below' (PHAK ch 8; IFH ch 5); holding a constant reading, the aircraft follows the falling pressure level down. One inch of mercury on the altimeter setting is approximately 1,000 feet of altitude (PHAK ch 8; IFH ch 5), so 30.12 minus 29.62 is 0.50 inch, about 500 feet lower than indicated, and about 10 feet for each 0.01 inch (computed). The pilot should frequently obtain current altimeter settings en route (PHAK ch 8); 14 CFR 91.121 requires the current reported altimeter setting of a station along the route and within 100 nautical miles of the aircraft; dialing the lower setting (29.62) into the window makes the same airplane read lower, from 6,500 to 6,000 for 0.50 inch. Adjustments to compensate for nonstandard pressure do not compensate for nonstandard temperature: since cold air is denser than warm air, when operating in temperatures colder than standard the altitude is lower than the altimeter indication (PHAK ch 8; IFH ch 5); there is no altimeter setting for temperature. If the air is colder than standard it is denser and the pressure levels are closer together (IFH ch 5); the cold temperature error is proportional to the height above the reporting station and to the temperature at the reporting station (IFH ch 5, AIM 7-3-1). The ICAO cold temperature error table (IFH Figure 5-7) gives, for a reported temperature of minus 20 degrees C, a possible error of 420 feet at 3,000 feet above the reporting station and 710 feet at 5,000 feet above it. In a teaching scenario (made up) with a 3,000 foot station, a 5,500 foot ridge, 6,500 feet indicated, a stale setting of 30.12 against 29.62 and minus 20 degrees C at the station (standard there is about plus 9 degrees C, 15 degrees C less 2 degrees per 1,000 feet), the margin over the crest is as little as 1,000 minus 500 minus 420, which is 80 feet (computed, worst case). If terrain or obstacle clearance is a factor in selecting a cruising altitude, particularly in mountainous terrain, a colder-than-standard temperature places the aircraft lower than the altimeter indicates, so a higher indicated altitude may be required to provide adequate terrain clearance (PHAK ch 8). Flown from a low pressure area to a high pressure area without adjustment, or in air warmer than standard, the actual altitude is higher than indicated (PHAK ch 8; IFH ch 5); that errs toward terrain clearance, but the pilot still resets to the current setting (14 CFR 91.121). A memory aid for temperature joins the pressure one: 'from hot to cold, look out below' (PHAK ch 8). Before flight, with the current altimeter setting set, the altimeter should read the field elevation within 75 feet; if it is off by more than 75 feet it should be referred to a certificated instrument repair station for recalibration (AIM 7-2-3; IFH ch 5). At and above 18,000 feet MSL all aircraft use the standard altimeter setting of 29.92 inches of mercury (14 CFR 91.121; IFH ch 5); over high, mountainous terrain certain atmospheric conditions can cause the altimeter to indicate 1,000 feet or more higher than the actual altitude, so a generous margin of altitude should be allowed (PHAK ch 8).

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 8
