article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Your altimeter turns air pressure into feet. Fly from high pressure into a low, an area of lower pressure, without resetting it, and the same reading puts you lower. Cold air does the same, and no setting fixes it.
Reset to the setting from a nearby airport's weather station as you go. In cold air over high ground, plan a higher altitude.

article.heading: Why a low takes altitude from you
paragraphs: An altimeter is a barometer. It measures the air pressure around the airplane and shows it as altitude, counted from the pressure you set in its window.
Hold a steady reading, and you fly along one pressure level, a height where the air pressure has one fixed value. Fly into a low without resetting, and that level sits lower, so you sink with it.

Settings are in inches of mercury, such as 29.92, and each inch is worth about 1,000 feet. Depart in a Cessna 172 with 30.12 set, cruise at 6,500 feet and fly on to where the setting is 29.62. That half inch leaves you about 500 feet lower than you read.

Below 18,000 feet, get the current setting from a station along your route, within 100 nautical miles, and dial it in. With 29.62 dialed in, the same airplane reads 6,000, so climb back to 6,500. That removes the pressure error, though not the cold-air error in the next section.

figure.caption: Under the low (L), this 172 is about 500 feet lower than its altimeter shows.
figure.alt: A Cessna 172 flying past a snowy ridge at night, with a blue letter L for low pressure above and a red label reading 500 FT.

article.heading: Why cold air puts you lower still
paragraphs: Setting the pressure does nothing for temperature. Standard air is 15 °C at sea level and cools about 2 °C per 1,000 feet. Colder air is denser, so its pressure levels sit closer together and the column of air below you is shorter.

Your altimeter still assumes standard spacing, so it shows more height above the station than is really there. The squeeze adds up with height, so the error grows the higher you are above the station and the colder it is there.

table.caption: Cold temperature error at a reported minus 20 °C

figure.caption: The cold air column (left) is shorter than the standard-day one (right). Dashed lines join matching marks, and the gap grows with height, biggest at the top.
figure.alt: Two vertical bars over a lit town at night, the left one shorter and labeled Cold air, the right one labeled Standard day. Dashed lines join their matching marks, a red line joins their tops, and the label Station sits below.

article.heading: What it adds up to over a ridge
paragraphs: Take the 172 at 6,500 feet on the altimeter over a 5,500-foot ridge, near a reporting station at 3,000 feet. Yesterday that left 1,000 feet. Tonight the setting there is 29.62, you still have 30.12 set, and it is minus 20 °C at the station.

With the right setting you would read 6,000, which is 3,000 feet above the station, so the table gives up to 420 feet. Worst case for these two errors, that leaves as little as 80 feet over the crest.

table.caption: Tonight's margin over the ridge, worst case
rows: Margin shown over the 5,500 ft ridge
Taken by the cold at 3,000 ft above the station, up to
Left over the crest, as little as

figure.caption: The low takes this 172 from the 6,500 shown to 6,000, and the cold up to 420 more. The bar's foot, close to the ridge, is where the 172 really is.
figure.alt: A tall red bar beside a snowy ridge at night, marked 6,500 at its top and 6,000 partway down, with red labels reading 500 FT and up to 420 FT.

article.heading: Three altimeter mistakes to avoid
paragraphs: Check the altimeter on the ground. With the local setting in, it should read within 75 feet of where you stand, usually the field elevation. That is the airport's published elevation above sea level. If it is off by 75 feet or more, have a certificated instrument repair station check it.
Keep resetting as you fly. Air traffic control tells you when there is a new setting, and on your own you can hear one on a nearby airport's weather broadcast.

Climb early when it's cold over high ground on a flight under visual flight rules. There is no knob for cold, so add the cold error for your height above the station to the altitude you need. Take it from the full cold temperature error table in the Aeronautical Information Manual, or work it out on a flight computer. Climb to that altitude before the ridge, or turn back.

figure.caption: The green bar, labeled Early climb, marks this 172's height over the ground, gained by climbing well before the ridge.
figure.alt: A Cessna 172 seen from above climbing over snowy forest toward a ridge, with a green line labeled Early climb.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. After flying from 30.12 into a 29.62 area without resetting, are you higher or lower than shown, and by how much?
2. With minus 20 °C reported at a station 3,000 feet below you and a current setting, can you trust the altimeter for terrain clearance?
3. What should happen if, before takeoff with the local setting dialed in, your altimeter reads 100 feet off the field elevation?
4. Flying from a low into a high without resetting, which way is your altimeter wrong?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Lower, by about 500 feet.
2. Not fully. The cold air puts you lower than shown, so plan a higher altitude.
3. It should go to a certificated instrument repair station.
4. You are higher than it shows. That is the safe side for terrain, but reset anyway, because other traffic flies the current setting.

posts.title: The emergency descent for an engine fire in a 172
posts.headline: Cut the fuel, then bank 30 to 45 degrees and descend at 100 knots, with a quick Mayday if there's time. Land flaps up at 70 knots.
posts.alt: A Cessna 172 in flight with flames and smoke coming from its engine cowling, under the chip Engine fire.
posts.related_text: An in-flight engine compartment fire is usually caused by a failure that allows a flammable substance, such as fuel, oil or hydraulic fluid, to come in contact with a hot surface, from a defective induction or exhaust system or a broken line; by the time a pilot becomes aware of it, it usually is well developed (AFH ch 18). Unless the AFM/POH directs otherwise, the first step on discovering a fire is to shut off the fuel supply by placing the mixture in idle cutoff and the fuel selector shutoff valve to OFF, which may starve the engine compartment of fuel and let the fire die naturally (AFH ch 18); the Cessna 172S ENGINE FIRE IN FLIGHT checklist reads 1 Mixture IDLE CUT OFF, 2 Fuel Shutoff Valve Pull Out (OFF), 3 Auxiliary Fuel Pump Switch OFF, 4 Master Switch OFF, 5 Cabin Heat and Air OFF (except overhead vents), 6 Airspeed 100 KIAS, 7 Forced Landing EXECUTE, and its first four items are memory items printed in bold (172S POH sec 3). If the flames are snuffed out, no attempt should be made to restart the engine (AFH ch 18; 172S POH sec 3). An emergency descent is a maneuver for descending as rapidly as possible to a lower altitude or to the ground for an emergency landing, and an uncontrollable fire is one reason for it (AFH ch 18); the 172S fire checklist has no descent steps of its own, so the descent flown is the emergency descent: a bank of approximately 30 to 45 degrees is established to maintain positive load factors (AFH ch 18; ACS PA.IX.A). Pushing the nose straight over reduces the load factor toward zero, at which nothing seems to have weight, so loose objects float (PHAK ch 5); in a 40 degree bank the load factor in level flight is about 1.3 (1 divided by the cosine of 40 degrees, computed). The 172S engine fire airspeed is 100 KIAS, not the 68 KIAS best glide; if the fire is not extinguished, the glide speed is increased to find an airspeed, within airspeed limitations, that gives an incombustible mixture (172S POH sec 3); the descent stays below the never-exceed speed and, in turbulence, below the maneuvering speed (AFH ch 18; 172S POH sec 2). On the FAA private pilot knowledge test, questions on emergency descent airspeed (ACS code PA.IX.A.K3) were missed 73.33 percent of the time from July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025 (FAA Frequently Missed Knowledge Test ACS Codes). Unless the fire is electrical or a crash landing is imminent, deactivating the electrical system prevents the use of the radios for distress messages, so a quick Mayday goes out first if there is time (AFH ch 18); a distress call is MAYDAY three times, the station addressed, the aircraft identification, the nature of the distress, intentions and position (AIM 6-3-1, 6-3-2). With the master switch off the 172S's electric wing flaps cannot be extended, so the forced landing is flown flaps up at 70 KIAS (172S POH sec 3 and sec 7); its EMERGENCY LANDING WITHOUT ENGINE POWER items include doors unlatched prior to touchdown, touchdown slightly tail low and brakes applied heavily (172S POH sec 3); a forward slip loses extra height (AFH ch 9); the airplane is expendable and the only thing that matters is the safety of those on board (AFH ch 18). Smoke, as from burning insulation in an electrical fire, is another situation that can require an emergency descent, with the engine still running (ACS PA.IX.A.K1; AFH ch 18). The emergency descent is practiced with an instructor: clear the area, reduce power to idle unless prohibited, touch the fuel and mixture controls without moving them in a simulated fire, and level off once stable (ACS PA.IX.A; AFH ch 18).

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: In a 172S with an engine fire in flight, cut the fuel first. Make a quick Mayday only if there's time, then switch the master off and close the cabin heat and air, except the overhead vents.
Get down fast. Fly an emergency descent at 100 knots, banked 30 to 45 degrees, then land flaps up at 70 knots and get out.

article.heading: Fuel first
paragraphs: Most engine fires start when fuel or oil leaks onto something hot, such as the exhaust. By the time you see one, it is usually well developed.

The first four checklist items are memory items. Idle cutoff, the mixture pulled fully out, stops fuel to the cylinders. The red fuel shutoff knob, pulled out, closes the supply line, and the auxiliary fuel pump goes off. That can starve a fuel-fed fire, though not an oil-fed one.

The fourth item is the master switch, the main electrical switch. If there's time, make a quick Mayday just before it goes off. Skip the call if the fire is electrical or a crash landing is close. Master off takes the radio, the transponder and the electric flaps.
Once the fire is out, don't restart the engine. A restart would pump fuel back to the leak, and a fire that seems out can flare up again.

table.caption: Engine fire in flight, a summary of the Cessna 172S checklist
rows: 100 knots indicated, higher within limits if the fire still burns
Then the checklist for a landing without engine power

figure.caption: The red fuel shutoff knob pulled out to off, under the 172S engine fire checklist with its first two steps ticked.
figure.alt: A close view of a red knob pulled out of the panel, under the label Fuel shutoff: pull out, beside a card titled 172S engine fire in flight listing seven steps.

article.heading: Why you bank on the way down
paragraphs: An emergency descent gets you down as fast as possible, here to land. The 172S fire checklist has no descent steps, so you fly the emergency descent pilots train.

Roll into a bank of about 30 to 45 degrees and let the nose drop into the turn. The tilted lift curves your path down while the wings stay loaded, with no sharp push forward. Use smooth elevator to hold the speed. The turn also lets you look below for traffic and a field.

Hold 100 knots, the checklist's speed, not the 68-knot best glide speed, the speed that glides farthest. You want down fast, not far. The extra speed adds drag. If the fire still burns, try a higher speed, within the limits, to put it out. Its heat may weaken the structure, so fly gently and never pass the red line, the never-exceed speed. In turbulence, stay below maneuvering speed, above which full or abrupt control movements can overstress the airplane. In a 172S it is 105 knots at 2,550 pounds, 98 at 2,200 and 90 at 1,900.

figure.caption: The descent flown in a bank, the arc showing the bank angle against the dashed horizon line.
figure.alt: A Cessna 172 trailing smoke in a steep bank over farmland, with an arc between its wing and a dashed horizon line.

article.heading: Landing with the master off
paragraphs: Master off leaves the electric flaps where they are, up for this descent, so the landing is flown flaps up at 70 knots.

Roll out high near the field, slow from 100 to 70 knots and lose any extra height with a forward slip. That is a bank with opposite rudder, which steepens the glide. Hold 70 knots with the elevator until the flare. Tighten the seat belts and unlatch the doors before touchdown. Touch down main wheels first, nose slightly high, brake hard and get out.

figure.caption: Gliding to the field at 70 knots with the flaps already up, under part of the 172S checklist for a landing without engine power.
figure.alt: A Cessna 172 gliding low over farmland with a green label reading 70 KT, under a card titled Emergency landing without engine power listing the airspeed, flaps, doors, touchdown and brakes.

article.heading: Four mistakes to avoid
paragraphs: Hold 100 knots in the descent, not best glide. On the private pilot knowledge test, emergency descent airspeed questions were missed 73 percent of the time in the year to June 2025.
Bank into the descent instead of shoving the nose straight down. An abrupt push unloads the airplane toward zero G, where loose items float.
Use the electrical fire checklist for smoke from burning wiring, since it has its own steps. It can still call for a fast descent, with the engine running.
Practice it with an instructor, after briefing a recovery altitude and clearing the area. In training, the power goes to idle first, and you touch each fuel control without moving it.

figure.caption: The descent at 100 knots, the 172S checklist's airspeed, with items 1 to 6 ticked and the first four marked as memory items.
figure.alt: A Cessna 172 diving in a bank under the 172S Engine Fire in Flight checklist, items 1 to 6 ticked and a Memory 1-4 tag, with 100 KT in green.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. What is the very first thing you do when your 172S's engine catches fire in flight?
2. Why do you bank 30 to 45 degrees instead of pushing the nose straight down?
3. Which three things that matter here do you lose when the master switch goes off?
4. What speed do you fly in the emergency descent, and what speed on final with the flaps up?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Cut the fuel, with the mixture to idle cutoff and the fuel shutoff valve pulled out to off.
2. A smooth banked entry keeps the wings loaded with no abrupt push, so loose items stay put.
3. The radio, the transponder and the electric flaps.
4. 100 knots in the descent, and 70 knots on final with the flaps up.

posts.title: When the controller goes silent but your radios work
posts.headline: On November 13, 2026, a ground network fault made controllers' voices and radar patchy nationwide. If nobody answers, check your radio, call again, then squawk 7600.
posts.alt: A see-through airliner's belly over a blue sky, its antennas wired to a radio rack inside, with the label No reply, marked Illustration.
posts.related_text: On November 13, 2026 the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop (ATCSCC Advisory 111, 20:54 UTC), citing communication issues affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers; approximately 3,500 aircraft were airborne and all landed safely; air traffic resumed as of 8:15 p.m. ET the same day, a little over four hours after the stop (FAA Q&A, November 15, 2026; ATCSCC advisories). A tower controls the runways and the airspace near them, an approach control handles the airspace around busy airports, and Air Route Traffic Control Centers handle the en route airspace between them, split into sectors; the ATC System Command Center in Warrenton, Virginia manages national traffic flow and issues ground stops (FAA; JO 7210.3). A Center controller's voice goes through the Center's voice switch over the FAA's telecommunications network to a remote radio site near the airspace, which transmits on VHF line of sight to the aircraft; a radio site has an antenna, an equipment shelter with network equipment, main and standby radios and backup batteries; sites overlap, and backup radios at another site can take over when a site's main radios or lines fail (JO 6500.28); on the airliner, blade antennas feed VHF radios in the electronics bay; radar and ADS-B put aircraft targets on the controller's display. Officials say the trouble began during routine maintenance switching FAA telecommunication lines from copper to fiber at a remote location, including the deployment of a new router, when data began flooding the FAA's network; the FAA's legacy equipment became unstable at 17 of its 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers; it was not a full outage, as some frequencies and radar feeds remained reliable; the two suspected source locations were blocked and the network stabilized (FAA Q&A, November 15, 2026). A two-way radio communications failure is when contact can't be restored, whatever the cause; a pilot who loses two-way contact tries to re-establish it, for example on the previously assigned frequency, on 121.5 MHz or through a flight service station, with no priority among the methods and all at once if possible (AIM 6-4-3); the transponder is set to 7600 (AIM 6-4-2), which ATC sees only where radar or ADS-B covers the aircraft. Under 14 CFR 91.185, if the failure occurs in VFR conditions or VFR conditions are met after it, the pilot continues the flight under VFR and lands as soon as practicable (AIM 6-4-1); otherwise the pilot flies the route of the last clearance, or if being radar vectored, direct from the point of failure to the fix, route or airway in the vector clearance; with no assigned route, the route ATC said to expect, and with neither, the route filed; for each route segment, at the highest of the altitude last assigned, the minimum altitude for IFR operations and the altitude ATC said to expect, where a higher expected altitude applies only from the time or fix given with it, and not at all if the failure comes after that time or fix (14 CFR 91.185; AIM 6-4-1). Standard separation that ATC sets up and the pilot keeps by flying the clearance is 1,000 feet vertically at FL350 in RVSM airspace and 5 nautical miles laterally with en route radar (JO 7110.65 4-5-1, 5-5-4); a predictable lost comms flight lets ATC keep it. TCAS II interrogates other aircraft's transponders directly, independent of ground ATC; it can give a traffic advisory and, when needed, a resolution advisory in the vertical, and between two TCAS II aircraft the resolution advisories are coordinated so they complement each other; the pilot follows the RA over an ATC instruction unless doing so would jeopardize safety, and tells ATC as soon as possible; TCAS gives no protection against an aircraft without a working transponder (FAA TCAS II v7.1 booklet; 14 CFR 91.123; AIM 4-4-16).

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: A controller's voice reaches you over the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA's) ground network and a radio site near your airplane. So a fault on the ground can silence the frequency while the radios on board work.

If nobody answers, check the frequency and volume and call again, trying the last frequency that worked and 121.5, the emergency frequency. If contact stays lost, squawk 7600 and fly the lost communications rules.

article.heading: How a controller's voice reaches you
paragraphs: An Air Route Traffic Control Center, or Center, handles traffic between airport areas. The controller's voice goes through the Center's voice switch, which connects each controller to the radio lines. Then the FAA's telecommunications network carries it to a remote radio site near your airspace.

That site holds network equipment, main and standby radios and backup batteries. It transmits on very high frequency (VHF) radio, which travels in straight lines, so terrain and the horizon can block it. Your antenna feeds the radio on board. Standby radios and batteries cover a failed radio or a power cut, not a broken network link.
On November 13, 2026, that ground link became unstable in many places at once. Officials say it began during copper-to-fiber line work, when data from new equipment flooded the FAA's network.

Voice and radar came and went at 17 of 22 Centers, though some frequencies kept working. The FAA stopped departures nationwide with a ground stop. About 3,500 aircraft were airborne, and all landed safely. Traffic resumed a little over four hours later.

figure.caption: Inside a remote radio site's shelter, with the network router, the main and standby radios and the backup batteries.
figure.alt: A see-through equipment shelter with racks labeled Network router and Main plus standby radios, and battery shelves at the left.

article.heading: What to do when nobody answers
paragraphs: A quiet frequency is normal, so silence alone is not a failure. If your calls go unanswered, try the last frequency that worked, 121.5 and a flight service station, all at once if you can.

Still nothing means a two-way radio communications failure, whatever the cause. Squawk 7600, which sets your transponder to the lost communications code. Air traffic control (ATC) sees it only where its radar or ADS-B still reaches the controller.

On an instrument flight, if you are in VFR conditions or reach them, continue under visual flight rules and land as soon as practicable. Otherwise, fly the route ATC assigned. If you were being vectored, steered by ATC headings, go direct from there to the fix, route or airway named in that vector clearance. With no assigned route, fly the route ATC said to expect, and with neither, the route you filed.

On each leg, fly the highest of the altitude last assigned, the minimum instrument altitude and any altitude ATC told you to expect. A higher expected altitude starts at the time or fix ATC gave with it, and doesn't apply if contact fails after that.

figure.caption: On an instrument flight in cloud, the white line is the route as cleared. The dashed line is a radar vector, and after a failure you fly straight to its fix.
figure.alt: An airliner's path curving toward a fix over the clouds, under the labels Route as cleared and Vectored, direct to fix.

article.heading: What TCAS can and cannot do
paragraphs: Flying the rules predictably lets ATC protect your route.

TCAS II, the Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System on airliners, asks other aircraft's transponders directly, so it works without the ground. A traffic advisory warns of nearby traffic, and if needed a resolution advisory gives a command such as climb or descend.
When two TCAS II jets meet, their units coordinate so their advisories work together. TCAS can't see an aircraft without a working transponder.

figure.caption: In this example, the two jets' TCAS units coordinate, so one is told to climb and the other to descend.
figure.alt: Two airliners far apart in a gray sky, the upper one under an up arrow labeled Climb, climb and the lower one at the bottom edge labeled Descend, descend, marked Illustration.

article.heading: Three mistakes when the radio goes quiet
paragraphs: Call again before deciding your radio has failed. First check the volume and the frequency you dialed.
Land as soon as practicable, not as soon as possible, after losing radio contact on an instrument flight in VFR conditions. The rule asks for a sensible landing, not a rushed one.
Follow a TCAS resolution advisory over an ATC instruction unless that would be unsafe, then tell ATC as soon as you can. Follow it promptly, whether or not the other aircraft has TCAS.

figure.caption: On an instrument flight with lost radio contact, in VFR conditions you continue under VFR and land as soon as practicable.
figure.alt: An airliner from behind over the clouds under green text reading Squawk 7600 and the label VFR conditions.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Why could your frequency go silent when the radios on board work?
2. Assigned 6,000 feet, with a minimum instrument altitude of 7,000 feet and no expected altitude, what do you fly after losing contact?
3. On an instrument flight in VFR conditions with no radio contact, how soon should you land?
4. If a TCAS resolution advisory conflicts with an ATC altitude instruction, which do you follow?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. The break can be on the ground, in the network or the radio site between the controller and you.
2. In cloud on that leg, 7,000 feet, the highest of the altitudes that apply.
3. As soon as practicable, continuing under VFR.
4. The resolution advisory, then tell ATC as soon as you can.

posts.title: IMSAFE and PAVE, explained
posts.headline: Pilot impairment contributes to many more accidents than aircraft system failures do.
posts.alt: Cover slide titled IMSAFE and PAVE. The house Cessna 172 parked on a small airport ramp at dawn, with a lone pilot seen from behind walking out to it carrying a flight bag. Text: Pilot impairment contributes to many more accidents than aircraft system failures do.
caption: The pressure to get there is the one risk that can make you ignore all the others.

Before you walk out to the airplane, check yourself: sick, on medication, stressed, tired or upset? When was your last drink? Even one beer can impair your flying. Then check the whole flight, from the airplane and the weather to whoever is waiting for you. Set your minimums in writing before the day. If you're still fit to fly but tired or rushed, add margin. Send this to someone you fly with.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
posts.related_text: Aircraft accident statistics show that pilots should be conducting preflight checklists on themselves as well as their aircraft, for pilot impairment contributes to many more accidents than failures of aircraft systems. One of the best ways single pilots can mitigate risk is to use the IMSAFE checklist to determine physical and mental readiness for flying: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, and Emotion. By incorporating the PAVE checklist into preflight planning, the pilot divides the risks of flight into four categories: Pilot-in-command (PIC), Aircraft, enVironment, and External pressures (PAVE). With the PAVE checklist, pilots have a simple way to remember each category to examine for risk prior to each flight. P = Pilot in Command: the pilot is one of the risk factors in a flight and must ask, 'Am I ready for this trip?' in terms of experience, recency, currency, physical, and emotional condition. The IMSAFE checklist provides the answers. Illness: Am I sick? Illness is an obvious pilot risk. Even mild symptoms may be sufficiently debilitating to create a 'P' hazard. The safest rule is not to fly while suffering from any illness. Medication: Am I taking any medicines that might affect my judgment or make me drowsy? Both prescription and non-prescription over-the-counter (OTC) drugs have side effects that can affect a pilot's physical and mental performance. No person may act or attempt to act as a crewmember of a civil aircraft while using any drug that affects the person's faculties in any way contrary to safety. Pilot performance can be seriously degraded by both prescribed and over-the-counter medications, as well as by the medical conditions for which they are taken; the safest rule is not to fly as a crewmember while taking any medication, unless approved to do so by the FAA. Stress: Am I under psychological pressure from the job? Do I have money, health, or family problems? Stress causes concentration and performance problems. While the regulations list medical conditions that require grounding, stress is not among them. Most pilots do not leave stress 'on the ground.' When more than usual difficulties are being experienced, a pilot should consider delaying flight until these difficulties are satisfactorily resolved. Stress and fatigue can be an extremely hazardous combination. Alcohol: Have I been drinking within 8 hours? Within 24 hours? As little as one ounce of liquor, one bottle of beer, or four ounces of wine can impair flying skills. Alcohol also renders a pilot more susceptible to disorientation and hypoxia. No person may act or attempt to act as a crewmember of a civil aircraft within 8 hours after the consumption of any alcoholic beverage, while under the influence of alcohol, or while having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. A pilot may still be under influence 8 hours after drinking a moderate amount of alcohol; therefore, an excellent rule is to allow at least 12 to 24 hours between 'bottle and throttle,' depending on the amount of alcoholic beverage consumed. Fatigue: Am I tired and not adequately rested? Fatigue continues to be one of the most insidious hazards to flight safety, as it may not be apparent to a pilot until serious errors are made. Fatigue may degrade cognitive skills and decision-making ability. Emotion: Am I emotionally upset? Any pilot who experiences an emotionally upsetting event should not fly until satisfactorily recovered from it. Emotions may affect normal pilot ability to focus. A = Aircraft: Is this the right aircraft for the flight? Am I familiar with and current in this aircraft? Is this aircraft equipped for the flight? Can this aircraft use the runways available with an adequate margin of safety, carry the planned load, operate at the altitudes needed, and does it have sufficient fuel capacity, with reserves, for the trip legs planned? V = EnVironment: weather is a major environmental consideration (the current ceiling and visibility, the possibility that the weather may be different than forecast, the crosswind component, thunderstorms, icing), along with terrain, the airports, the airspace and any temporary flight restrictions (TFRs) along the route, and night. External pressures are influences external to the flight that create a sense of pressure to complete a flight, often at the expense of safety. They include someone waiting at the airport for the flight's arrival, a passenger the pilot does not want to disappoint, the desire to demonstrate pilot qualifications or to impress someone, the desire to satisfy a specific personal goal ('get-home-itis,' 'get-there-itis,' and 'let's-go-itis'), the pilot's general goal-completion orientation, and pride. Management of external pressure is the single most important key to risk management because it is the one risk factor category that can cause a pilot to ignore all the other risk factors. External pressures put time-related pressure on the pilot and figure into a majority of accidents. Pilots subject to external pressures sometimes fail to consider the other three major categories of hazards. Personal standard operating procedures supply a release for the external pressures of a flight: allow time for an extra fuel stop or an unexpected landing because of weather; have alternate plans for a late arrival or backup airline reservations; plan to leave early enough to drive if necessary; advise those waiting at the destination that the arrival may be delayed; manage passengers' expectations. The key to managing external pressure is to be ready for and accept delays. Once a pilot identifies the risks of a flight, he or she needs to decide whether the risk, or combination of risks, can be managed safely and successfully. If not, make the decision to cancel the flight. One way a pilot can control the risks is to set personal minimums for items in each risk category. These are limits unique to that individual pilot's current level of experience and proficiency. Pilots who understand the difference between what is 'smart' or 'safe' based on pilot experience and proficiency establish personal minimums that are more restrictive than the regulatory requirements. One of the most important concepts that safe pilots understand is the difference between what is 'legal' in terms of the regulations, and what is 'smart' or 'safe' in terms of pilot experience and proficiency. Example situations calling for additional safety margins: Pilot: illness, use of medication, stress, or fatigue; lack of currency (e.g., have not flown for several weeks). Aircraft: an unfamiliar airplane or an aircraft with unfamiliar avionics or other equipment. enVironment: unfamiliar airports and airspace; different terrain or other unfamiliar characteristics. External Pressures: 'must meet' deadlines, pressures from passengers. If you are facing these, adjust baseline personal minimums by adding at least 500 feet to ceiling, adding at least 1/2 mile to visibility, adding at least 500 feet to runway length, and subtracting at least 5 knots from winds. These margins are for a pilot who is otherwise fit and legal to fly; they are not a fix for illness or impairing medication, and the safest rule is not to fly while suffering from any illness. The example situations and additional safety margins only provide a starting point; pilots may develop their own adjustment factors, and if multiple special conditions apply, a pilot could make an adjustment for each factor. For a night cross-country flight to an unfamiliar airport, departing after a full workday, the suggested adjustment is adding 1,000 feet to the ceiling value, one mile to visibility, and 1,000 feet to required runway length. The pilot should not adjust personal minimums to complete a specific flight. The time to consider adjustments is not while under pressure to fly, but rather when time and objectivity permit an honest self-analysis. Make adjustments to one variable at a time, and seek training and consult with a flight instructor before making a significant adjustment to personal minimums. Established personal minimums enable the pilot to make a no-go or divert decision rather than departing with a sense of unease regarding the outcome of a flight. A written set of personal minimums can also make it easier to explain tough decisions to passengers who depend on the pilot's judgment. For example, the aircraft may have a maximum crosswind component of 15 knots listed in the aircraft flight manual (AFM), and the pilot has experience with 10 knots of direct crosswind. The 10 knot crosswind experience level is that pilot's personal limitation until additional training with a certificated flight instructor (CFI) provides the pilot with additional experience. Human factors have been documented as a primary contributor to more than 70 percent of aircraft accidents. Using all four PAVE checklist categories before a flight captures most hazards normally encountered. A pilot had only 4 hours of sleep the night before being asked by the boss to fly to a meeting in a city 750 miles away. The reported weather was marginal and not expected to improve. After assessing fitness as a pilot, it was decided that it would not be wise to make the flight; the boss was initially unhappy, but was later convinced by the pilot that the risks involved were unacceptable. Aftereffects of alcohol consumption (dehydration, hangover, and headaches, etc.) may trigger a 'P' hazard for longer than eight hours after consumption. Some publications combine Emotion with Stress as the 'S' in IMSAFE and leave the 'E' to remind pilots about 'Eating.'

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 2

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: An impaired pilot contributes to many more accidents than a failed aircraft system, so your preflight starts with you. IMSAFE checks your fitness, and PAVE sorts the whole flight's risks into four buckets.
Personal minimums, your own limits, are written before the day and tighter than the regulations. When you're otherwise fit to fly but face a PAVE hazard, add at least the margins below.

table.caption: How far to widen your written minimums on a hazard day

article.heading: Why you preflight yourself first
paragraphs: Human factors, such as fatigue and stress, are a primary contributor to more than 70 percent of aircraft accidents. IMSAFE covers the ones you carry, from illness and medication through stress, alcohol, fatigue and emotion. Some versions fold emotion into the S and use the E for eating.

Even mild symptoms can make you the hazard, so the safest rule is not to fly ill. Prescription and over-the-counter medicines, and the conditions they treat, can degrade you. The law grounds you while a drug affects you, and it's safest to fly on none unless the FAA approves it.
Stress from work, money, health or family hurts concentration, yet no regulation grounds you for it. When troubles run heavier than usual, consider delaying the flight until they're resolved.

As little as one ounce of liquor, one bottle of beer or four ounces of wine can impair your flying skills. You may not act as a crewmember within 8 hours of drinking, under the influence, or at an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. A moderate amount can outlast 8 hours, so the better rule is at least 12 to 24 hours, depending on how much you drank.
Fatigue can hide until you make serious errors, and with stress it can be an extremely hazardous combination. After an upsetting event, wait until you've recovered, since emotion can pull your focus.

figure.caption: IMSAFE checks you, the pilot, and PAVE checks the whole flight around you.
figure.alt: A pilot seen from behind on the ramp a few steps from a white high-wing Cessna 172, with the runway, hills and morning sky beyond. One tag marks the pilot as IMSAFE, and a wider tag spans the airplane, runway and sky as PAVE.

article.heading: How PAVE covers the whole flight
paragraphs: Running all four buckets before a flight catches most hazards you'll normally meet. P is you, the pilot in command, judged on experience, recent flying and your IMSAFE answers.

A asks whether the airplane suits the trip in equipment, runway margin, load, altitude and fuel with reserves. V, the environment, covers weather, terrain, airports, airspace, temporary flight restrictions and night.

E, external pressures, are influences outside the flight that push you to finish it, often at the cost of safety. They include someone waiting, a passenger you don't want to let down, and get-home-itis.
Manage this bucket above the others, since it alone can blind you to the other three. It adds time pressure and figures into a majority of accidents.

figure.caption: One scene, four buckets: the pilot, the airplane, the low cloud and the passengers waiting.
figure.alt: A wide view of a wet ramp: the pilot walking out on the left, a Cessna 172 in the middle, low cloud over the hills beyond the runway, and two passengers with bags by the terminal door. Each is tagged with its PAVE letter, the cloud in blue and the passengers in amber.

article.heading: Minimums you write before the day
paragraphs: Your airplane's flight manual lists a 15 knot maximum crosswind component, and you have flown 10 knots of direct crosswind. Ten knots stays your limit until more training with an instructor. Personal minimums are limits like that one, fitted to your own experience and proficiency.
A six-step worksheet, starting with the weather, builds them. Written down, they let you call a no-go or divert instead of departing uneasy.

You plan a night cross-country to an unfamiliar airport, leaving after a full workday. Each hazard can take its own margin. Here the suggested raise is 1,000 feet of ceiling, one mile of visibility and 1,000 feet of runway length.

table.caption: Situations that call for the extra margin
rows: Stress or fatigue, or lack of currency (not having flown for several weeks)
An unfamiliar airplane or an aircraft with unfamiliar avionics or other equipment
Unfamiliar airports and airspace, different terrain or other unfamiliar features

figure.caption: On a tired day the minimum rises by at least 500 feet, above today's ceiling, so the flight waits.
figure.alt: An airport seen from far off under a flat grey cloud deck. A blue line marks today's ceiling. An amber dashed line just below it marks the pilot's written minimum, and a second amber line inside the cloud, with an arrow up to it, marks the tired-day minimum. A tag says the drawing is not to scale.

article.heading: Two mistakes that undo the check
paragraphs: Leave your minimums alone once a specific flight is on the line. Adjust them later, one value at a time, and see an instructor before any big change.
Tell your passengers, and whoever waits, that you may be late. Being ready to accept a delay is the key, so plan for an extra fuel stop, a backup airline seat or time to drive.

figure.caption: Packed bags and waiting passengers are the pressure that can make you ignore the low cloud ahead.
figure.alt: Two passengers seen from behind loading weekend bags into a Cessna 172 on the ramp, while a low grey cloud deck sits on the hills beyond the runway and hides their tops.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Your last beer was a little over 8 hours before your planned takeoff. What does the better rule tell you to do?
2. After 4 hours of sleep, your boss asks you to fly to a meeting 750 miles away. With the weather marginal and not expected to improve, which PAVE buckets flag?
3. You haven't flown for several weeks, and today's ceiling sits right at your written minimum. What happens to that minimum?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Wait at least 12 to 24 hours, depending on how much you drank. Eight hours meets only the time limit.
2. P, V and E all flag, so stay down. A pilot in this spot declined, and the boss later agreed.
3. Stay down. Several weeks without flying is a P hazard, so your minimum rises above today's ceiling.

posts.title: Inside the 172 engine and what low oil pressure means
posts.headline: If the oil pressure drops in flight, check the oil temperature. A normal one may point to the gauge, a rising one to a failing engine. Land either way.
posts.alt: The front of a Cessna 172 with its cowling lifted away, labeled Upper cowl and Lycoming O-320, with oil temperature and pressure gauges above.
posts.related_text: The 1981 Cessna 172P's engine is a Lycoming O-320-D2J: horizontally opposed, four cylinders, air cooled, carburetor equipped, rated 160 BHP at 2,700 RPM (172P POH sec 1 and 7); it is a direct drive engine, the propeller driven straight off the crankshaft (Lycoming O-320 Operator's Manual 1-1). In a reciprocating engine the valves, spark plugs and pistons are in the cylinders and the crankshaft and connecting rods in the crankcase; on the power stroke the burning fuel-air mixture forces the piston down, creating the power that turns the crankshaft (PHAK ch 7). The O-320's camshaft is located above and parallel to the crankshaft and actuates hydraulic tappets, which operate the valves through push rods and valve rockers (Lycoming O-320 Operator's Manual 1-1). Engine oil lubricates the moving parts and also cools, by reducing friction and removing heat from the cylinders (PHAK ch 7). In the 172P, oil is drawn from the sump through a suction strainer screen into the engine-driven pump; a bypass valve sends cold oil straight to the full-flow filter and hot oil out to the oil cooler and back to the filter; a pressure relief valve regulates oil pressure by letting excess oil return to the sump while the rest is circulated to the engine parts; residual oil returns to the sump by gravity (172P POH sec 7). Pressure oil is fed to the main oil gallery and on to the crankshaft's main bearings and rod journals, the camshaft and hydraulic tappets, and through the hollow push rods to the valve mechanism (Lycoming O-320 Operator's Manual 1-2). The 172P's oil pressure gauge, fed by a direct pressure oil line from the engine, is marked: minimum idling pressure 25 PSI (red line), normal operating range 60 to 90 PSI (green arc), maximum 115 PSI (red line); the oil temperature gauge beside it is marked green 100 to 245 degrees F, red line 245 degrees F (172P POH sec 7). With low oil pressure and normal oil temperature there is a possibility the oil pressure gauge or relief valve is malfunctioning; a leak in the line to the gauge is not necessarily cause for an immediate precautionary landing, because an orifice in this line prevents a sudden loss of oil from the sump, but a landing at the nearest airport is advisable to inspect the source of trouble (172P POH sec 3). If a total loss of oil pressure is accompanied by a rise in oil temperature, there is good reason to suspect an engine failure is imminent: reduce engine power immediately, select a suitable forced landing field and use only the minimum power required to reach the desired touchdown spot (172P POH sec 3). Unlike oil pressure, changes in oil temperature occur more slowly (PHAK ch 7), so a normal temperature soon after a pressure drop does not clear the engine and the pilot keeps watching it on the way to the airport (an inference from that lag, stated as such).

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 7

posts.credits: 3D model: “Cessna172” by KOG_THORNS (sketchfab.com), CC BY 4.0, modified.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: If the oil pressure in your 172 drops below its green arc, the normal range, in flight, check the oil temperature. A normal temperature may point to the gauge, its line or the relief valve, but it doesn't prove the engine is fine. Land at the nearest airport.
If the pressure is gone and the temperature is climbing, the engine may fail soon. Reduce power now, pick a landing spot and use only the power you need to reach it.

article.heading: How the engine turns the propeller
paragraphs: The 172P's Lycoming O-320 has four cylinders, laid flat in two opposed pairs and cooled by air. It is rated 160 horsepower at 2,700 revolutions per minute. Other 172 models have other engines and gauge markings, so check your own airplane's handbook.

In each cylinder, the burning fuel and air push a piston, a sliding plug, toward the crankshaft, the engine's main turning shaft. Its connecting rod pushes on an offset part of the crankshaft, which turns the push into rotation. The engine is direct drive, so the crankshaft turns the propeller itself.
Above the crankshaft runs the camshaft. Through hollow tubes called pushrods, it opens each cylinder's valves, which let the fuel and air in and the burned gas out.

figure.caption: The crankshaft and one of its connecting rods, inside the see-through crankcase.
figure.alt: A see-through engine with a steel crankshaft labeled Crankshaft and a rod below it labeled Connecting rod.

article.heading: Where the oil goes
paragraphs: Two of oil's jobs matter here. It lubricates the moving parts, and it carries heat away from the cylinders.
The engine-driven pump draws it from the sump, the oil reservoir at the bottom of the engine, through a screen. Cold oil goes straight to the filter, and hot oil goes through the cooler first.

A relief valve limits the pressure by spilling the extra oil back to the sump. The rest flows into the main oil gallery, the engine's main oil passage. From there it reaches the bearings, the smooth supports for the turning shafts, the camshaft and, through the hollow pushrods, the valves.
Then it drains back to the sump by gravity. So if the oil stops flowing, the parts rub, the heat stays in the engine and the temperature climbs.

figure.caption: Oil (tan) in the main oil gallery and the passages that feed the bearings, with the oil pressure gauge (right) in its green arc.
figure.alt: Tan oil passages running through a see-through crankcase, labeled Oil gallery and Bearings, below two small gauges labeled Oil press.

article.heading: What the two oil gauges tell you
paragraphs: The oil pressure gauge reads straight from the engine through a line. It shows pressure, not how much oil is left. The oil temperature gauge beside it is your cross-check.

With a normal temperature, a faulty gauge can read low falsely, or a faulty relief valve can make the pressure really low. A leak in the gauge line isn't necessarily a reason to land at once. An orifice, a narrow restriction in that line, lets so little oil through that a leak can't drain the sump quickly.
If the pressure is gone and the temperature is rising, an engine failure may be close.

table.caption: Cessna 172P oil gauge markings, in pounds per square inch (PSI) and degrees Fahrenheit

figure.caption: Low indicated oil pressure (right) with a normal temperature (left). Only a mechanic can tell a false reading from a real loss.
figure.alt: Two round gauges, oil temperature and oil pressure, over a faint see-through engine with a valve labeled Relief valve and a line labeled Gauge line.

article.heading: Three mistakes with low oil pressure
paragraphs: Keep watching the temperature after a normal first reading. Oil temperature changes more slowly than pressure, so a normal reading soon after the drop doesn't clear the engine.
Reduce power at once if the temperature climbs with the pressure gone, and get ready to land without engine power.
Land at the nearest airport even when the gauge looks like the culprit. Treat any abnormal reading as a reason to cut the flight short.

figure.caption: With no oil pressure showing and the oil temperature rising, the engine may fail soon.
figure.alt: A see-through Cessna 172 over farmland under the oil temperature and oil pressure gauges, with a red label reading Temp rising.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. How can a faulty gauge and a faulty relief valve each show low oil pressure?
2. What does the orifice in the oil pressure gauge line do?
3. Why doesn't a normal oil temperature right after a pressure drop clear the engine?
4. What do you do when the oil pressure is gone and the temperature is climbing?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. A faulty gauge can read low when the pressure is fine, and a faulty relief valve can make the pressure really low.
2. It lets so little oil through that a leaking gauge line can't drain the sump quickly.
3. Oil temperature changes more slowly than pressure, so keep watching it.
4. Reduce power now, pick a field and use only enough power to reach it.

posts.title: How full flaps can stall an iced tail
posts.headline: Ice on the tail and a fresh full-flap setting can stall the tail and drop the nose. A tail stall's recovery is partly the opposite of a wing stall's.
posts.alt: A see-through Cessna 172 in gray icing weather with its horizontal tail glowing red and broken airflow swirling around it, labeled Tail stall.
posts.related_text: Most aircraft have a nose-down pitching moment from the wings because the CG is ahead of the center of pressure; it is the role of the tailplane to counteract this moment by providing a downward force (downward lift), so the tail works at a negative angle of attack, its air meeting it from above (IFH ch 4; AC 91-74B 3-7). Extending the flaps changes the direction of the wing's wake airflow (downwash) at the tail (172S POH sec 3) and may increase the negative angle of attack of the tail, as may increasing speed (actions which move the wing away from stall, such as deployment of flaps or increasing speed, may increase the negative AOA of the tail): deployment of flaps lets the wing fly at a less positive angle of attack, decreasing the probability of a wing stall, while the angle of attack at the tailplane is more negative (IFH ch 4; AC 91-74B 5-12). Since the tailplane is ordinarily thinner than the wing, it is a more efficient collector of ice, and on most aircraft it is not visible to the pilot (IFH ch 4; AC 91-74B 3-7); a relatively small ice accretion can significantly reduce the maximum lift coefficient and the angle of attack at which the surface stalls (IFH ch 4); an ice-contaminated tailplane stall occurs when a tailplane with accumulated ice is placed at a sufficiently negative angle of attack (AC 91-74B 5-12). With ice on the tailplane, it may stall after full or partial deployment of flaps, and the nose pitches down (IFH ch 4); it rarely occurs until the flaps are fully extended on susceptible airplanes, and there are no known incidents in cruise (AC 91-74B 5-11, 5-12); with a severe ice build-up on the horizontal tail, the change in wing wake airflow direction caused by flap extension could result in a loss of elevator effectiveness (172S POH sec 3). Symptoms that, singly or in combination, may warn of tailplane icing include elevator control pulsing, oscillations or vibrations, an abnormal nose-down trim change, unusual pitch anomalies, a reduction or loss of elevator effectiveness, a sudden change in elevator force (the control would move nose-down if unrestrained) and a sudden uncommanded nose-down pitch (IFH ch 4). The tailplane stall recovery: immediately retract the flaps to the previous setting and apply appropriate nose-up elevator pressure; increase airspeed appropriately for the reduced flap extension setting; apply sufficient power for the aircraft configuration and conditions (high power settings may adversely affect the response at high airspeed in some designs; observe the manufacturer's recommendations) (IFH ch 4); these procedures are in some respects opposite from a wing stall recovery, and applying the incorrect procedure can seriously compound the upset (AC 91-74B 5-13). Since most icing accidents have been attributed to wing stall, a pilot should always suspect a wing stall with any vibration or buffet if full flaps have not just been deployed, and a wing stall recovery reduces the angle of attack by reducing the aircraft pitch (AC 91-74B 5-12, 5-13). Pilots of airplanes not certificated for flight in icing, such as the Cessna 172, must avoid icing conditions and immediately exit icing if inadvertently encountered (AC 91-74B 3-13); the 172S POH's inadvertent icing procedure turns the pitot heat on and turns back or changes altitude, and with ice on board it says to leave the wing flaps retracted for the landing, to approach at 65 to 75 KIAS depending upon the amount of accumulation, and to be prepared for a significantly higher stall speed and a longer landing roll (172S POH sec 3); limited or no flaps will likely mean a higher-than-normal approach speed, and longer runways may be necessary (AC 91-74B 5-12).

citations.ref: Cessna 172S POH sec 3 inadvertent icing encounter
citations.title: Cessna 172S Pilot's Operating Handbook
