article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Your horizontal tail holds the nose up by lifting downward. Lowering the flaps makes the air meet it more steeply. With ice on the tail, full flaps can push it past its own stall, and the nose drops.
To recover, put the flaps back where they were and hold back pressure. Then fly the speed that flap setting needs, with only the power it takes.

article.heading: Why the tail pushes down
paragraphs: Most airplanes balance on a center of gravity, their balance point, that sits ahead of the wing's center of pressure, where its lift acts. With the weight ahead of the lift, the nose tries to drop.
The horizontal tail holds against it. Its air meets it from above, at a negative angle of attack, the angle between a surface and the air meeting it. So it works like a small wing lifting downward.

figure.caption: Air meeting the tail from above (cyan) makes it push down (green arrow), which holds the nose up.
figure.alt: A tail airfoil drawn over a see-through Cessna 172 in gray weather, with cyan airflow lines meeting it from above, a label Air from above and a green arrow labeled Pushes down.

article.heading: What flaps and speed do to the tail
paragraphs: Lower the flaps and the wing throws its air down harder. That downwash, the air the wing pushes down behind it, now reaches the tail at a steeper angle.
The tail's negative angle of attack grows, bringing it closer to its own stall. The flaps do the opposite for the wing, which can now fly at a smaller angle of attack, farther from a wing stall.

More speed does the same to the tail as flaps do. At higher speed the wing needs a smaller angle of attack, so the nose sits lower and the tail meets its air more from above. So lowering the nose to gain speed steepens the tail's angle, which is why a tail stall's fix differs from a wing stall's.

figure.caption: The lowered flap (lower left) bends the wing's air (cyan) down toward the tail, which is drawn large at the top.
figure.alt: A wing section with its flap drooped at the lower left, cyan airflow bending down from it toward the tail, the same tail drawn large at the top, and the label Flaps down.

article.heading: How ice brings the tail's stall closer
paragraphs: The tail is thinner than the wing, so it collects ice faster. On most airplanes you can't see it from the seat.
Even a little ice can cut a surface's maximum lift and lower the angle of attack at which it stalls. On the tail, that moves the stall closer to where the tail already works.
So a tail stall usually comes right after the flaps go to full, and there are no known cases in cruise.

figure.caption: Ice (violet) lowers the tail's stall angle (red line). With full flaps, the air (cyan) now meets the tail steeply enough to reach that line.
figure.alt: A tail airfoil with violet ice on its leading edge, a red stall line at the front, cyan airflow lines meeting it steeply and the chip Ice plus full flaps: tail stall risk.

article.heading: How a tail stall feels
paragraphs: Right after the flaps go down, hints can come first. Watch for a pulsing yoke, an abnormal nose-down trim change or odd pitch bobbing.
When the tail stalls, the airflow breaks away from it and its downward push fades. The nose pitches down on its own, and the elevator gets weak or stops working.

The control force changes suddenly, and left alone, the yoke would move forward, nose-down. A wing stall can come at any flap setting and may shake the airframe with buffet, the shudder as its airflow breaks away. With ice, that warning can come late or not at all.

figure.caption: The yoke tugs forward in your hands as the tail's push fades.
figure.alt: A see-through cockpit with two control yokes, an arrow showing the pull on them and the label Felt: forward tug.

article.heading: Four mistakes in an iced airplane
paragraphs: Get out of icing at once in a 172, which isn't approved for flight in icing. Turn on the pitot heat, which keeps the airspeed probe clear, then turn back or change altitude.

Land an iced 172 with the flaps up, because flaps with ice on the tail can cost elevator control. Approach at 65 to 75 knots indicated, faster with more ice, and expect a higher stall speed and a longer landing roll.

Bring the flaps back up to their previous setting at once, rather than leaving them down, and resist the yoke's forward pull. Then fly the airspeed that setting needs, with enough power for it, making any nose-down change slowly. High power can make it worse in some designs, so follow your airplane's manual.

Treat a buffet as a wing stall unless you have just lowered full flaps. Most icing accidents have been wing stalls, and their recovery lowers the nose. Using the wrong recovery can seriously worsen the upset.

figure.caption: The two stalls side by side, each with its clue and its first move.
figure.alt: A see-through Cessna 172 over icy farmland with a two-column card: Wing stall, buffet, no fresh full flaps, lower nose; Tail stall, fresh full flaps, forward tug, flaps back, back pressure.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. What do you do first if the yoke tugs forward and the nose drops just after you lower full flaps with ice aboard?
2. Which stall do you suspect when you feel a buffet in icing with the flaps still up?
3. Why might the tail carry more ice than the wing you can see from your seat?
4. How do you set the flaps and the approach speed for landing a 172 with ice on board?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Put the flaps back to the previous setting and hold back pressure. Then fly the speed that setting needs, with the power for it.
2. A wing stall, since you haven't just lowered full flaps. Lower the nose.
3. The tail is thinner, so it collects ice faster, and on most airplanes you can't see it.
4. Flaps up, and approach at 65 to 75 knots, faster with more ice. Expect a longer landing roll.

posts.title: The impossible turn after an engine failure
posts.headline: At 400 feet, turning back to the runway after an engine failure takes more turning and more height than it seems. Lower the nose and land straight ahead instead.
posts.alt: An illustrative view of farmland with a runway labeled Runway, an airplane at a 400 FT marker just after takeoff, and an orange turn back that reaches the ground at a red X short of the runway.
posts.related_text: After an engine failure on takeoff, altitude and airspeed are seldom sufficient to execute a 180 degree gliding turn necessary to return to the runway (172S POH sec 3, amplified procedures); the AFH calls the turn back 'the impossible turn', which presents many challenges (AFH ch 18). In the AFH's example at 65 knots and a standard-rate turn, the radius of the turn is 2,100 feet, so at the completion of a 180 degree turn the airplane is 4,200 feet to one side of the runway; it needs to turn another 45 degrees to head toward the runway, a total change in direction of 225 degrees, and a turn back may require more than a 180 degree change in direction (AFH ch 18). At the standard rate (3 degrees of change in direction per second) it takes 1 minute to turn 180 degrees, and 225 degrees takes 75 seconds plus a 4-second reaction time (AFH ch 18); the 172S glides about 20 nautical miles from 12,000 feet at 68 KIAS (POH Figure 3-1), about 10 to 1, which is about 690 feet a minute at 68 to 70 knots, so 79 seconds of gliding, the 75-second turn plus the 4-second reaction, costs about 900 feet, more than twice 400 feet (computed); the AFH's example starts at 300 feet AGL, sinks 1,000 feet a minute, takes 79 seconds including the reaction time, loses 1,316 feet and ends 1,016 feet below the runway (AFH ch 18). A turn back, if attempted, requires a turn with a higher bank angle; a standard rate or shallow turn consumes too much time, requires too much distance and generates an unacceptable solution (AFH ch 18). Cessna 172S stall speeds at 2,550 lb, power off, flaps up, in KIAS: 48 at 0 degrees of bank, 52 at 30, 57 at 45 and 68 at 60 (POH Figure 5-3); the engine failure immediately after takeoff checklist's airspeed is 70 KIAS with the flaps up and 65 KIAS with the flaps down (POH sec 3), so in a 60 degree bank the stall speed is just under the glide speed. In a 60 degree level turn the load factor is 2 and the stall speed is about 41 percent higher than in level flight (AFH ch 5). If the pilot does not lower the nose sufficiently during the turn, an accelerated stall and fatal crash may occur; pilots should be alert for and respond appropriately to any stall warning and reduce wing loading during the turn as necessary (AFH ch 18); altitude loss during a stall recovery may be as much as 230 feet (172S POH Figure 5-3, note 1). Prompt lowering of the nose to maintain airspeed and establish a glide attitude is the first response to an engine failure after takeoff; in most cases the landing should be planned straight ahead with only small changes in direction to avoid obstructions, and the checklist ends 'Land, STRAIGHT AHEAD' (172S POH sec 3); continuing straight ahead or making a slight turn gives the pilot time to establish a safe landing attitude, and the landing occurs under control and as slowly as possible, which usually represents the option with the lowest risk (AFH ch 18). The 172S ENGINE FAILURE IMMEDIATELY AFTER TAKEOFF checklist has eight items: airspeed 70 KIAS flaps up (65 flaps down), mixture idle cut off, fuel shutoff valve off, ignition off, wing flaps as required, master switch off, cabin door unlatch, and land straight ahead; it assumes time to secure the fuel and ignition systems before touchdown (172S POH sec 3). A pilot might turn back only if certain the airplane can reach the field from its current position and the pilot has trained and practiced the turn back maneuver, practicing turns in both directions at a safe altitude in the make and model flown with an authorized flight instructor; a turn back at low altitude presents an unacceptable risk for student pilots, low-time pilots and untrained pilots (AFH ch 18).
posts.credits: 3D model: “Cessna172” by KOG_THORNS (sketchfab.com), CC BY 4.0, modified.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: If the engine quits 400 feet above the ground just after takeoff, the runway behind you is the hardest place to reach. In this example, a gentle turn back needs about 225 degrees and more than twice your height, and a steep one can stall.
Lower the nose right away to hold the engine-failure speed, 70 knots in a 172S with the flaps up. Pick a field ahead, keep the turns small and land straight ahead, slow and under control.

article.heading: Why turning back is more than 180 degrees
paragraphs: A turn has width. Even at a slow 65 knots, a standard-rate turn, 3 degrees a second, has a radius of about 2,100 feet.

So a 180-degree turn leaves you about 4,200 feet to one side of the runway. In this no-wind example, you need about another 45 degrees just to point back at it, a total of about 225 degrees. Reaching the runway and lining up take more.

figure.caption: The dashed line across the circle is the turn's width. After 180 degrees you are off to the side, so in this example pointing back takes about 225 degrees.
figure.alt: An aerial view of farmland with an orange turn arc and dashed lines back toward the runway, labeled 225 degrees.

article.heading: Why a gentle turn costs too much height
paragraphs: At the standard rate, 180 degrees takes a minute and 225 degrees takes 75 seconds. Add about 4 seconds to react, and you are gliding for 79 seconds.

A 172S glides about 10 feet forward for every foot it comes down. At 70 knots that is about 700 feet a minute, so 79 seconds of gliding costs over 900 feet. That is more than twice the 400 feet you had.
That is a straight-glide figure. A banked glide sinks faster, and the glide to the runway after the turn needs more height still.

figure.caption: The white bar is the 400 feet the airplane had. The orange bar is the height a gentle turn back uses at that sink rate, over twice as much.
figure.alt: A low view over farmland with a 400 FT marker beside a much taller orange marker labeled Over 2 times, and a red X where a sloping glide path meets the ground.

article.heading: Why a steep turn back can stall
paragraphs: So a turn back has to be steep to be quick.

Banking tilts the wing's lift, so a turn needs more lift, and the stall speed rises, as the table shows for a 172S. Held level at 60 degrees of bank, the wing carries twice the airplane's weight, which raises the stall speed about 41 percent. That puts it at 68 knots, just 2 knots under the 70-knot engine-failure speed.

With your eyes on the runway, it is easy to pull back on the control wheel to tighten the turn and keep the nose up. That can bring an accelerated stall, when the wing meets the air at too great an angle under the turn's extra load. One wing may drop.

table.caption: Cessna 172S stall speeds at 2,550 lb, power off, flaps up, in a level coordinated turn

figure.caption: At 2,550 pounds with the flaps up, this 172S stalls at about 68 knots in a level 60-degree bank. It is flying at 70.
figure.alt: A Cessna 172 in a steep bank against the sky, marked 60 degrees, beside a card reading Stall 68 kt, your speed 70 kt.

article.heading: What to fly instead
paragraphs: Lower the nose at once. Hold the engine-failure speed, 70 knots with the flaps up or 65 with them down, until the flare. That is the raise of the nose just before touchdown.
Plan the landing straight ahead, with only small changes in direction to miss obstacles.

If there is time while you keep flying, pull the mixture to idle cutoff, close the fuel shutoff valve and switch off the ignition. Set the flaps, then turn off the master switch, since the flaps need its power, and unlatch the door. Touch down under control at the slowest speed you can.

figure.caption: Fly first. Nose down to the engine-failure speed, a field ahead with small turns, then straight ahead, slow and in control.
figure.alt: A Cessna 172 gliding low over a field below a card reading 172S, nose down, 70 kt, flaps up; field ahead, small turns; straight ahead, slow, in control.

article.heading: Three mistakes after an engine failure on takeoff
paragraphs: Lower the nose first, before anything else. It keeps the airspeed you need to glide and stay clear of the stall.

At the first stall warning in a turn, ease the back pressure until the warning stops, then roll toward wings level. Less load on the wing lowers the stall speed. A stall this close to the ground can drop a wing. With the nose swinging sideways, it can become a spin, with no height left to recover.

Brief your engine-failure plan before every takeoff, and leave the turn back to pilots who have practiced it. They have practiced it at a safe altitude with an instructor, in that make and model. Even they turn back only when certain of making the runway.

figure.caption: Pulling harder during a turn can stall the wing, and red marks the stalled wing.
figure.alt: A see-through Cessna 172 banked steeply over farmland and a river, with red wing surfaces and a label reading Stalled.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. When the engine quits at 400 feet just after takeoff, what is your very first action?
2. Why doesn't a 180-degree turn leave you pointing at the runway?
3. Using the table, how far is 70 knots above the stall speed in a 60-degree bank?
4. Is it fine to make a small turn toward a good field just left of your nose?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Lower the nose to the engine-failure speed, 70 knots indicated with the flaps up.
2. The turn carries you off to one side, about 4,200 feet at 65 knots, so in this example pointing back takes about 225 degrees.
3. About 2 knots, which is almost no margin.
4. Yes. Small changes in direction to reach a field or miss obstacles are part of landing straight ahead.

posts.title: The thunderstorm life cycle, explained
posts.headline: A towering cumulus can reach the mature stage, a thunderstorm at its most violent, in about 15 minutes.
posts.alt: Cover slide titled Thunderstorm life cycle. A mature thunderstorm with a broad flat anvil towers over a small rural airfield at dusk, rain falling from its base in the distance, with the house Cessna 172 parked on the ramp in the foreground, chocked and tied down. Text: A towering cumulus can reach the mature stage, a thunderstorm at its most violent, in about 15 minutes.
caption: That towering cumulus near your route can be a mature thunderstorm, at its most violent, in about 15 minutes.

One cell typically lasts about 30 minutes, but almost every storm is multicell, with new cells forming as long as the ingredients last. And data-linked radar can be 15 to 20 minutes older than the time it shows. That's long enough for a new cell to reach the mature stage. Swipe through the three stages, what a mature storm throws at you and how far to stay away. Then send it to a pilot you fly with.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
posts.related_text: A thunderstorm is a local storm, invariably produced by a cumulonimbus cloud, and always accompanied by lightning and thunder, usually with strong gusts of wind, heavy rain, and sometimes hail. Thunderstorm cell formation needs three ingredients: sufficient water vapor, unstable air, and a lifting mechanism. Lifting mechanisms include converging winds around surface lows and troughs, fronts, upslope flow, drylines, outflow boundaries generated by prior storms, and local winds, such as sea breeze, lake breeze, land breeze, and valley breeze circulations. A conditionally unstable air mass needs a lifting mechanism strong enough to release the instability. A rising convective current continues upward until it reaches a level where its temperature cools to the same as that of the surrounding air; if it cools to saturation, a cumuliform cloud forms. A thunderstorm cell undergoes three distinct stages during its life cycle: towering cumulus (also called the cumulus stage), mature, and dissipating. The total life cycle is typically about 30 minutes. The distinguishing feature of the towering cumulus stage is a strong convective updraft, a bubble of warm, rising air concentrated near the top of the cloud, and updraft speeds can exceed 3,000 fpm. In this stage, continuous, strong updrafts prohibit moisture from falling. Within approximately 15 minutes of the cumulus stage beginning, the thunderstorm reaches the mature stage, which is the most violent time period of the thunderstorm's life cycle. The cell transitions to the mature stage when precipitation reaches the surface. Precipitation descends through the cloud and drags the adjacent air downward, creating a strong downdraft alongside the updraft. In the mature stage, the downdraft spreads out along the surface, well in advance of the parent thunderstorm cell, as a mass of cool, gusty air, and its arc-shaped leading edge is called a gust front. Gust fronts often move far ahead (up to 15 mi) of associated precipitation and cause a rapid and sometimes drastic change in surface wind ahead of an approaching storm. Cumulonimbus tops frequently penetrate into the lower stratosphere as an overshooting top, where strong winds aloft distort the cloud top into an anvil shape. Weather hazards reach peak intensity toward the end of the mature stage. The dissipating stage is marked by a strong downdraft embedded within the area of precipitation. Subsiding air replaces the updraft throughout the cloud, cutting off its supply of moisture; precipitation tapers off and ends, and the cloud gradually vaporizes from below, leaving only a remnant anvil cloud. Single-cell thunderstorms are rare; almost all thunderstorms are multicell. In an organized multicell cluster, as the first cell matures it is carried downwind and a new cell forms upwind to take its place, and a multicell cluster may have a lifetime of several hours (or more). New cells will continue to form as long as the three necessary ingredients exist. Uplift along the gust front may trigger the formation of new cells, sometimes well ahead of the parent cell. Turbulence is present in all thunderstorms, and severe or extreme turbulence is common. Outside the cloud, shear turbulence has been encountered several thousand feet above and up to 20 mi laterally from a severe storm; additionally, clear-air turbulence (CAT) may be encountered 20 or more miles from the anvil cloud edge. Hail may be encountered in clear air several miles from the thunderstorm, and hailstones 0.75 in in diameter and larger can cause significant damage to aircraft. Rain at the surface does not mean the absence of hail aloft, and pilots should anticipate possible hail with any thunderstorm, especially beneath the anvil of a large cumulonimbus. Every thunderstorm produces lightning and thunder by definition. Lightning can puncture the skin of an aircraft and damage communications and electronic navigational equipment, and nearby lightning can blind the pilot, rendering the pilot momentarily unable to navigate either by instrument or by visual reference. Thunderstorms produce abundant supercooled liquid water above the freezing level, and the abundance of supercooled water makes clear icing very rapid between 0°C and -15°C. Thunderstorm icing can be extremely hazardous. A microburst is a small-scale, intense downdraft that spreads outward when it reaches the surface. It has a lifespan of about 5-15 minutes, during which it can produce downdrafts of up to 6,000 fpm. Avoiding thunderstorms is the best policy. Avoid by at least 20 miles any thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo, especially under the anvil of a large cumulonimbus. Don't land or take off in the face of an approaching thunderstorm: a sudden gust front of low level turbulence could cause loss of control. Don't attempt to fly under a thunderstorm even if you can see through to the other side, and don't attempt to fly under the anvil of a thunderstorm, where there is a potential for severe and extreme clear air turbulence. If unable to navigate around an area of thunderstorms, divert and wait out the thunderstorms on the ground. If flying around a thunderstorm is not an option, stay on the ground until it passes. Never regard any thunderstorm lightly. All thunderstorms have conditions that are hazards to aviation; while not every thunderstorm contains all hazards, it is not possible to visually determine which hazards a thunderstorm contains, and the visual appearance is not a reliable indicator of the turbulence inside a thunderstorm. Data-linked NEXRAD mosaic imagery shows where the weather was, not where the weather is; the weather conditions depicted may be 15 to 20 minutes older than indicated on the display. A good rule of thumb is to circumnavigate thunderstorms identified as severe or giving an extreme radar echo by at least 20 nautical miles (NM), since hail may fall for miles outside of the clouds. If flying around a thunderstorm is not an option, stay on the ground until it passes. Air mass thunderstorms occur at random in unstable air, last for only an hour or two, and are generally a result of surface heating; steady-state thunderstorms are associated with weather systems, where fronts, converging winds, and troughs aloft force upward motion, spawning storms that often form into squall lines. Even a single-cell (ordinary) thunderstorm may be severe and produce hail and microburst winds, and all thunderstorms are hazardous to aircraft. It is impossible to fly over thunderstorms in light aircraft: severe thunderstorms can punch through the tropopause and reach 50,000 to 60,000 feet depending on latitude. A typical microburst has a horizontal diameter of less than 2.5 mi and a nominal depth of 1,000 ft, and it can produce increasing headwind and headwind losses of 30-90 kt. Avoid by at least 20 mi any thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense, heavy, or extreme radar echo; such echoes should be separated by at least 40 mi before flying between echoes. Regard as extremely hazardous any thunderstorm with tops 35,000 ft or higher, whether the top is visually sighted or determined by radar. Supercooled water can exist at temperatures as cold as -40°C in the presence of vigorous upward vertical motion, such as in a thunderstorm updraft; supercooled water freezes on impact with an aircraft. The strongest turbulence within the cloud occurs between updrafts and downdrafts. If unable to avoid penetrating a thunderstorm, establish power settings for the turbulence penetration airspeed recommended in the aircraft manual before entering and don't change them inside; maintain a constant attitude and allow the altitude and airspeed to fluctuate, because maneuvering to hold a constant altitude greatly increases stress on the aircraft. In the dissipating stage, compression warms the subsiding air and the relative humidity drops, and the convective cloud gradually vaporizes from below. Don't use data-linked NEXRAD mosaic imagery as the sole means for negotiating a path through a thunderstorm area; do use it for route selection to avoid thunderstorms entirely. Don't attempt to fly under a thunderstorm: turbulence and wind shear under the storm could be hazardous.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 12

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Every thunderstorm cell goes through three stages. As a towering cumulus, it grows on a strong updraft. It turns mature when its rain reaches the ground, and it dies once sinking air has taken over.

Keep at least 20 miles from any thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo. A good rule of thumb is 20 nautical miles, since hail may fall for miles outside the cloud. If you can't get around the storms, divert and wait them out on the ground.

article.heading: What starts a cell and builds it
paragraphs: A storm needs enough water vapor, unstable air and a push to lift it. The push can be a front, wind up a slope, converging winds, a sea or lake breeze, or cool air spreading from an older storm. Storms that pop up at random in unstable air are generally a result of surface heating.
Pushed hard enough, unstable air keeps rising until it is no warmer than the air around it. If it cools to saturation on the way, a cumulus cloud forms.
In the towering cumulus stage, the updraft is a warm bubble near the cloud's top that can exceed 3,000 feet per minute (fpm). It is strong enough to hold the rain up.

figure.caption: A towering cumulus: air pushed up the slope rises into the cloud, and the updraft holds the rain up.
figure.alt: A tall cumulus tower over a wooded ridge with no rain under its flat base. Blue arrows show air rising up the slope into the base and on up through the tower.

article.heading: How a cell matures, dies and is replaced
paragraphs: Within about 15 minutes, the drops grow too heavy for the updraft to hold, and their fall brings on the mature stage. The rain drags air down with it, making a downdraft beside the updraft. The strongest turbulence in the cloud lies between the two.

At the ground, the downdraft spreads well ahead of the cell as cool, gusty air. Its curved leading edge is the gust front. Up high, strong winds flatten the top into an anvil, and the hazards peak late in this stage.

In the dissipating stage, sinking air fills the cloud and cuts off its moisture supply. The downdraft stays strong in the rain as the rain tapers off. Warmed as it sinks, the air dries the cloud from below until only the old anvil is left.

From first tower to old anvil typically takes about 30 minutes, but single-cell storms are rare. In an organized cluster, new cells form upwind as old ones drift downwind, or rise on the lift along a gust front. Such a cluster can last several hours.

figure.caption: A dying cell sinks and evaporates under its old anvil while a new tower builds beside it.
figure.alt: An old storm's fraying anvil with thin wisps and virga under it and blue arrows sinking to the ground, and beside it a young cumulus tower, labelled new cell, with a blue arrow rising through it.

article.heading: What a mature storm throws at you
paragraphs: Not every storm holds every hazard in the table, and none shows from outside which it holds. Over the top is no escape in a light airplane: severe storms can reach 50,000 to 60,000 feet.

Icing builds fast because the updraft carries water that is still liquid above the freezing level, and it freezes on impact. Caught inside, keep the power set for the manual's turbulence penetration airspeed and hold a constant attitude. Let altitude and airspeed vary.

table.caption: What each hazard of a mature storm does, and where it can reach you.
rows: In every thunderstorm, often severe or extreme
Several thousand feet above and up to 20 mi beside a severe storm, and in clear air 20 mi or more from the anvil edge
Stones 0.75 in and larger cause significant damage
Aloft even when only rain reaches the ground, and in clear air several miles out, especially under the anvil
Can puncture the skin, damage radios and navigation equipment, and blind you for a moment
Clear ice, very rapid between 0°C and -15°C
Above the freezing level, and in the updraft as cold as -40°C
A rapid, sometimes drastic change in the surface wind
Up to 15 mi ahead of the rain
A downdraft of up to 6,000 fpm that spreads out at the ground, with headwind losses of 30-90 kt
Typically less than 2.5 mi across, for about 5-15 minutes

figure.caption: The mature stage: rain drags air down beside the updraft, and the cool outflow spreads along the ground, led by its gust front.
figure.alt: A mature thunderstorm with a flat anvil top and a rain shaft under one side. Blue arrows show the updraft, the downdraft in the rain and the outflow along the ground, its leading edge labelled gust front.

article.heading: Four mistakes near a thunderstorm
paragraphs: Stay out from under a storm and its anvil, even when you can see daylight beyond. Turbulence and wind shear make the air under the storm hazardous. Under the anvil, severe and extreme turbulence can strike in clear air.
Don't take off or land in front of an approaching storm. Its gust front arrives first, and a sudden burst of low-level turbulence can cost you control.

Plan your route around storms with the datalink radar picture, never using it alone to thread between cells. It can lag the age it shows by 15 to 20 minutes. Never fly between severe or intense echoes less than 40 miles apart.
Treat every thunderstorm as dangerous, even when its radar echo is light. A lone cell can still be severe, with hail and microburst winds.

figure.caption: Not to scale: at least 20 miles from a severe storm, and never under it or its anvil.
figure.alt: A storm on the right with its anvil spreading left, the air around it hatched red as off limits, an amber line at least 20 miles beyond the anvil's edge, and a Cessna 172 flying away beyond the line.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. A cumulus ahead has a hard, growing top and no rain under its base. Which stage is it in, and what holds the rain up?
2. You're holding short when the windsock swings and a cool, gusty wind arrives, with the rain still miles off. What reached you, and should you take off?
3. The cell you've watched has stopped raining and is breaking up, while new towers build beside it. Is the area about to clear?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. The towering cumulus stage. Its strong updraft keeps the drops from falling.
2. A gust front, and no. Wait on the ground until the storm passes, because its turbulence can cost you control.
3. No. It's a multicell storm, and those new towers are new cells that will mature in turn.

posts.title: How full fuel tanks can still starve the engine
posts.headline: A 172 with both tanks full can still starve its engine. A clear vent, the fuel selector on BOTH for takeoff and landing, and water-free fuel samples keep it fed.
posts.alt: A see-through Cessna 172 over farmland with both wing tanks in blue, a red label Starving at the engine and the chip Both tanks full.
posts.related_text: The Cessna 172P's standard fuel system has two removable aluminum tanks, one in each wing, 21.5 US gallons each, 43 total, 40 usable, and fuel flows by gravity from the two wing tanks to a four-position selector valve and through a strainer to the carburetor (172P POH sec 2 and 7). Fuel system venting is essential to system operation: blockage of the system results in decreasing fuel flow and eventual engine stoppage (172P POH sec 7); if the fuel vent is stopped with the engine running, the engine can lose power and eventually stop from fuel starvation (Cessna 172 Service Manual sec 12). The tanks are vented by an overboard vent line in the left tank, which protrudes from the bottom surface of the left wing near the wing strut, an interconnecting line that joins the right tank's air space to the left tank's, and a vented right filler cap (172P POH sec 7; Cessna 172 Service Manual sec 12); the vent's opening is checked on the walkaround. Each tank feeds through a screened outlet at its inboard end, nearest the cabin; when the tanks are 1/4 full or less, prolonged uncoordinated flight such as slips or skids can uncover the fuel tank outlets (172P POH sec 7). Takeoff and landing are made with the fuel selector valve on BOTH, the setting for takeoff, climb, landing and maneuvers that involve prolonged slips or skids (172P POH sec 2 and 7); on BOTH, the other tank keeps feeding; with one tank 1/4 full or less selected, or a tank run dry, slips and skids are kept to 30 seconds or less (172P POH sec 2 fuel limitations and sec 7 note). The selector valve sits beneath the floorboard; inside, a rotor with drilled passages lines up with the left inlet, both inlets, the right inlet or neither (OFF), with a spring-loaded seal at each tank's inlet (Cessna 172 Service Manual sec 12). From the selector the fuel goes to the fuel strainer at the firewall, then to the carburetor; the strainer's screen catches sediment, and water, being heavier than fuel, settles in the bottom of the strainer; water also settles in each tank's sump, the tank's low point (172P POH sec 7; Cessna 172 Service Manual sec 12; PHAK ch 7); water that reaches the carburetor can stop the engine (PHAK ch 7). Before the first flight of the day and after each refueling, fuel is drained from each tank sump into the sampler cup to check for water, sediment and the proper grade, whose color shows it (100LL blue, 100 green), and the strainer drain knob is pulled for about four seconds to clear the strainer of water and sediment, then checked closed (172P POH sec 2 and 4); if water is found, draining continues until no more shows (PHAK ch 7).

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Fuel can only leave a tank as fast as air gets in to take its place. So in a 172 with both tanks full, a blocked vent can still starve the engine. A slip on a low tank, or water in the fuel, can do the same.

Check the fuel vent tube under the left wing on every walkaround, and take off and land with the fuel selector on BOTH. Before the day's first flight and after refueling, drain each tank's sump, its lowest point, and the strainer, a filter by the engine.

article.heading: How the tanks breathe
paragraphs: In the carbureted 172P, gravity does the work, with no fuel pump. Other 172 models differ, so check your own airplane's handbook. Fuel runs from an aluminum tank in each wing down to the carburetor, which mixes it with air for the cylinders. On the way it passes the selector valve, which you set to LEFT, RIGHT, BOTH or OFF, then the strainer.

As fuel leaves a tank, air has to come in behind it. If it can't, the pressure above the fuel drops, and that low pressure holds the fuel back against gravity. The tanks breathe through a vent tube under the left wing, near the strut that braces it.
A crossover line links the two tanks' air spaces, so the right tank breathes through the same tube. The right filler cap has a small safety vent too, but the tube is the main air inlet.
Block the vent tube and the flow can fade. The engine loses power and can stop from fuel starvation, with both tanks still full.

figure.caption: Thin blue lines carry fuel from both tanks to the engine, and the white line across the cabin links their air spaces. The red ring marks the blocked vent tube.
figure.alt: A see-through Cessna 172 from above with its wing tanks in blue and a red label Blocked at the vent tube under the left wing.

article.heading: Why you take off and land on BOTH
paragraphs: The selector valve sits under the floor. Inside, a rotor, a disc the handle turns, lines up its drilled passages for each setting.

Each tank feeds from a screened outlet at its inboard end, the end nearest the cabin. A slip or skid is flight with the ball in the turn coordinator off center, and the fuel shifts the same way the ball does. At a quarter tank or less, a long one can slide one tank's fuel toward its tip, away from its outlet.

Both outlets sit near the cabin, so the same shift pushes the other tank's fuel onto its outlet. On BOTH, that tank keeps feeding, one reason you take off and land there. On LEFT or RIGHT with that tank at a quarter or less, keep any slip or skid to 30 seconds or less. The same limit applies whenever either tank is dry, even on BOTH.

figure.caption: The selector is on LEFT and that tank is low. In a slip, its fuel has run out toward the wingtip, leaving the outlet by the cabin uncovered.
figure.alt: A see-through Cessna 172 with the fuel selector dial on LEFT and a red label Outlet uncovered at the left tank's inboard end, its fuel out toward the tip.

article.heading: Where water hides, and how you drain it
paragraphs: From the selector, fuel passes the strainer on the firewall, the metal wall between the engine and the cabin. Its screen catches dirt. Water is heavier than fuel, so it sinks to the bottom of the strainer's bowl.
Water that reaches the carburetor can stop the engine. Water from condensation also settles in each tank's sump.

Drain each sump into the sampler cup. Look for the right color for the grade, 100LL blue or 100 green, with no water and no dirt. Water can show as clear beads or a clear layer at the bottom of the cup, or as cloudy fuel. Then pull the strainer drain for about four seconds, and check that it's closed.

figure.caption: The fuel strainer on the firewall, cut away. Dirt clings to its screen, and water pools at the bottom of the bowl.
figure.alt: A cutaway of a fuel strainer's bowl full of blue fuel, with dark bits of dirt on its screen and a bead of water at the bottom labeled Water.

article.heading: Three fuel mistakes to avoid
paragraphs: Look at the vent tube's opening under the left wing on every walkaround.
Take off and land on BOTH, not on LEFT or RIGHT. If you ran on one tank in cruise, set BOTH again before you land.
Keep draining while the cup shows water. More can sit behind the first sample, so drain the strainer, the sumps and the selector valve's drain until it's gone.

figure.caption: Pushing the sampler cup's pin into the sump drain catches fuel from the bottom of the tank.
figure.alt: A see-through wing from below with a sampler cup, part full of blue fuel, under the sump drain, labeled Sampler cup.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Why can a 172 with both tanks full still lose power from fuel starvation?
2. What makes BOTH the right setting for takeoff and landing?
3. With the selector on LEFT and that tank a quarter full, how long may a slip or skid last?
4. What do you do when the first sample from a sump shows water?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. A blocked vent stops air from replacing the fuel, so the flow fades and the engine can stop.
2. A long slip with a low tank can uncover its outlet, and on BOTH the other tank keeps feeding.
3. 30 seconds at most.
4. Keep draining until no water shows, since more may be in the tank.

posts.title: How ice closes the coffin corner
posts.headline: High enough, a jet's low-speed buffet and high-speed Mach buffet come within a few knots of each other. Ice raises the slow edge, so the two edges meet lower.
posts.alt: A business jet above the clouds beside an airspeed tape under a Coffin corner chip, its red stall and Mach buffet bands nearly meeting, with an ice label at its foot.
posts.related_text: At a given indicated (calibrated) airspeed the true airspeed is higher the higher you fly, because the thinner air requires a faster true airspeed to give the same pitot pressure for the same KCAS (PHAK ch 5, Mach Buffet Boundaries); at 41,000 feet in the standard atmosphere, 200 knots calibrated is about Mach 0.687, about 394 knots true (computed). The speed of sound varies with temperature: under standard conditions of 15 degrees C it is 661 knots at sea level, and at 40,000 feet, where the temperature is minus 55 degrees C, it decreases to 574 knots (PHAK ch 5). The Mach number is the ratio of the true airspeed to the speed of sound at flight conditions; up high the airplane's speed limit is a Mach number (MMO), and in a constant Mach number climb the indicated airspeed falls off (PHAK ch 5; AC 61-107B). Critical Mach is the speed at which the airflow over any part of the aircraft first reaches Mach 1.0 (PHAK ch 5); Mach buffet arises when airflow separates on the upper surface of a wing behind a shock wave, and the shock wave strength increases as the local airflow speed ahead of it increases (AFH ch 16). At low-speed cruise the flow has a greater turn to make to follow the wing's upper surface; the air speeds up to do that and may exceed Mach 1 over the upper surface, because the true airspeed is still high, giving low-speed Mach buffet, a prestall buffet, which comes at a higher indicated airspeed as altitude increases (AFH ch 16; PHAK ch 5). If an airplane flew any faster it would exceed MMO, leading to high-speed Mach buffet; any slower and it would need an angle of attack leading to low-speed Mach buffet; this region is known as coffin corner (AFH ch 16), only a few knots below the onset of Mach buffet and a like speed above stall buffet (AWH ch 19). The aerodynamic ceiling, where the edges meet, is higher than the altitude limit in the AFM (AC 61-107B); increasing either gross weight or load factor increases the low-speed buffet speed and decreases the Mach buffet speed, so a bank or turbulence narrows the gap and cruise altitude and speed are chosen to leave margin for maneuvering and turbulence (AC 61-107B). Between 0 and minus 10 degrees C clouds consist mainly of supercooled water droplets, between minus 10 and minus 20 degrees C liquid droplets coexist with ice crystals, and below minus 20 degrees C clouds are generally all ice crystals (AWH ch 20); a jet meets the icing range climbing or descending through cloud, and at 40,000 feet, about minus 55 degrees C (PHAK ch 5), ice picked up on the climb does not melt off. Ice no thicker or rougher than a piece of coarse sandpaper can reduce lift by 30 percent and increase drag up to 40 percent (AWH ch 20); a reduction of the maximum lift coefficient by 30 percent is not unusual (AC 91-74B); since lift grows with the square of airspeed, stall speed varies as one over the square root of the maximum lift coefficient, and 1 divided by the square root of 0.70 is about 1.2, a stall speed about 20 percent higher (computed). A wing contaminated with ice ordinarily stalls at a lower angle of attack, and thus at a higher airspeed, and the stall may occur before stall warning devices activate (AC 91-74B). At high altitudes little excess thrust may be available (AC 61-107B); ice no thicker or rougher than coarse sandpaper can increase drag up to 40 percent and larger accretions far more (AWH ch 20; AC 91-74B), and in many icing events airspeed decreased from cruise to stall in less than 3 minutes (AC 91-74B). Anti-icing systems are to be activated prior to entering icing conditions, while deicing systems are normally activated at the first sign of ice accretion, as the AFM or POH directs; any remaining ice increases the stall speed, so the extra margin the flight manual gives is flown with ice on board, and the pilot exits the icing conditions (AC 91-74B). Anti-ice equipment keeps ice from forming; de-ice equipment removes ice that has formed (AC 91-74B). If the airspeed decays at high altitude, select maximum continuous thrust (MCT) to increase available thrust and stop the decay; if the airspeed still deteriorates, the only option is to descend, and lower down the speed window is wider (AC 61-107B); if the wing stalls or a stall is impending at the slow edge, reducing the angle of attack (nose down) is the priority, until the impending stall indications are eliminated, then thrust as needed and a gentle return to the desired flight path to avoid a secondary stall; at high altitude an extended nose-down recovery may be needed, and the recovery will likely require losing several thousand feet (AC 120-109A); pilots should understand the cause of any buffet in order to respond appropriately, since a buffet at the fast edge is Mach buffet (AFH ch 16). At the slow edge the stall recovery template starts with disconnecting the autopilot and autothrottle, then reducing the angle of attack and rolling the wings level (AC 120-109A); in icing conditions, buffet or shudder is treated as an imminent wing stall (AC 91-74B), and Mach buffet may come from two conditions in cruise, high speed (the fast edge) and low speed (the slow edge) (AFH ch 16); if the speed cannot be held, the pilot descends, declaring an emergency if necessary rather than delaying the recovery for an ATC clearance (AC 120-109A).

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 5

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Climb a jet high enough and its speed limits close in. A few knots slower and the wing shakes, or buffets, on its way to a stall. A few knots faster and shock waves cause high-speed Mach buffet.
That narrow speed window is the coffin corner. Ice raises the slow edge, so the window shuts at a lower altitude and with less warning.

article.heading: Why speed works differently up high
paragraphs: Thin air pushes less on the airspeed indicator. So your indicated airspeed, the dial's reading, sits far below your true airspeed, your speed through the air. At 41,000 feet on a standard day, 200 knots indicated is almost 400 knots true.
The fast edge depends on how close you are to the speed of sound. So up high your limit is a Mach number, your true airspeed as a fraction of the speed of sound.
Hold a constant Mach number in a climb, and the fast edge falls to a lower indicated airspeed.

table.caption: Sound travels slower in colder air (standard day)

figure.caption: Left, the dial's reading. Right, the true airspeed. The bar, not to scale, sets that speed against the speed of sound.
figure.alt: A business jet above the clouds with two readouts, 200 kt indicated and about 400 kt true, over a bar marked Sound speed.

article.heading: The fast edge, high-speed Mach buffet
paragraphs: The air flowing over the top of the wing moves faster than the airplane. Speed up, and that air reaches the speed of sound first. The airplane's Mach number at that moment is its critical Mach number.
Past it, a shock wave forms on the upper surface, a thin line where the air suddenly slows. As the shock grows, the airflow behind it breaks away and the wing shakes.

figure.caption: Over the wing's top, the air goes faster than sound (blue). A shock wave stands at the back of that region, and behind it the flow separates (red).
figure.alt: A wing section on a dark grid with a blue region over its top labeled Supersonic, a line labeled Shock wave and a red mark behind it labeled Separated flow.

article.heading: The slow edge, and where they meet
paragraphs: Slow down, and the wing needs a higher angle of attack, the angle between the wing and the oncoming air, to keep its lift. The air then has a sharper turn to make over the top, so it speeds up more.

Lower down, a wing stalls at about the same indicated airspeed at any height. Up high, true airspeed stays high even at a slow indicated airspeed, so that air can pass Mach 1. The wing then buffets before it stalls, at a higher indicated airspeed the higher you climb.
Climb on and the edges close in until a few knots separate them, the coffin corner.

The aerodynamic ceiling, where the edges meet, comes lower as weight rises. A bank or a bump of turbulence loads the wing and narrows the gap. So cruise where your flight manual's buffet data for your weight leaves room to maneuver.

figure.caption: Altitude against indicated airspeed, not to scale. The two edges meet at the top, the coffin corner, with only a narrow gap below it around the jet (white dot).
figure.alt: A graph of altitude against indicated airspeed, not to scale, with two red curves meeting at the top under a Coffin corner chip, a label Narrow gap at the apex and a white dot inside.

article.heading: What ice does to the window
paragraphs: A jet picks up most of its ice climbing or descending through cloud between 0 °C and -20 °C. At cruise altitude it is far below freezing, so that ice stays on.
Even a thin layer as rough as coarse sandpaper can cut the wing's maximum lift by as much as 30 percent. Lift grows with the square of airspeed, so the stall speed can rise by about 20 percent.
The slow edge jumps at every altitude, and the corner moves lower. An iced wing can also stall at a lower angle of attack, before a stall warning set for a clean wing sounds.

Thin, rough ice can add up to 40 percent more drag, and engines make far less thrust in thin air. Hold altitude once drag passes the thrust, even on the autopilot, and the speed bleeds away. In many icing events, cruise turned to stall in under 3 minutes.

figure.caption: The violet curve is the iced slow edge. The red mark is a speed that was safe on a clean wing and is now a stall.
figure.alt: The same altitude and indicated airspeed graph with a violet curve inside the red ones, a red mark labeled Stall and a label Corner drops.

article.heading: Four mistakes near the coffin corner
paragraphs: Turn on anti-ice, which keeps ice from forming, before you enter icing. De-ice systems, which remove ice that has formed, are normally used at the first sign of ice.

Ask air traffic control for a lower altitude while ice is still on the wing, since the clean-wing margins no longer apply. Lower down, keep the extra speed margin your jet's ice speeds call for. If the speed keeps decaying at maximum continuous thrust, the most thrust allowed with no time limit, descend at once. Then tell ATC, declaring an emergency rather than waiting for a clearance.

Treat any buffet or shudder in icing conditions as a stall about to happen. Outside icing, the trend is a clue to the edge. Speed decaying into a buffet points to the slow edge, and Mach rising into it points to the fast edge.

If the wing stalls or is about to, disconnect the autopilot and autothrottle, the automatic throttle, while holding the attitude. Then lower the nose until the warning and buffet stop and the speed builds. Roll the wings level, set thrust as needed and retract any speed brakes. Return gently to level flight, below the Mach limit. Expect to lose several thousand feet.

figure.caption: The white dot is the jet after a descent. The white bracket under it is the room left between the iced slow edge (violet) and the fast edge.
figure.alt: A business jet above the clouds below an inset of the altitude and airspeed graph with a point lowered inside the curves and the label Descend: wider window.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. At 41,000 feet with 200 knots on the airspeed indicator, roughly how fast are you moving through the air?
2. Near the coffin corner, which edge are you at when a buffet comes as the airspeed trends down?
3. Why does ice picked up in cloud at -10 °C still matter once you reach cruise?
4. High up, with the airspeed still decaying at maximum continuous thrust, what do you do?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Almost 400 knots, about twice what the dial shows.
2. The slow edge, so recover as from a stall about to happen, then descend gently, below the Mach limit.
3. It won't melt off up there, so the stall speed stays high.
4. With the speed still decaying, descend at once and tell ATC, declaring an emergency rather than waiting for a clearance.

posts.title: What makes the left engine critical
posts.headline: On a twin whose propellers both turn clockwise, losing the left engine yaws the airplane hardest and takes the most rudder. That makes it the critical engine.
posts.alt: Two see-through twins over farmland, one above the other: the top one labeled Left engine out with its left engine outlined red, the bottom one labeled Right engine out with its right engine outlined red.
posts.related_text: The critical engine is the engine whose failure has the most adverse effect on directional control; on twins with each engine rotating in conventional, clockwise rotation as viewed from the pilot's seat, the critical engine is the left engine (AFH ch 13). Under power at positive angles of attack, as when slow and nose high, the descending propeller blade meets the air at a higher angle of attack and produces more thrust than the ascending blade (P-factor, asymmetric loading); with clockwise rotation as seen from the seat the descending blade is on the right side of each propeller disc, so the center of thrust moves to the right of each propeller's hub (PHAK ch 5; AFH ch 13). In a nose-high attitude the relative wind meets the disc from a little below its axis (the geometry is our inference, stated). The descending blade of the right engine is farther from the center of gravity than the descending blade of the left engine, so it has a longer moment arm; failure of the left engine leaves the most asymmetrical thrust and the most adverse yaw toward the dead engine, and with the right engine failed the left engine's thrust acts on a shorter arm, so there is less yaw to hold (AFH ch 13). Whichever engine fails, the pilot holds the airplane straight primarily with rudder pressure on the side of the airplane with the operating engine ('dead foot, dead engine'), with a small bank of up to 5 degrees toward the operating engine; with the left (critical) engine inoperative the yaw is greatest, so it takes more rudder than with the right engine inoperative (AFH ch 13). After an engine failure the pilot identifies the failed engine ('dead foot, dead engine') and verifies it by retarding that engine's throttle before feathering (AFH ch 13); if the yaw cannot be controlled with full rudder, reducing power on the operating engine and lowering the nose is the recovery (AFH ch 13). Prevention comes first: the airspeed must stay above VMC, and the pitch attitude for VYSE, the blue line, has to be lowered from that of VY (AFH ch 13); verification is that retarding the suspected engine's throttle brings no change in performance (AFH ch 13). As the airplane slows and control effectivity decays, the yawing tendency must be met with additional rudder pressure; the more rudder deflection it takes to hold the airplane straight, the higher the speed at which the rudder runs out of travel, so with the critical engine inoperative directional control is lost first, at the highest speed; VMC, marked with a red radial line on most airspeed indicators, is the minimum speed at which directional control can be maintained after the critical engine suddenly fails with the remaining engine at takeoff power, published for a maximum of 5 degrees of bank toward the operative engine (with the wings level it is significantly higher); and the AFM/POH-published VMC is determined with the critical engine inoperative (AFH ch 13). Many twins have a counter-rotating right engine; on the Piper PA-44-180 Seminole the left engine turns clockwise and the right engine counterclockwise as viewed from the cockpit, which puts each propeller's descending blade on the inboard side, gives balanced thrust and eliminates the critical engine factor: neither engine is worse to lose (AFH ch 13; Seminole POH 7.5, 7.7).

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 5

citations.ref: Piper PA-44-180 Seminole POH sec 7 engines and propellers
citations.title: Piper PA-44-180 Seminole Pilot's Operating Handbook

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: On most twins both propellers turn clockwise, seen from the pilot's seat. On those twins, losing the left engine is worse. Slow and nose high, each propeller pulls harder on its right side, an effect called P-factor.

So the right engine's pull sits farther from the airplane's balance point. Lose the left engine, and that pull swings the nose hardest. That makes the left engine the critical engine, and a twin's VMC, its minimum control speed, is set with it dead.

article.heading: What the critical engine is
paragraphs: The critical engine is the engine whose failure hurts directional control the most. Directional control means keeping the nose pointed where you want it.

With one engine dead, all the thrust pulls on one side. This one-sided pull is asymmetric thrust, and it yaws, or swings, the nose toward the dead engine. The question is which engine leaves the harder swing.

figure.caption: Left engine out. The yellow line is the right engine's thrust, and the bracket marks its longer arm, explained below. The violet arrow is the nose swinging left.
figure.alt: Top view of a see-through twin on a dark grid under the chip Left engine out, its red left engine labeled Critical engine, a bracket labeled Longer arm on the right side and a violet arrow at the nose pointing left.

article.heading: How P-factor moves each engine's thrust
paragraphs: Slow and nose high, each propeller's shaft points a little above the flight path. So the air reaches the propeller disc, the circle the blades sweep, from slightly below.

As the propeller turns clockwise, the blade on the right side moves down into that upward-slanting air. It meets the air at a bigger angle of attack, the angle between the blade and the oncoming air. The blade going up on the left meets it at a smaller one.

The descending blade takes the bigger bite and makes more thrust. So each engine's thrust shifts to the right of its hub. This is P-factor, and it is strongest slow and nose high, as right after takeoff.

figure.caption: Nose high, the propeller's axis (dashed line) points above the oncoming air, the relative wind (cyan). So that air reaches the propeller from slightly below.
figure.alt: A see-through twin from the side on a dark grid under the chip Nose high, with a dashed line labeled Prop axis tilted up and a cyan arrow labeled Relative wind meeting the propeller.

article.heading: Why the left engine's loss yaws harder
paragraphs: The arm is the sideways distance from the airplane's center of gravity, its balance point, to the line an engine's thrust acts along. With the thrust shifted right, the right engine's thrust moves outboard, away from the cabin, and the left engine's moves inboard, toward it. So the right engine's arm is longer.

Lose the left engine, and the right engine's thrust pulls on that longer arm. The pull is the same, but on a longer arm it turns the airplane harder, like a longer wrench. So the nose swings hardest toward the dead engine.
Lose the right engine instead, and the left engine's thrust works on a shorter arm, with a weaker swing.

table.caption: One engine out on a twin whose propellers both turn clockwise
rows: Right engine, on the longer arm
Left engine, on the shorter arm

figure.caption: Right engine out. The left engine's thrust (yellow) sits on the shorter arm, closer to the middle, so the swing toward the dead right engine (violet) is weaker.
figure.alt: Top view of a see-through twin under the chip Right engine out, its right engine red, a yellow thrust arrow on the left engine, a bracket labeled Shorter arm and a violet arrow pointing right.

article.heading: Why the critical engine sets VMC
paragraphs: Whichever engine fails, you hold the airplane straight mainly with rudder on the good engine's side, plus a small bank toward the good engine.
The rudder also weakens as the airplane slows. The more rudder the yaw takes, the sooner the rudder reaches its stop. With the critical engine dead, the rudder runs out first, at the highest speed.

VMC is the slowest speed at which you can keep directional control after the critical engine suddenly fails, with the good engine at takeoff power. Most twins mark it with a red radial line on the airspeed indicator.

That red line holds only for the conditions it was set under, including up to 5 degrees of bank toward the good engine. Lower the nose promptly to hold the blue line, the best climb speed on one engine. If full rudder can't stop the yaw, reduce power on the good engine and lower the nose further.

figure.caption: At the VMC mark, the left-engine-out bar reaches full rudder while the right-engine-out bar has rudder to spare. The green arrow is the rudder's push on the tail, which swings the nose back to the right.
figure.alt: Top view of a see-through twin under the chip Set with left engine out, with a panel of two green bars labeled Rudder needed, Left engine out and Right engine out against a Full rudder mark, an airspeed dial labeled VMC and a green arrow at the tail.

article.heading: Three mistakes about the critical engine
paragraphs: Stop the yaw with the rudder pedal on the good engine's side. The idle foot then points to the dead engine, which pilots remember as dead foot, dead engine. Close that engine's throttle before you shut anything down. If nothing changes, you found the dead engine. If the airplane sinks or the yaw changes, you closed the good one, so push that throttle back up.
Bank a few degrees toward the good engine rather than holding the wings level. With the wings level, the real VMC is much higher than the red line.

Check which way your twin's propellers turn. Some twins, such as the Piper Seminole, turn the right propeller counterclockwise. Each descending blade is then on the inboard side, so the arms match and there is no critical engine.

figure.caption: A Seminole-style twin with a counter-rotating right propeller. Both descending blades are inboard, the arms are equal, and no engine is critical.
figure.alt: Top view of a see-through twin under the chip Seminole-style twin, No critical engine, with a yellow thrust arrow on each engine set inboard of its hub and a bracket labeled Equal arms.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Slow and nose high, which side of a clockwise propeller's disc makes more thrust?
2. When two identical twins whose propellers both turn clockwise lose opposite engines at the same slow speed, which one needs more rudder?
3. When your left engine fails in the climb, which rudder pedal do you press?
4. Does a Seminole, with its right propeller turning counterclockwise, have a critical engine?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. The right side, where the descending blade meets the air at a bigger angle of attack.
2. The one that lost its left engine, because the right engine's thrust then sits on the longer arm and yaws it harder.
3. The right pedal, on the good engine's side, so the idle left foot matches the dead left engine.
4. No, because both descending blades are inboard and the arms match.

posts.title: How a constant-speed propeller holds its RPM
posts.headline: Flyweights, a spring and engine oil twist the blades to hold your RPM steady, until the blades run out of room.
posts.alt: A retractable-gear Cessna over farmland under the chip Constant speed and 2,500 RPM, with a manifold pressure gauge and a tachometer.
posts.related_text: The propeller control does not set a blade angle directly while the propeller is governing: the pilot controls the engine rpm indirectly by means of a propeller control connected to the propeller governor, and once a specific rpm is selected the governor automatically adjusts the propeller blade angle as necessary to maintain it; the governor is on the engine, geared to the engine crankshaft (AFH ch 12; PHAK ch 7). In the Cessna 172RG the control is a knob labeled PROP RPM, PUSH INCR (172RG POH 7-23); a blue, fluted knob is the standard configuration for the propeller control. The pitch of a fixed-pitch propeller is set by the manufacturer and cannot be changed, and its rpm is regulated by the throttle (PHAK ch 7); with the throttle left alone the propeller has a natural tendency to slow down as the aircraft climbs and to speed up as the aircraft dives, because the load on the engine varies (FAA-H-8083-32 ch 7). An aircraft with a constant-speed propeller has two controls: the throttle controls power output, indicated by the manifold pressure gauge, and the propeller control regulates engine rpm (PHAK ch 7); when the airplane is nosed up into a climb the governor decreases the blade angle just enough to keep the engine speed constant, and when it is nosed down into a dive the governor increases the blade angle (AFH ch 12); a low blade angle keeps the blade angle of attack small and efficient at low speed, and a higher blade angle suits the higher speed (AFH ch 12). 2,500 RPM is the 172RG's normal climb setting (172RG POH 4-9). As airspeed increases the load on the engine is lightened because of the small blade angle; the governor senses this and increases the blade angle (AFH ch 12). The 172RG's normal climb power is 25 inches of manifold pressure and 2,500 RPM (172RG POH 4-9). The governor is sensitive to small changes in engine rpm and changes the blade angle just enough to keep the engine speed constant (AFH ch 12); the reel's 2,630 and 2,390 RPM readings exaggerate the swing so it can be seen. Pushing the 172RG's propeller control in decreases blade pitch, giving a higher RPM (172RG POH 7-23). The propeller control sets the tension of the governor's speeder spring, which opposes two engine-driven flyweights flung outward as they turn; on speed, the force on the flyweights and the spring's tension are balanced; in an underspeed the flyweights tilt inward, and the pilot valve, forced down by the speeder spring, meters oil flow to decrease propeller pitch and raise engine rpm (FAA-H-8083-32 ch 7). In an overspeed, the centrifugal force on the flyweights is greater than the speeder spring force; the flyweights tilt outward and raise the pilot valve, which meters oil flow to increase propeller pitch and lower engine rpm until on speed (FAA-H-8083-32 ch 7); the governor controls engine oil, boosted to high pressure by the governing pump, to or from a piston in the propeller hub, and oil pressure on the piston twists the blades toward high pitch, low RPM (172RG POH 7-23); the oil reaches the hub through a hollow engine shaft (FAA-H-8083-32 ch 7); the constant-speed propellers on almost all single-engine airplanes are of the oil-pressure-to-increase-pitch design (AFH ch 13). When oil pressure to the piston in the propeller hub is relieved, centrifugal force, assisted by an internal spring, twists the blades toward low pitch, high RPM (172RG POH 7-23); the blades have an inherent centrifugal twisting moment that tends to flatten them toward low pitch (AFH ch 12); on speed, the pilot valve is neither directing oil to nor from the propeller's hydraulic cylinder, so the blade angle holds (FAA-H-8083-32 ch 7). Once the propeller blades reach their pitch-stop limit, the engine rpm increases or decreases with changes in airspeed and propeller load similar to a fixed-pitch propeller (AFH ch 12). The Cessna 172RG's McCauley two-blade constant-speed propeller runs from 12.0 degrees low pitch to 26.5 degrees high pitch at the 30-inch station, on an engine rated 180 BHP at 2,700 RPM (172RG POH 1-3), with the tachometer's red line at 2,700 RPM (172RG POH section 2). If a descent is too rapid, the maximum blade angle is not enough to hold the rpm constant and the rpm responds to any change in throttle setting (AFH ch 12). A combination of high manifold pressure and low rpm can induce damaging detonation, so when increasing power, increase the rpm first and then the manifold pressure, and when decreasing power, decrease the manifold pressure first and then the rpm; the cruise power charts in the AFM/POH give the approved combinations (AFH ch 12); for maximum takeoff power the propeller control is moved all the way forward to the low pitch, high rpm position (AFH ch 12); detonation is the uncontrolled, explosive burning of the fuel-air charge (PHAK ch 7).
