article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: With a constant-speed propeller, the throttle sets the power and the blue propeller knob sets the RPM. The knob doesn't set the blade angle directly. That is the angle each blade makes with the circle it spins in.

A governor on the engine sets it. It twists the blades steeper, a bigger bite of air each turn, or flatter, a smaller bite. So the RPM holds as you climb and descend, as long as the blades have room to twist.

article.heading: Why a fixed-pitch propeller's RPM wanders
paragraphs: A fixed-pitch propeller has one blade angle, or pitch, set by the manufacturer. That angle is most efficient at only one airspeed and RPM, and you control the RPM with the throttle alone.

Leave the throttle where it is and the RPM follows the airspeed. Climb and slow down, and the air meets the blades at a bigger angle of attack, the angle between blade and oncoming air. The heavier load drags the RPM down. Lower the nose and speed up, and the RPM rises.

figure.caption: The round dial shows a blade seen from its tip, with its path as a dashed line and the air it meets in blue. On a fixed-pitch propeller the blade angle, blade to path, never changes.
figure.alt: A Cessna in flight over farmland under the chip Fixed pitch, with a round dial showing a blade from its tip and a tachometer reading 2,500 RPM.

article.heading: How the governor holds the RPM
paragraphs: The governor sits on the engine, geared to the crankshaft. Inside it, two small flyweights spin with the engine, and the faster they spin, the harder they swing outward.
A speeder spring presses against them from the other side. The blue knob sets how hard that spring presses, and pushing the knob in squeezes it harder.

The flyweights and the spring position a small pilot valve between them. It sends engine oil to the propeller hub or lets oil drain from it. In the 172RG, as in most single-engine airplanes, oil in the hub pushes a piston that twists the blades to a bigger bite. When oil drains, the blades' own spin and a hub spring twist them flatter.
When the flyweights balance the spring, the propeller is on speed, at the RPM you set. The valve sits centered and the blade angle holds.
Push the knob in and the spring wins. Oil drains from the hub, the blades flatten and the RPM rises until the flyweights balance the stiffer spring. Pull the knob out and it all runs the other way.

figure.caption: Inside the governor, the blue speeder spring presses against the two flyweights. The blue line is the cable from the knob, and the yellow line carries oil to the hub.
figure.alt: A see-through propeller governor on the engine under the chip Push: RPM up, with a blue coil labeled Speeder spring, two weights labeled Flyweights, a yellow oil line and a tachometer reading 2,500 RPM.

article.heading: When the nose goes down and RPM rises
paragraphs: Lower the nose and the airplane speeds up. The faster air meets the blades at a smaller angle of attack, so they load the engine less. The propeller starts to spin faster than the RPM you set, which mechanics call an overspeed condition.
The flyweights swing outward and move the pilot valve. Engine oil, boosted by the governor's own pump, flows to the hub through the hollow engine shaft.
This incoming oil pushes the piston, which twists both blades steeper. The extra load slows the propeller, and the RPM settles back where you set it.

figure.caption: Nose down, the flyweights swing out and the governor's pump sends oil up the yellow line toward the hub. The picture exaggerates the rise to 2,630 RPM, which a working governor catches quickly.
figure.alt: A see-through governor with a label Pump at its base, arrows along a yellow line labeled Oil running up toward the propeller hub, and a tachometer reading 2,630 RPM.

article.heading: When the nose comes up and RPM falls
paragraphs: Raise the nose and the airplane slows. Now the slower air meets the blades at a bigger angle of attack, and the extra load slows the propeller below your RPM. That is an underspeed condition.
The flyweights fall inward, and the speeder spring pushes the pilot valve the other way. That opens a path for the oil to leave the hub.
Now the blades twist toward a smaller bite, pushing the piston back and the oil out. The lighter load lets the RPM climb back to the setting.

figure.caption: Nose up, the slow air meets the still-steep blade at a big angle, as the dial shows. The hub spring and the blade's spin now twist it flatter. The picture exaggerates the drop to 2,390 RPM, which a working governor catches quickly.
figure.alt: A see-through propeller hub and blade with labels Hub spring and Its own spin, the oil line behind it and a tachometer reading 2,390 RPM.

article.heading: Mistakes with the throttle and the blue knob
paragraphs: Set power with the manifold pressure gauge as you move the throttle, and cross-check the tachometer. It shows the pressure in the engine's intake, in inches of mercury, and power depends on it and the RPM together.
Change power in the right order. To add power, raise the RPM first and then the manifold pressure. To reduce it, bring the manifold pressure down first and then the RPM.

Avoid high manifold pressure at low RPM. It can cause detonation, where the fuel-air charge explodes instead of burning smoothly, and damage the engine. Use the power charts in your Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH).
Push the knob full forward for takeoff, to the low-pitch, high-RPM setting. In the 172RG the knob is labeled PROP RPM, PUSH INCR.
Expect the RPM to follow the airspeed at a pitch stop, the end of the blades' travel. There the governor can twist them no further, as with a fixed-pitch propeller.

table.caption: The Cessna 172RG's propeller numbers
rows: 25 inches of manifold pressure and 2,500 RPM
Low-pitch stop, the flattest blade angle
12.0 degrees, measured 30 inches out from the hub center
High-pitch stop, the steepest blade angle
26.5 degrees, measured 30 inches out from the hub center

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. With a constant-speed propeller, what did the blades just do if you lowered the nose and the RPM held at 2,500?
2. What happens to the blade angle and the RPM when you push the blue knob in?
3. Why could the RPM start falling in a slow climb when you haven't touched the knob?
4. When adding power with a constant-speed propeller, which do you raise first, the RPM or the manifold pressure?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. They twisted to a bigger bite. In the 172RG the governor sent oil to the hub to keep the propeller from speeding up.
2. The blades flatten to a smaller angle and the RPM rises.
3. The blades may have reached their low-pitch stop. From there the RPM follows the airspeed, as with a fixed-pitch propeller.
4. The RPM first, then the manifold pressure. High manifold pressure at low RPM can cause detonation.

posts.title: Wake turbulence, explained
posts.headline: Behind a larger airplane, its wake can roll yours harder than your ailerons can counter.
posts.alt: Cover slide titled Wake turbulence. A large twin-engine airliner low on final approach over a misty airfield at dusk, a curling trail of mist streaming back and down from each wingtip; the right wingtip's trail is labelled as a wingtip vortex. Text: Behind a larger airplane, its wake can roll yours harder than your ailerons can counter. Labels: WINGTIP VORTEX.
caption: Behind a larger airplane, its wake can roll yours harder than your ailerons can counter.

The vortices sink and spread out near the ground. Be especially alert in calm or light winds, when they can stay in the touchdown zone. A light quartering tailwind is the worst case: it can push them into the touchdown zone and leave them along your final. Landing behind one, stay at or above its path and land beyond where it touched down. Landing after one takes off, touch down well before where it rotated. Swipe to the check: tower clears you for takeoff right after a business jet's touch-and-go. Do you go? Send this to someone who shares a runway with bigger airplanes.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
posts.related_text: Every aircraft generates wake turbulence while in flight. Wake turbulence is a function of an aircraft producing lift, resulting in the formation of two counter-rotating vortices trailing behind the aircraft. Wake turbulence can impose rolling moments exceeding the roll-control authority of encountering aircraft, causing possible injury to occupants and damage to aircraft. The usual hazard is induced rolling moments that can exceed the roll-control authority of the encountering aircraft; in rare instances a wake encounter could cause catastrophic inflight structural damage. Lift comes from a pressure differential over the wing surface: the lowest pressure occurs over the upper wing surface and the highest pressure under the wing. This pressure differential triggers the roll up of the airflow at the rear of the wing, resulting in swirling air masses trailing downstream of the wingtips; after the roll up is completed, the wake consists of two counter-rotating cylindrical vortices, with most of the energy within a few feet of the vortex core. The vortex circulation is outward, upward and around the wingtips when viewed from either ahead or behind the aircraft. At altitudes greater than a wingspan from the ground, the vortices remain spaced a bit less than a wingspan apart, drifting with the wind. An aircraft generates vortices from the moment it rotates on takeoff to touchdown, since trailing vortices are a by-product of wing lift. Prior to takeoff or touchdown, pilots should note the rotation or touchdown point of the preceding aircraft. Weight, speed, wingspan, and shape of the generating aircraft's wing all govern the strength of the vortex, and extending flaps or other wing configuring devices changes it. Vortex strength increases proportionately to an increase in operating weight or a decrease in aircraft speed. Since the turbulence from a 'dirty' aircraft configuration hastens wake decay, the greatest vortex strength occurs when the generating aircraft is heavy, clean, and slow. The ability of an aircraft to counteract the roll imposed by a wake vortex depends primarily on its wingspan and counter-control responsiveness. Counter control is usually effective and induced roll minimal when the encountering aircraft's wingspan and ailerons extend beyond the rotational flow field of the vortex; it is more difficult for aircraft with a short wingspan (relative to the generating aircraft) to counter the imposed roll. Flight tests have shown that the vortices from larger aircraft sink at a rate of several hundred feet per minute, slowing their descent and diminishing in strength with time and distance behind the generating aircraft. Pilots should fly at or above the preceding aircraft's flight path, altering course as necessary to avoid the area directly behind and below the generating aircraft. Avoid the area below and behind the wake-generating aircraft, especially at low altitude, where even a momentary wake encounter could be catastrophic. When the vortices of larger aircraft sink close to the ground (within 100 to 200 feet), they tend to move laterally over the ground at a speed of 2 or 3 knots. A crosswind decreases the lateral movement of the upwind vortex and increases the movement of the downwind vortex. Thus a light wind with a cross-runway component of 1 to 5 knots could result in the upwind vortex remaining in the touchdown zone for a period of time and hasten the drift of the downwind vortex toward another runway. A tailwind condition can move the vortices of the preceding aircraft forward into the touchdown zone, and the light quartering tailwind requires maximum caution. A light quartering tailwind presents the worst case, as the wake vortices could be present along a significant portion of the final approach and extended centerline, not just in the touchdown zone. Pilots should be particularly alert in calm wind conditions and situations where the vortices could remain in the touchdown area, drift from aircraft operating on a nearby runway, sink into the takeoff or landing path from a crossing runway, sink into the traffic pattern, or sink into the flight path of VFR aircraft operating on the hemispheric altitude 500 feet below. Landing behind a larger aircraft on the same runway: stay at or above the larger aircraft's final approach flight path, note its touchdown point, and land beyond it. Landing behind a larger aircraft when a parallel runway is closer than 2,500 feet: consider possible drift to your runway, stay at or above the larger aircraft's final approach flight path, and note its touchdown point. When landing beyond the point of landing of the preceding heavier aircraft, ensure you have adequate runway remaining if conducting a touch-and-go landing, or adequate stopping distance available for a full stop landing. Departing behind a larger aircraft: note the larger aircraft's rotation point and rotate prior to it, continue climbing above the larger aircraft's climb path until turning clear of its wake, and avoid subsequent headings which will cross below and behind it. Landing behind a departing larger aircraft on the same runway: note its rotation point and land well prior to it. Departing or landing after a larger aircraft executing a low approach, missed approach, or touch-and-go landing: because vortices settle and move laterally near the ground, the vortex hazard may exist along the runway and in your flight path, particularly in light quartering wind conditions. You should ensure that an interval of at least 2 minutes has elapsed before your takeoff or landing. Pilots may request additional separation (for example, 2 minutes instead of 4 or 5 miles) for wake turbulence avoidance. This request should be made as soon as practical on ground control and at least before taxiing onto the runway. The pilot in command of an aircraft is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of that aircraft. Tower gives VFR aircraft it is talking to, which in its opinion may be adversely affected by wake turbulence from a larger aircraft, the larger aircraft's position, altitude and direction of flight, followed by "CAUTION - WAKE TURBULENCE". Whether or not a warning or information has been given, the pilot is expected to adjust aircraft operations and flight path as necessary to preclude serious wake encounters, and a pilot who accepts a clearance to visually follow a preceding aircraft accepts responsibility for separation and wake turbulence avoidance. En route VFR, avoid flight below and behind a large aircraft's path; if a larger aircraft is observed above on the same track (meeting or overtaking), adjust your position laterally, preferably upwind. If persistent vortex turbulence is encountered, a slight change of altitude (upward) and lateral position (upwind) should provide a flight path clear of the turbulence. In forward flight, departing or landing helicopters produce a pair of strong, high-speed trailing vortices similar to the wingtip vortices of larger fixed-wing aircraft. Pilots of small aircraft should avoid operating within three rotor diameters of any helicopter in a slow hover taxi or stationary hover. Pilots should notify ATC when a wake event is encountered, and be as descriptive as possible (bank angle, altitude deviations, intensity and duration of the event). Controllers may anticipate separation and need not withhold a takeoff clearance for an aircraft departing behind a large, heavy, or super aircraft if there is reasonable assurance the required separation will exist when the departing aircraft starts takeoff roll.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 14

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Every wing that makes lift trails two vortices that spin opposite ways, from rotation until touchdown. Behind a larger airplane they can roll yours harder than your ailerons can counter, and low down even a moment in one could be catastrophic.
So stay at or above a larger airplane's path, land beyond its touchdown point and lift off before its rotation point.

article.heading: How it forms, and whose is worst
paragraphs: Lift comes from lower pressure over the wing and higher pressure under it. That difference rolls the air up behind the wingtips into two counter-rotating vortices, with most of their energy within a few feet of each core. Seen from ahead or behind, the air turns outward, upward and around each tip.

Weight, speed, wingspan and wing shape set the strength. It grows as weight rises and speed falls. A dirty configuration makes the wake decay sooner. So the strongest wake comes from an airplane that is heavy, clean and slow.

How well you fight the roll depends mostly on your wingspan and how quickly your controls respond. The shorter your wingspan next to the larger airplane's, the harder the roll is to counter. A helicopter departing or landing in forward flight trails a strong pair too.

figure.caption: Seen from behind, the air curls up around each wingtip from the high pressure under the wing to the low pressure on top.
figure.alt: A large airliner seen from behind at dusk, a corkscrew of mist trailing from each wingtip, with arrows curling outward, up and around each tip and labels for the low pressure above the wing and the high pressure below it.

article.heading: Where the wake goes
paragraphs: The vortices from larger airplanes sink at several hundred feet per minute, slowing and weakening with time and distance. Higher than a wingspan above the ground they stay a bit less than a wingspan apart and drift with the wind.

Within 100 to 200 feet of the ground they tend to move sideways at 2 or 3 knots. A crosswind slows the upwind vortex and speeds the downwind one. So 1 to 5 knots of crosswind can hold the upwind vortex in the touchdown zone for a while. A tailwind can move the wake forward into the touchdown zone. A light quartering tailwind needs maximum caution, since it can leave the wake along much of final. Be particularly alert in calm wind, too. A wake can also drift in from a nearby runway, or sink into your path from a crossing runway or into the traffic pattern.

figure.caption: Both vortices sink. Near the ground, a light crosswind can hold the upwind one over the touchdown zone while the downwind one drifts off.
figure.alt: Looking down a runway at dusk: two vortex symbols sink from where a larger airplane passed, drifting a little with a light crosswind from the left; near the ground the upwind one lingers over the runway and the downwind one moves off past the edge.

article.heading: Landing and departing behind one
paragraphs: Landing behind a larger airplane, stay at or above its final approach path. Note its touchdown point and land beyond it, leaving room to stop. With a parallel runway closer than 2,500 feet, expect drift to yours and fly the same way. Landing behind one that is taking off, note its rotation point and land well before it.

Departing behind one, rotate before its rotation point and climb above its path until you turn clear of its wake. Then avoid headings that cross below and behind it. After a larger airplane's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go, wait at least 2 minutes before you take off or land. Stay at least three rotor diameters from a hovering helicopter.

figure.caption: Stay at or above the larger airplane's path and land beyond its touchdown point, clear of the wake that sinks below that path.
figure.alt: A side view of a runway: a dashed line traces a larger airplane's approach path to its touchdown point, with a faint red wedge below it where its wake sinks, and a Cessna 172 flies a parallel path above it to a point beyond.

article.heading: Three mistakes with wake turbulence
paragraphs: Avoid the wake yourself, warning or not. A caution from tower is information, and accepting a visual approach or an instruction to follow traffic makes the wake avoidance yours.
Ask for time before you taxi onto the runway, instead of taking a clearance that comes too soon. You may request extra separation of 2 minutes. A takeoff clearance does not mean the wake has gone.

Move aside, preferably upwind, when a larger airplane passes above you on your track, because its wake can sink to VFR traffic 500 feet below. In persistent wake turbulence, a slight climb and a move upwind should take you clear. Tell ATC about any wake encounter.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Where do you aim when a larger airplane ahead of you touches down near the 1,000-foot markers?
2. A 3-knot wind blows across the runway just after a larger airplane lands. Where can its wake be?
3. Departing after a business jet, you doubt you can stay above its climb path. What do you ask for?
4. Holding short, you watch a larger airplane do a touch-and-go and tower clears you at once. What now?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Beyond those markers, staying at or above its approach path and leaving enough runway to stop.
2. The upwind vortex can stay in the touchdown zone for a while.
3. Ask for more time, such as 2 minutes, before you taxi onto the runway.
4. Stay holding short and ask for at least 2 minutes. Its vortices can still be sitting on the runway.

posts.title: What is parasite drag?
posts.headline: A blunt wheel, a rough skin and a wing root all slow an airplane down.
posts.alt: A see-through Cessna 172 seen low from the side, with the teardrop cover over a main wheel labelled Wheel fairing and a pink parasite-drag arrow trailing behind it through cyan air lines.
posts.related_text: Parasite drag is the drag not associated with making lift; it is called parasite because it in no way functions to aid flight, and there are three types: form drag, interference drag and skin friction (PHAK ch 5 p 5-6). Form drag comes from the airplane's shape and the airflow around it: the air separates to move around a body and rejoins behind it, and how quickly and smoothly it rejoins is representative of the resistance; it is the easiest kind to reduce when designing an aircraft, by streamlining as many parts as possible (PHAK p 5-6, Fig 5-7, the sphere with a fairing). A blunt body has higher pressure on its front, where the air piles up, than in the separated, low-pressure wake behind it, and the integrated pressure difference resolved in the drag direction is the form drag (AFH glossary). The Cessna 172R's optional speed fairings, the wheel and brake fairings, increase its cruise speeds by approximately 2 knots; without them, cruise speeds are 2 knots lower (172R POH (1996) Section 1 Performance-Specifications, Fig 5-8 note, Section 6 equipment list). Wheel pants are covers used to reduce aerodynamic drag (AFH ch 2). Skin friction drag is the resistance due to moving air in contact with the airplane's surface; every surface is rough under a microscope; the air in contact with the surface is virtually motionless and each layer above moves slightly faster until it moves at the speed of the air around the aircraft, a layer called the boundary layer (PHAK p 5-6). The boundary layer starts as smooth laminar flow and some distance back from the leading edge breaks down into turbulent flow with swirls or eddies; laminar flow creates less skin friction drag than turbulent flow (PHAK p 5-46). Designers use flush mount rivets, remove irregularities that protrude above the wing surface and use a smooth, glossy finish; dirt disrupts the free flow of air and increases drag, so keep the surfaces clean and waxed (PHAK p 5-7). Interference drag comes from the intersection of airstreams that creates eddy currents, turbulence or restricts smooth airflow; the wing root has significant interference drag, as air flowing around the fuselage collides with air flowing over the wing; the most is observed where two surfaces meet at perpendicular angles; with two identical wing tanks the overall drag is greater than the sum of the individual tanks; fairings and distance between lifting surfaces and external components reduce it (PHAK p 5-6). Parasite drag increases as the square of the airspeed: if the speed doubles, parasite drag increases four times (GFH ch 3 p 3-5; PHAK p 5-8), as from 100 to 200 knots it becomes four times as great (PHAK ch 11 p 11-5). Induced drag varies inversely with the square of the airspeed: at twice the speed it is one-fourth (PHAK p 5-8, 11-6). Arithmetic: D proportional to V^2, (2)^2 = 4. Frost, snow and ice on the leading edge or upper surface of the wing no thicker or rougher than a piece of coarse sandpaper can reduce lift by 30 percent and increase drag up to 40 percent (Aviation Weather Handbook FAA-H-8083-28 ch 20 p 20-7); frost disrupts the airflow over the wing, reduces lift and increases drag, and an aircraft must be thoroughly cleaned and free of frost before beginning a flight (PHAK ch 12, Dew and Frost).

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapters 5, 11 and 12

citations.ref: Cessna 172R POH (1996) sec 1, 5 and 6 speed fairings
citations.title: Cessna 172R Pilot's Operating Handbook (1996)

posts.credits: 3D model: “Cessna172” by KOG_THORNS (sketchfab.com), CC BY 4.0, modified. Sky: Kloofendal 38d Partly Cloudy (Pure Sky) by Greg Zaal (polyhaven.com), CC0.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Parasite drag is all the drag that does not come from making lift. It does nothing to help the airplane fly, and it comes in three kinds: form drag, skin friction and interference drag.
Every blunt shape, rough patch and joint adds some, and all of it grows quickly with speed.

article.heading: Form drag comes from shape
paragraphs: Form drag comes from an object's shape and the way the air flows around it.
A bare wheel is blunt.

Air piles up against its front at higher pressure, then tears away behind it into a churning, low-pressure wake. With more pressure pushing on the front than on the back, the wheel is pushed backward, and that push is form drag.

Form drag is the easiest kind for a designer to reduce, by streamlining. A teardrop cover around the wheel, called a wheel fairing or wheel pant, lets the air close in smoothly behind it, so the wake shrinks and so does the drag. On a Cessna 172R, the optional teardrop covers on the wheels are worth about 2 knots of cruise speed.

figure.caption: A cross-section of the bare wheel's flow, drawn flat and two-dimensional: the air piles up in front at higher pressure (amber) and tears away into a churning, low-pressure wake (light blue). The pink arrow is the drag.
figure.alt: A Cessna 172 main wheel seen from the side, with cyan air lines flowing past it, an amber glow in front labelled Higher pressure, a light-blue churning wake behind labelled Lower pressure, and a pink drag arrow pointing aft.

article.heading: Skin friction and the boundary layer
paragraphs: Skin friction is the drag of moving air in contact with the airplane's surface.

The air touching the skin is almost still. Each layer above it moves a little faster, until the air moves at the speed of the air flowing around the airplane. That thin region is the boundary layer, and as its layers slide over each other they rub.

Near the leading edge the boundary layer flows smoothly, which is called laminar flow. Some way back it breaks down into swirls and eddies, which is turbulent flow, and turbulent flow makes more skin friction than laminar flow.
So designers use flush rivets, remove anything that sticks up above the wing surface and give the airplane a smooth, glossy finish.

figure.caption: The boundary layer (lime), drawn much thicker than it really is. Each arrow's length is the air's speed at that height, zero at the skin. Near the leading edge (left) the profile is laminar; farther back the layers break into swirls, and the turbulent profile (right) is fuller close to the skin, so it rubs harder.
figure.alt: A magnified circle on the top of a Cessna 172 wing with three columns of lime arrows, short at the skin and longer above: a laminar profile on the left under the label Laminar, small swirls in the middle, and a fuller turbulent profile on the right under the label Turbulent.

article.heading: Interference drag where parts meet
paragraphs: Interference drag comes from airstreams meeting, which sets up eddies and turbulence or blocks the smooth flow. The wing root makes a lot of it. There, air flowing around the fuselage collides with air flowing over the wing.
It is worst where two surfaces meet at a right angle, and the joined parts make more drag than the same parts would apart.
Smooth, curved fairings at the joints reduce it, and so does more distance between a lifting surface and anything hung near it.

figure.caption: Where the air along the cabin meets the air over the wing, it churns (the curls). A smooth, curved fairing (white) along the joint keeps that churn small.
figure.alt: The root of a Cessna 172 wing where it meets the cabin top, with cyan air lines from the fuselage and the wing, small orange curls beside the joint, and a curved white fairing labelled Fairing along it.

article.heading: Two mistakes that add drag
paragraphs: Clear every trace of frost off the wings, tail and other surfaces before takeoff, however thin. Frost, snow or ice on the leading edge or top of the wing, even a layer no thicker or rougher than coarse sandpaper, can cut lift by as much as 30 percent and add up to 40 percent more drag.
Keep the airplane clean and waxed. Dirt disrupts the smooth flow of air over the surface and adds drag.

article.heading: What speed does to drag
paragraphs: All three kinds grow with the square of the airspeed. Double an airplane's airspeed, say from 60 to 120 knots, and its parasite drag becomes four times as great.
Induced drag, the drag that comes with making lift, does the opposite. In level flight at the same weight, at twice the speed it is about a quarter of what it was.

figure.caption: At twice the speed, parasite drag (pink) grows to four times its size and induced drag (violet) falls to a quarter. Each arrow is compared only with its own dashed starting arrow.
figure.alt: A see-through Cessna 172 with doubled cyan air streaks, a long pink arrow under it marked 4x beside a dashed ghost of its shorter length, and a short violet arrow above the wing, labelled Induced drag, beside a dashed ghost of its longer length.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. At the same altitude you fly twice as fast. How much bigger does the parasite drag get?
2. Why does a teardrop cover make less drag than a bare wheel?
3. Why do designers use flush rivets and a smooth, glossy finish?
4. A thin layer of frost as rough as coarse sandpaper covers the wing before a morning flight. What do you do?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. About four times bigger, because parasite drag grows with the square of the airspeed.
2. The air closes in smoothly behind it, so the low-pressure wake shrinks and so does the form drag.
3. Anything that sticks up or roughens the skin adds skin friction drag.
4. Clean every bit of it off before the flight, because even that much frost adds drag and cuts lift.

posts.title: What causes induced drag
posts.headline: Induced drag is the price of lift. It gives the power curve its back side, and losing some of it near the ground is why a fast flare floats.
posts.alt: A see-through Cessna 172 in level flight: a green lift arrow leaning back from a dashed vertical, a short violet arrow closing it at the top, and a violet wingtip vortex trailing back from the near wingtip.
posts.related_text: A wing making lift has higher pressure on its lower surface than on its upper surface; air moves from high pressure toward low, and the path of least resistance is toward the tips, so air flows spanwise outward under the wing, inward toward the fuselage over it, and spills up round each tip into a vortex (PHAK ch 5 p 5-7/5-8). Seen from behind, the vortices turn counterclockwise about the right tip and clockwise about the left (PHAK p 5-7). The vortices induce an upward flow beyond the tips and a downwash behind the wing that extends forward to its trailing edge and over the top of the wing (PHAK p 4-9; p 5-8: 'This downwash over the top of the airfoil at the tip has the same effect as bending the lift vector rearward'); the downwash points the average relative wind down from the flight path, and lift, which is always perpendicular to the relative wind, tilts aft. Its rearward component is induced drag (PHAK p 5-7/5-8; PHAK ch 4 p 4-9; GFH ch 3 Fig 3-6). Induced drag is inseparable from lift: it is present whenever a wing makes lift (PHAK p 5-7). The lower the airspeed, the higher the angle of attack needed for lift equal to the weight, the stronger the vortices and the greater the induced drag; it varies inversely with the square of the airspeed, so in level flight at the same weight and altitude half the airspeed gives four times the induced drag (PHAK p 5-8). Arithmetic: D_i = W^2 / (q pi b^2 e) with q = rho V^2 / 2, so (V / (V/2))^2 = 4. A heavier airplane needs more lift at the same speed, so a higher angle of attack and more induced drag; vortex strength is directly proportional to weight and inversely proportional to wingspan and speed (PHAK p 5-9), and at the same airspeed, altitude and wing the induced drag goes with the weight squared: a Cessna 172P from an illustrative 1,900 lb to its 2,400 lb maximum takeoff weight (POH p 1-5, Takeoff, Normal Category: 2400 lbs.) is about 26 percent heavier ((2400/1900) = 1.263, about a quarter) and carries about 60 percent more induced drag ((2400/1900)^2 = 1.596). Parasite drag increases as the square of the airspeed, so near the stall total drag rises mainly because of the sharp rise in induced drag, and induced drag predominates at low speed (PHAK p 5-8, 5-11); flight speeds below the speed for maximum endurance (the lowest point on the power curve) require more power with a decrease in airspeed: the region of reversed command, the back side of the power curve (PHAK ch 11 p 11-11, Fig 11-14; AFH glossary). On a low, slow approach, merely lowering the nose without power gives a rapid sink and loss of altitude, and applying power may reduce or stop the descent; but even full power may not let the airplane climb or hold altitude, and then the only recourse is to lower the pitch attitude to regain airspeed, which inevitably costs altitude (PHAK p 11-12). Ground effect normally occurs up to a height of one wingspan above the surface (AFH); the surface restricts the vertical airflow, reducing the downwash, the wingtip vortices, the induced angle of attack and the induced drag: 1.4 percent less at a height equal to the span, 23.5 percent less at a quarter of the span (PHAK p 5-11); with the reduced drag and the lack of power-off deceleration, excess speed at the flare can mean a considerable float (PHAK p 5-12). A Cessna 172S's wing span is 36 ft 1 in (POH Fig 1-1). An increase in aspect ratio decreases the drag, especially at high angles of attack (PHAK p 5-21); a high-performance glider's wing has a high aspect ratio, 39:1 on an 86.9 ft span in the GFH's Fig 3-10, with minimal induced drag, and winglets reduce induced drag by altering the airflow near the tips (GFH ch 3; PHAK ch 4 p 4-9), but they are not a means to decrease the wake vortex hazard: studies on approach and landing show no discernible difference with or without them (AC 90-23G par 14). The Cessna 172's wing (36 ft 1 in, 174 sq ft) has an aspect ratio of about 7.5 (36.08^2 / 174 = 7.48). Every aircraft in flight generates wake vortices; they are strongest when the generating aircraft is heavy, clean (flaps up) and slow, and behind a large aircraft they sink several hundred feet per minute; fly at or above the larger aircraft's flight path, use a slight lateral change (preferably upwind) to clear persistent turbulence, and when landing behind it on the same runway stay at or above its final approach path, note its touchdown point and land beyond it (AC 90-23G par 3, 5a, 7b, 7c, 8e, 8f; PHAK p 5-9).

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Induced drag is the drag that comes with making lift. The wingtip vortices tilt the air the wing meets downward, the lift leans back with it, and its backward part is induced drag.
It grows as you slow down. In level flight, half the airspeed means four times the induced drag.

article.heading: Where the wingtip vortices come from
paragraphs: A wing making lift has higher air pressure under it than on top. Air moves from high pressure toward low, and the easiest way around the wing is past its tips.
Under the wing the air slides outward, away from the fuselage, while on top it slides inward. At each tip the air from below curls up and over the top and sets up a whirlpool called a wingtip vortex.
Seen from behind, the vortex turns counterclockwise at the right tip and clockwise at the left. Both trail behind the airplane whenever the wing makes lift.

figure.caption: The air under the wing (amber) curls up round the tip and rolls into a wingtip vortex (violet), drawn exaggerated and slowed.
figure.alt: A see-through Cessna 172 wing seen from behind and above, light blue on top, with amber lines sliding out under it and violet coils rolling up behind the right wingtip.

article.heading: How the vortices tilt the lift back
paragraphs: The vortices push air up beyond the tips and down behind the wing, and that downwash reaches forward over the wing itself. So the relative wind, the local air the wing meets, arrives tilted slightly down from the flight path.
Lift always acts at a right angle to the relative wind. When the relative wind tilts down, the lift leans back by the same small angle.
Split the leaning lift in two. The upward part holds the airplane up, and the rearward part, pulling against the direction of flight, is induced drag.

figure.caption: The vortices bend the air across and behind the wing downward (cyan), so the wing meets air tilted slightly downhill.
figure.alt: A side view of a see-through Cessna 172 with cyan streaks arriving level ahead of the wing and bending down over it and behind it.

article.heading: Why slow and heavy make more of it
paragraphs: To hold altitude at a lower speed, the wing needs a higher angle of attack, its angle to the relative wind. The vortices get stronger and the lift leans back further.
Induced drag varies inversely with the square of the airspeed.

Weight makes more of it too, because more weight needs more lift at the same speed. At one airspeed the induced drag grows with the weight squared. Load a 172P from 1,900 lb to its 2,400 lb maximum takeoff weight, about a quarter heavier, and its induced drag rises about 60 percent.

Parasite drag, from pushing the airplane through the air, grows with the square of the airspeed instead. So at low speed induced drag takes over. Below the best-endurance speed, the bottom of the power curve, flying slower takes more power. That is the back side.

Wing shape matters too. A high-performance glider's long, narrow wing, with an aspect ratio of 39 to 1 against a 172's 7.5, makes little of it. Winglets reduce it too, but they do not noticeably weaken a jet's wake.

figure.caption: The lift (green) stands square to the local air (cyan), so it leans back from the vertical. Its backward part, along the flight path, is the induced drag (violet), drawn larger than life.
figure.alt: A wing section on a white dashed flight-path line, a cyan arrow of local air arriving tilted down, a green lift arrow leaning back from a dashed vertical and a short violet arrow labelled INDUCED DRAG at its top.

article.heading: Three mistakes near the ground and behind jets
paragraphs: The first mistake is arriving at the flare fast. Within about one wingspan of the runway, 36 feet for a 172, the ground restricts the downwash and the vortices. Induced drag drops, by 23.5 percent at a quarter of the span, so extra speed carries you far down the runway.

The second is letting a low, slow approach get slower. On the back side it keeps slowing unless you act. Add power early. Lowering the nose alone makes you sink fast, but when full power is not enough, it is the only way to regain speed, even near the ground.

The third is flying below a big jet's flight path. Its vortices are strongest when it is heavy and slow with its flaps up, and they sink several hundred feet per minute. If a big jet passes above you on the same track, move sideways, preferably upwind. Landing behind it, land beyond its touchdown point.

figure.caption: In the flare the ground restricts the downwash, so the induced drag (violet) shrinks from the dotted length it had higher up to the solid arrow.
figure.alt: A see-through Cessna 172 low over a runway with its markings, cyan streaks passing over and behind the wing, a green lift arrow leaning back from a dashed vertical, and at its top a violet arrow shorter than the dotted violet line that marks its length higher up.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. In level flight at the same weight, what happens to induced drag when you cut your airspeed in half?
2. Why does the lift lean back on a wing that trails wingtip vortices?
3. You reach the flare with extra speed. Why does the airplane keep floating?
4. A heavy airliner has just landed ahead of you on the same runway. Where do you touch down?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. It gets four times bigger, because induced drag varies inversely with the square of the airspeed.
2. The vortices tilt the relative wind down, and lift stays at a right angle to the relative wind.
3. Close to the ground the downwash and vortices shrink, so induced drag drops and the airplane slows down less.
4. Beyond its touchdown point, after staying at or above its approach path. It made vortices until its wheels touched.

posts.title: How a carburetor works
posts.headline: A carburetor meters fuel with a pressure drop. In humid air, that drop and the evaporating fuel can ice it even on a hot day, and carb heat clears it.
posts.alt: A see-through cutaway of the up-draft carburetor under a Cessna 172P's engine: cyan air streaks speeding up through the narrow throat, a green fuel passage from the float bowl to the nozzle, and white frost crusting the throttle plate and the throat.
posts.related_text: In the 172P's up-draft carburetor, air speeds up through a narrow throat, the venturi, and its pressure drops; the float bowl beside it is vented, so its higher pressure pushes fuel up a passage and out of the discharge nozzle into the throat. The throttle is a butterfly plate above the nozzle: opening it lets more air through, and more fuel comes with it. As the airplane climbs the air gets thinner while the carburetor meters about the same fuel, so the mixture turns too rich; the 172P's handbook keeps it rich in the climb below 3,000 feet and leans above it; leaning with the red mixture knob cuts the fuel back to match, and full out (idle cut-off) stops the fuel to shut the engine down; in cruise the 172P's handbook leans until the RPM peaks, then further until it drops 25-50 RPM (POH p 4-16). The venturi's pressure drop and the fuel's evaporation can cool the air by up to about 70 °F, so ice can form in the throat and on the throttle plate on days as warm as 100 °F; a nearly closed throttle in a descent is the most sensitive; PHAK ch 7: carburetor ice 'is most likely to occur when temperatures are below 70 degrees Fahrenheit ... and the relative humidity is above 80 percent' (an outside air temperature, unlike the 70 °F of cooling). In a 172 with a fixed-pitch propeller the first sign is an unexplained drop in RPM; full carb heat brings warm air from a shroud around an exhaust pipe, the RPM dips at first because warm air is less dense, then rises as the ice melts, and the 172P's handbook clears it with full throttle and full heat; it calls for full heat as required in the descent and full heat before reducing power for landing, and PHAK ch 7 says: 'If carburetor icing conditions are suspected and closed-throttle operation anticipated, adjust the carburetor heat to the full ON position before closing the throttle'; with the throttle closed 'the engine cools rapidly' and 'is more susceptible to carburetor icing'.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: An older Cessna 172, like the 172P, has a carburetor under its engine. Gravity feeds it fuel, and a difference in air pressure pushes that fuel into the airflow.
You manage it with three knobs: the throttle, the red mixture knob and carb heat, which clears ice that can form inside it even on a hot day.

article.heading: How the carburetor meters fuel
paragraphs: As the pistons draw air in, outside air comes through a filter and up into the bottom of the 172P's up-draft carburetor. On the way it squeezes through a narrow throat called the venturi. It speeds up to get through, and its pressure drops.

Beside the throat sits the float bowl, where a float holds the fuel at a steady level. The bowl is vented, so the air above its fuel stays at a higher pressure than the air in the throat. That difference pushes fuel up a passage and out of the discharge nozzle into the airstream, where it breaks up and evaporates.
Above the nozzle, the throttle knob turns a flat butterfly plate. Push the knob in and the plate turns toward edge-on. More air flows, the pressure drop grows, and more fuel comes with it.

figure.caption: The carburetor cut open: air (cyan) speeds up through the throat, the venturi, where its pressure drops (violet). The higher pressure on the fuel in the float bowl (white arrows) pushes it up the passage and out of the nozzle (green).
figure.alt: A cutaway of a carburetor: on the left the narrow throat with cyan streaks and a violet dashed line, a green fuel passage curving from the bottom of a float bowl up into the throat, and on the right the bowl with green fuel, a float and white arrows pressing down on the fuel.

article.heading: Why you lean the mixture up high
paragraphs: The engine burns fuel by the weight of air it gets, but the venturi meters the volume of air. As you climb, each cubic foot of air weighs less, yet it still draws about the same fuel. The mixture turns rich, too much fuel for the air, and the engine can run rough.

Pulling the red mixture knob out turns a valve in the carburetor that cuts the fuel back, which leans the mixture. The 172P's handbook keeps it rich in the climb below 3,000 feet and leans for best RPM above that. In cruise it leans past peak RPM until the RPM drops 25 to 50. Pulled full out to idle cut-off, the knob stops the fuel to shut the engine down.
Coming down from altitude, push it back in. Too lean a mixture can run rough and overheat the engine.

article.heading: Why it can ice on a hot day
paragraphs: The venturi's pressure drop chills the air, and so does the fuel evaporating into it. Together they can chill it by as much as 70 Fahrenheit degrees. If the air is humid, its water vapor can freeze onto the throat and the throttle plate, even on a 100 °F day.
The risk is worst with the throttle nearly closed in a descent. The air gets past the plate only through a small gap at its edge, and a little ice can block it.

The 172P's propeller is fixed-pitch, so lost power shows as lower RPM. The first sign is a drop in RPM with the throttle where you left it, then roughness. Pull the carb heat knob all the way out. It swaps the filtered air for unfiltered air warmed by a shroud around an exhaust pipe. The 172P's emergency checklist adds full throttle, then turns the heat off once the engine runs smoothly.

figure.caption: Ice (white) on the throttle plate and the throat wall, drawn exaggerated, with the air (cyan) still flowing past. Reel credits: 3D model “Cessna172” by KOG_THORNS (sketchfab.com), CC BY 4.0, modified. Engine sound “1978 Cessna 172 Departure” by Wingspan Adventures & Flight (youtube.com), CC BY 3.0, modified.
figure.alt: A close view inside a cut-open carburetor: the round throttle plate on its shaft, crusted with thick white frost, with white rime on the wall behind it and cyan streaks of air around it, under the words BELOW FREEZING.

article.heading: Three mistakes with carb ice
paragraphs: Keep full carb heat on when the RPM dips. Warm air is less dense, so the RPM drops first, then rises slowly as the ice melts.

Put full carb heat on before you close the throttle when icing is possible, without waiting for a symptom. A throttled-back engine cools quickly, which makes icing more likely. The 172P's handbook does so before reducing power to land.
Expect carb ice well above freezing. Carb ice is most likely with outside air below about 70 °F and humidity above 80 percent. Other airplanes differ, so follow the handbook for yours.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. What pushes the fuel into the venturi?
2. Why does the mixture get richer as you climb?
3. In cruise, the RPM slowly drops though you haven't touched the throttle. What do you do, and what will the RPM do next?
4. Why put carb heat on before you close the throttle for a descent?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. The higher air pressure in the vented float bowl, against the lower pressure in the venturi's throat.
2. The venturi meters air by volume, so thinner air draws about the same fuel but brings less weight of air.
3. Pull full carb heat. The RPM dips first, because warm air is less dense, then rises as the ice melts.
4. A little ice can block the small gap at the nearly closed plate, and a throttled-back engine cools, inviting ice.

posts.title: How gyro instruments work
posts.headline: In a 172P, a low suction reading means the attitude and heading indicators can't be trusted. The electric turn coordinator still shows your turns.
posts.alt: An X-ray view through the see-through instrument panel of a banking Cessna 172P: inside the attitude indicator's case a gold spinning wheel in two silver rings stays level, and the blue and brown horizon on the face stays level with it.
posts.related_text: The attitude indicator's horizon stays level because its gyro, a heavy wheel spinning at about 18,000 RPM in two gimbal rings, holds its plane in space while the airplane pitches and rolls around it. The heading indicator's gyro spins on its edge in a vertical plane, and its compass card, geared to the gyro, holds its direction while the airplane turns around it; it drifts slowly, so it is checked against the magnetic compass about every 15 minutes. On the Cessna 172P one engine-driven vacuum pump draws air through a filter and across the rotors' buckets to spin both the attitude and heading indicators, and the suction gauge shows the suction, 4.5 to 5.4 inches of mercury in the 172P. If that pump fails, both gyros slowly spin down and wander, and the 172P has no low-vacuum warning light, so a level airplane can look as if it is turning. The turn coordinator runs on electricity and shows the rate of turn through precession: the turn's force on its rotor acts 90 degrees later in the direction of rotation and leans the gyro against a spring, more for a faster turn; with low suction, believe it rather than the attitude indicator.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Three of the six instruments in front of you in a Cessna 172P hold a gyro, a heavy wheel spinning very fast. In the attitude and heading indicators it resists being tilted, so the airplane moves around it. The turn coordinator uses a different trick, precession.

Two of them, the attitude indicator and the heading indicator, are spun by air from one vacuum pump on the engine. The third, the turn coordinator, is electric. So if the suction gauge reads low, believe the turn coordinator, not the attitude indicator.

article.heading: Why the horizon and the heading hold still
paragraphs: Inside the attitude indicator a rotor spins at about 18,000 RPM, revolutions per minute. That speed, with most of its weight at the rim, makes it hold its plane in space.

The rotor hangs in two hinged rings, called gimbals, one inside the other. When you bank or pitch, the airplane and the case turn around the rotor while the rotor stays put. The horizon bar is fixed to the gyro, so it stays level with the real horizon, and to you the horizon picture tilts in the case.
Just below, the heading indicator's rotor spins on its edge, in a vertical plane. Its compass card is geared to the gyro, so the card holds its direction while the nose swings around it.
It has no magnets, and a little friction in its bearings makes it precess, so it drifts slowly. Check and reset it against the magnetic compass about every 15 minutes.

figure.caption: The attitude indicator's gyro in its two gimbal rings (white), drawn see-through. The rings let the airplane pitch and roll around the wheel without tilting it.
figure.alt: A close view inside a see-through attitude indicator case: a gold spinning wheel held in two white rings, one inside the other, on a dark grid.

article.heading: One pump spins both
paragraphs: On the 172P a vacuum pump on the engine pulls air out of both instrument cases and vents it overboard. That draws cabin air in through a filter on the firewall and across little buckets cut into each rotor's rim, spinning it like a water wheel. A relief valve keeps the suction from going too high.

The suction gauge on the panel's left shows the suction. The 172P's handbook wants 4.5 to 5.4 inches of mercury. Outside that range, it says, the attitude and heading indicators should not be considered reliable.
If the pump fails, both gyros slowly spin down and wander. The 172P has no low-vacuum warning light, only the gauge, so a level airplane can look as if it is turning.

figure.caption: The vacuum system drawn see-through: the engine-driven pump, the filter and the air (light blue) on its way to both gyros. The hose routing is simplified. In the 172P, air comes in through the filter, spins both gyros and goes on to the engine-driven pump, with a relief valve on that line. Reel credits: 3D model “Cessna172” by KOG_THORNS (sketchfab.com), CC BY 4.0, modified. Engine sound “1978 Cessna 172 Departure” by Wingspan Adventures & Flight (youtube.com), CC BY 3.0, modified.
figure.alt: An X-ray view behind a Cessna 172P panel: the attitude and heading indicators with gold rotors, light-blue arrows of air at the black hoses, a white filter labelled Filter below and a labelled vacuum pump on the engine.

article.heading: Why the turn coordinator is electric
paragraphs: The turn coordinator is the third gyro. On the 172P it runs on the electrical system, so one failure cannot take all three. Its face says D.C. ELEC. In another airplane, check the handbook for what powers each gyro.

Its gimbal is angled up about 30 degrees, so it senses roll as well as yaw. When the airplane turns, it pushes on the spinning rotor's rim, and the rotor reacts 90 degrees further around, in the direction it spins. That tilts the gimbal against a spring, more for a faster turn. The little airplane shows your rate of turn, not your bank angle, and gives no pitch information.

article.heading: Three mistakes with the gyros
paragraphs: Stop trusting the vacuum gyros when the suction drops. Once the rotors slow down, the attitude and heading indicators wander, and the little horizon can show a bank that isn't there. Use the turn coordinator for turns and the magnetic compass for heading. Take pitch from the outside horizon, or from airspeed, altitude and vertical speed.
Make the suction gauge part of your scan. Many small airplanes have no vacuum failure warning, so the gauge is your alarm.
Reset the heading indicator only on the ground, stopped or taxiing straight, or in straight and level flight at a steady speed. In a turn or a climb, the compass's own errors get copied in.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Why does the attitude indicator's horizon stay level when you bank?
2. What spins the heading indicator's gyro in a 172P?
3. The suction gauge reads 2 inches of mercury, the attitude indicator shows a gentle left bank, and the turn coordinator's little airplane is level. Which do you trust, and what else has failed?
4. Why is the turn coordinator electric?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Its gyro holds its plane in space and the horizon bar is fixed to it, so the airplane rolls around it.
2. Air from the engine-driven vacuum pump, the same pump that spins the attitude indicator.
3. Trust the turn coordinator. With suction that low, the attitude indicator and the heading indicator are both unreliable.
4. So a vacuum pump failure cannot take all three gyros at once.

posts.title: How magnetos work
posts.headline: Two engine-driven magnetos fire two plugs in every cylinder. OFF only works through a ground wire, so a broken one leaves a magneto live.
posts.alt: An X-ray view of the back of a Cessna 172P's Lycoming engine, its cylinders and wiring in grey, with the two gold magnetos ringed and labelled Magnetos and their spark-plug leads running forward.
posts.related_text: The Cessna 172P's Lycoming O-320-D2J gets its sparks from two engine-driven magnetos on the rear of the engine, and a magneto makes its current independently of the airplane's electrical system, so the engine keeps running with the master switch off. Inside a magneto a rotating magnet builds current in a coil; when the breaker points open, the coil sends a high-voltage pulse that jumps a spark plug's gap. Each cylinder has two spark plugs and each magneto fires one of them, so if one magneto fails the other keeps every cylinder firing. On the run-up check at 1,700 RPM the engine slows a little on one magneto because one spark plug per cylinder burns the mixture more slowly; the 172P allows a drop of up to 125 RPM on either magneto and up to 50 RPM between them. Ignition OFF stops a magneto by grounding it through its own wire, the P-lead; if that wire breaks, OFF cannot stop that magneto and moving the propeller by hand can start the engine, and no RPM drop on the check may mean faulty grounding.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: A piston engine like the Cessna 172P's makes its own sparks. Two magnetos, driven by the engine, fire two spark plugs in every cylinder, and they need nothing from the battery or the alternator. That is why the engine keeps running with the master switch off.
The ignition switch stops a magneto by grounding it through a wire. If that wire breaks, OFF no longer stops that magneto, so you treat every propeller as if the engine could start.

article.heading: How a magneto makes a spark
paragraphs: The 172P's Lycoming O-320 carries its two magnetos on the back of the engine, where the engine turns them. Inside each one a magnet spins past a coil and builds up current in its first winding.

A small switch called the breaker points then snaps open, and that current stops all at once. The magnetic field through the coil flips fast, and a second winding of thousands of turns, wound over the first, turns that change into a high-voltage pulse. A rotating distributor sends each pulse down the lead to the right spark plug, where it jumps the plug's gap.

The magneto makes all of this itself, so once the engine runs, the battery and the alternator play no part in the sparks. The battery still matters for starting, because the starter only cranks the engine with the master switch on.

figure.caption: The breaker points, the small switch inside a magneto, drawn as a simplified schematic and shown open. Opening them is what makes the coil fire a spark.
figure.alt: A close view inside a see-through magneto: a small hinged steel arm swung away from its contact, labelled Points open, beside the spinning shaft, with gold magneto parts around it.

article.heading: Two plugs in every cylinder
paragraphs: Each of the four cylinders has two spark plugs, eight in all. On the 172P the right magneto fires the lower right and upper left plugs, and the left magneto fires the lower left and upper right plugs.

So each magneto fires one plug in every cylinder. If one magneto quits, the other keeps all four cylinders firing. That is the point of having two. Two flame fronts also burn the mixture faster than one, which is why the engine slows a little when only one plug fires in each cylinder.

article.heading: Three mistakes with the ignition switch
paragraphs: Return to BOTH between the R and L checks. The 172P's Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH) makes the magneto check at 1,700 RPM, engine revolutions per minute. Select R and note the RPM, then go back to BOTH to clear the other set of plugs. Then select L, note the RPM, and return to BOTH. The drop should not exceed 125 RPM on either magneto or 50 RPM between them.

Treat a check with no drop at all as a fault, though it feels like good news. Turning the key to OFF connects each magneto to the airplane's metal frame through its own wire, the P-lead, which stops its sparks. Selecting one magneto grounds the other the same way. So if nothing changes when you select one magneto, the one you tried to switch off may still be firing. The POH treats an absent drop as a sign of faulty grounding, or of timing set to fire the sparks earlier than specified.

Treat every propeller as live, even with the key OFF. If a P-lead breaks, OFF cannot silence that magneto. It stays live: it can still produce sparks when the propeller is turned, even with the key OFF. Moving the propeller by hand can then start the engine with fuel left in a cylinder. The POH says to treat the propeller as if the ignition switch were on and to stay out of its arc. A normal shutdown does not rely on the key alone. The POH pulls the mixture to IDLE CUT-OFF first, which stops the fuel and so the engine, then turns the ignition switch OFF.

figure.caption: The key is at OFF, but this magneto's ground wire (green) is broken at the red mark, so the magneto can still produce sparks when the propeller is turned. The wire's route is drawn for illustration. Reel credits: 3D model “Cessna172” by KOG_THORNS (sketchfab.com), CC BY 4.0, modified. Engine sound “1978 Cessna 172 Departure” by Wingspan Adventures & Flight (youtube.com), CC BY 3.0, modified.
figure.alt: A gold magneto with its green ground wire running down toward the cockpit, a red ring labelled Break where the wire is broken at the magneto, and an inset of the ignition key turned to OFF.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Does the engine stop if you turn the master switch off in flight?
2. Why does the engine slow a little when you select one magneto?
3. On the run-up the RPM does not change at all when you select L. What could that mean?
4. The key is OFF and in your pocket. Is the propeller safe to turn by hand?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. No. The magnetos make their own current, so the engine keeps running. You lose the airplane's electrical power, not the ignition.
2. With one magneto, only one plug fires in each cylinder, so the mixture takes longer to burn.
3. The right magneto may not be grounding, so it may still be firing. That is a fault to get fixed before flight.
4. No. A broken P-lead leaves a magneto live, so treat every propeller as if the engine could start.

posts.title: Density altitude, explained
posts.headline: On a 70°F day at a 5,883-foot field, altimeter 30.10, your airplane performs as if it's at about 7,700 feet.
posts.alt: Cover slide titled Density altitude. A small airfield in a high mountain valley: the house Cessna 172 climbs out over the runway toward rising, pine-covered ground under high peaks. Text: On a 70°F day at a 5,883-foot field, altimeter 30.10, your airplane performs as if it's at about 7,700 feet.
caption: You can't detect the effect of high density altitude on your airspeed indicator. On a 70°F day at a 5,883-foot field, altimeter 30.10, your airplane performs as if it's at about 7,700 feet.

You lift off and climb at your usual indicated speeds, but you're faster over the ground, with less power and thrust to get there. So you need more runway and climb at a shallower angle. Your landing roll is longer too. Work out your takeoff distance for today's conditions before you go. Taking off from a field above 3,000 feet? If your airplane's procedure calls for it, lean for maximum rpm in a full-throttle runup before takeoff. Send this to someone who flies from a hot or high field.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
posts.related_text: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. It is the vertical distance above sea level in the standard atmosphere at which a given density is to be found. Under standard conditions, pressure altitude and density altitude identify the same level. Regardless of the actual altitude at which the aircraft is operating, it will perform as though it were operating at an altitude equal to the existing density altitude. Density altitude is a measure of air density. It is not to be confused with pressure altitude, true altitude, or absolute altitude, and it is not to be used as a height reference, but as a determining criteria in the performance capability of an aircraft. The conditions that result in a high density altitude are high elevations, low atmospheric pressures, high temperatures, high humidity, or some combination of these factors. Lower elevations, high atmospheric pressure, low temperatures, and low humidity are more indicative of low density altitude. Density is directly proportional to pressure: if the pressure is lowered, the density is lowered (at a constant temperature). Increasing the temperature decreases the density (at a constant pressure). Pilots can expect the density to decrease with altitude. Temperature is the most important factor, since temperature has the greatest effect on density horizontally in the atmosphere. On hot days, the air becomes less dense, causing high density altitudes; on cold days, the air is denser, causing lower density altitudes. Water vapor is lighter than air, so moist air is lighter than dry air: as the water content of the air increases, the air becomes less dense, increasing density altitude and decreasing performance. Humidity alone is usually not considered an important factor in calculating density altitude and aircraft performance, but it is a contributing factor. In the handbook's humidity example, at 8,000 feet with a temperature of 80° and a dew point of 75°, the density altitude is 11,564 feet; with no humidity, the density altitude would be almost 500 feet lower. As air becomes less dense, it reduces power because the engine takes in less air, thrust because a propeller is less efficient in thin air (there is less air for the propeller to work with), and lift because the thin air exerts less force on the airfoils. A pilot cannot detect the effect of high density altitude on the airspeed indicator. The aircraft lifts off, climbs, cruises, glides, and lands at the prescribed indicated airspeeds, but at a specified indicated airspeed, the true airspeed and groundspeed increase proportionally as density altitude becomes higher. High density altitude lengthens the takeoff and landing rolls and reduces the rate of climb. Before lift-off the plane must attain a faster groundspeed and needs more runway, and the reduced power and thrust add a need for still more runway; at a prescribed indicated airspeed it flies at a faster true airspeed, which means climbing at a shallower angle. An average small airplane requiring 1,000 feet for takeoff at sea level under standard atmospheric conditions will require a takeoff run of approximately 2,000 feet at an operational altitude of 5,000 feet. Density altitude is determined by first finding pressure altitude and then correcting it for nonstandard temperature. The pressure altitude can be determined by any of the three following methods: by setting the barometric scale of the altimeter to 29.92 "Hg and reading the indicated altitude, by applying a correction factor to the indicated altitude according to the reported altimeter setting, or by using a flight computer. Using a flight computer, density altitude can be computed by inputting the pressure altitude and outside air temperature; it can also be determined from a density altitude chart. In the handbook's density altitude chart example, an airport elevation of 5,883 feet with an altimeter setting of 30.10 "Hg reads -165 in the conversion column, so subtracting 165 feet gives a pressure altitude of 5,718 feet; at an outside air temperature of 70°F, the chart gives an approximate density altitude of 7,700 feet. The pilot must make an accurate prediction of takeoff distance from the performance data of the AFM/POH, regardless of the runway available. The most critical conditions of takeoff performance are the result of some combination of high gross weight, altitude, temperature, and unfavorable wind. Although an aircraft is certified for a specified maximum gross takeoff weight, it may not safely take off at this weight under all conditions: conditions that affect takeoff and climb performance, such as high elevations, high temperatures, and high humidity (high density altitudes), may require a reduction in weight before flight is attempted. Maximum surface air temperature usually occurs during the midafternoon, and minimum surface air temperature usually occurs shortly after sunrise. Advancing or delaying a departure may reduce risk likelihood, and canceling a flight is necessary if the pilot cannot mitigate risk sufficiently by other means. Any attempt to take off below the recommended speed means that the aircraft could stall, be difficult to control, or have a very low initial rate of climb. In the handbook's case study, a takeoff at maximum gross weight from Animas Air Park (elevation 6,684 feet, where July temperatures result in a high density altitude) had a calculated takeoff distance of 4,700 feet, and the pilot's 20 percent safety factor produced a desired runway length of 5,640 feet, which exceeds the available 5,000-foot runway. She reduced the departure fuel load and had her passengers board at an airport with a 9,200-foot runway instead. At airports with elevations of 2,000 feet and higher, control towers and FSSs broadcast the advisory "Check Density Altitude" when the temperature reaches a predetermined level; the pilot retains the responsibility to compute density altitude, when appropriate, as a part of preflight duties. The handbook's sample takeoff distance chart notes that prior to takeoff from fields above 3,000 feet elevation, the mixture should be leaned to give maximum rpm in a full throttle, static runup.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapters 4, 10 and 11

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature: the height in the standard atmosphere where today's air density would be found. Your airplane performs as if it were there, whatever its real altitude. It is a measure of air density, not a height to fly by. High elevation, heat, humidity and low pressure all raise it. A high density altitude means a longer takeoff and landing roll and a weaker climb.

figure.caption: The field's own elevation, and the higher density altitude the airplane performs at on a hot day.
figure.alt: A valley airfield seen from the side under a mountain face. A white line along the runway is labelled FIELD ELEVATION; a dashed amber line higher up, with an arrow up to it, is labelled PERFORMS AS IF HERE.

article.heading: What raises it
paragraphs: High elevations, low pressure, high temperatures and high humidity all raise density altitude. Lower elevations, high pressure, low temperatures and low humidity point to a low one.

Temperature is the most important of the weather factors. Hot days make the air less dense, and cold days make it denser. Low pressure thins the air too, so an altimeter setting below 29.92 inches pushes density altitude up.

Humidity is a smaller factor. Water vapor is lighter than air, so moist air is less dense than dry air. In the handbook's example, at 8,000 feet with a temperature of 80° and a dew point of 75°, the density altitude is 11,564 feet. With no humidity it would be almost 500 feet lower.

figure.caption: A high field in hard afternoon sun: two of the four things that raise density altitude.
figure.alt: A Cessna 172 parked on the ramp of a high mountain-valley airfield in hard afternoon light, with bare peaks behind. Labels read 1 HIGH FIELD and 2 HOT AFTERNOON SUN.

article.heading: What it does to the airplane
paragraphs: Thin air takes power from the engine, because the engine takes in less air. It takes thrust from the propeller and lift from the wing.

You can't detect the effect on the airspeed indicator. You lift off, climb and land at the usual indicated airspeeds, but your true airspeed and groundspeed are higher. So you need more runway to get airborne, and the lost power and thrust add still more. At a given indicated airspeed you climb at a shallower angle, and the landing roll is longer too.
Take an average small airplane that needs 1,000 feet to take off at sea level on a standard day. At an operational altitude of 5,000 feet, it needs about 2,000.

figure.caption: The same runway, two takeoffs. At a high density altitude the roll is longer and the climb shallower. The angles are drawn steeper than real to show the difference.
figure.alt: A runway seen from the side. A dashed white path labelled LOW DENSITY ALTITUDE leaves the runway early and climbs steeply, with a faint Cessna 172 on it. An amber path labelled HIGH DENSITY ALTITUDE leaves much further along and climbs at a shallower angle, with a solid Cessna 172 on it. An amber bracket under the runway marks the EXTRA ROLL.

article.heading: Working it out
paragraphs: First find pressure altitude. Set the altimeter to 29.92 inches and read it, correct the field elevation for the reported altimeter setting, or use a flight computer. Then correct it for temperature with a density altitude chart or a flight computer.

In the handbook's chart example, the airport elevation is 5,883 feet and the altimeter setting is 30.10 inches. The conversion column reads minus 165, so the pressure altitude is 5,718 feet. At 70°F, the chart gives about 7,700 feet.
At airports 2,000 feet and higher, towers and flight service stations broadcast "Check density altitude" when the temperature climbs. Working it out is still part of your own preflight.

article.heading: Three mistakes on a hot, high day
paragraphs: Run the numbers before you decide. Take the takeoff distance and climb from your POH whatever the runway length, then add a margin. Read the charts at the real pressure altitude and temperature, with your weight and today's wind. Allow for the runway's slope and surface too. Being certified for a maximum gross weight doesn't mean you can take off at it today.

Change the plan when the numbers don't fit. Take less weight, use a longer runway or go when it's cooler. The day's lowest temperature usually comes shortly after sunrise, and the highest in the midafternoon. If none of that is enough, don't go.

Lift off at the recommended speed, not before it. Below that speed the airplane could stall, be hard to control or climb very slowly. Lean as your POH says. The handbook's sample takeoff chart, for one airplane, leans for maximum rpm in a full-throttle static runup before takeoff from fields above 3,000 feet.

figure.caption: Just after sunrise is usually the coolest time of the day to take off.
figure.alt: A Cessna 172 on the runway of the same airfield just after sunrise, the sun clearing the peaks on the left, labelled USUALLY THE DAY'S COOLEST.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for what?
2. Which weather factor matters most to density altitude?
3. Why does a high density altitude lengthen the takeoff roll when you still lift off at the usual indicated airspeed?
4. Your takeoff distance is 4,700 feet, you add a 20 percent margin and the runway is 5,000 feet. Do you go?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Nonstandard temperature, once you have the pressure altitude.
2. Temperature, because hot days make the air less dense.
3. Your true airspeed and groundspeed are higher at that indicated airspeed, and the engine and propeller give you less power and thrust to reach it.
4. Not like that, because 4,700 feet plus 20 percent is 5,640 feet. Take less weight, use a longer runway or wait for cooler air, and if it still doesn't fit, don't go.

posts.title: How the pitot tube works
posts.headline: Block the tube's front with its drain clear and the needle reads zero. Seal the drain too and it acts like an altimeter.
posts.alt: The 172P's airspeed indicator over a Cessna 172 climbing in grey cloud. The needle points at 158 on the red line, which is ringed in white, beside the gold label 158 KT and RED LINE, while a glowing cyan outline needle labelled 70 KT marks the airplane's real speed. Not to scale.
posts.related_text: On the Cessna 172P the pitot tube is mounted on the lower surface of the left wing and the static port on the lower left side of the forward fuselage, and the airspeed indicator needs both. Pressure from the pitot tube fills a diaphragm inside the airspeed indicator, the case around it is kept at static (outside) pressure from the static port, and the needle shows the difference, the dynamic pressure that grows with speed. Moisture including ice, dirt or insects can block the tube; at Brisbane Airport, mud-nesting keyhole wasps fully blocked 3D-printed replica pitot probes 93 times in 39 months, and the first mud in a probe is enough to upset the airspeed reading. With the front opening and the drain hole both blocked, the pressure in the tube is trapped and, with the static port clear, the airspeed indicator works like an altimeter: it reads higher in a climb and lower in a descent, whatever the real speed. Computed in the standard atmosphere, a tube sealed at 70 KIAS at 3,000 ft reads about 158 KIAS after a 1,000 ft climb with no change in real speed; 158 KIAS is the 172P's red line.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 8

citations.ref: House, Ring and Shaw (2020), keyhole wasps and pitot probes, PLOS ONE 15(11) e0242063
citations.title: House, Ring and Shaw (2020), PLOS ONE 15(11): e0242063
citations.note: the keyhole wasp study at Brisbane Airport

posts.credits: 3D model: “Cessna172” by KOG_THORNS (sketchfab.com), CC BY 4.0, modified.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: The airspeed indicator compares two pressures. Air rammed into the pitot tube under the left wing fills a diaphragm, and outside air from a static port fills the case around it. The needle shows the difference between them.

Block the tube's front with its drain hole clear and the needle falls to zero. Block the drain too and the needle follows altitude. Sealed at 70 KIAS (knots indicated airspeed), a 1,000 ft climb reads about 158, the 172P's red line.

article.heading: How the needle reads two pressures
paragraphs: On the Cessna 172P, the pitot tube hangs under the left wing. A pitot tube has a front opening and a small drain hole for moisture. The static port is a small hole low on the left side of the forward fuselage.
The front opening catches ram air at total pressure, the outside air's static pressure plus dynamic pressure, the extra pressure from motion.
