A line carries it into a thin diaphragm inside the airspeed indicator. The case around it holds static pressure from the port, so the static part cancels and only dynamic pressure pushes. Fly faster and it grows. The diaphragm swells, and a linkage turns the needle.

figure.caption: Inside the airspeed indicator. Ram air (gold) fills the diaphragm, static air (light blue) fills the case around it, and the needle shows the difference. The cutaway follows the FAA handbook's generic airspeed indicator, not a Cessna parts drawing.
figure.alt: A cutaway of an airspeed indicator: a gold line labelled Ram air feeds a gold diaphragm inside a case filled light blue and labelled Static air, a linkage runs to the needle on the 172P's dial, and a banner above reads RAM minus STATIC to AIRSPEED.

article.heading: A blocked front reads zero
paragraphs: Ice, dirt or insects can block a pitot tube. A nest in the front can leave the drain hole as the only opening. The air inside vents through the drain to outside pressure. Both sides of the diaphragm match, so the needle reads zero.

At Brisbane Airport, 3D-printed replica probes, not the airplanes' real ones, were watched for 39 months. Mud-nesting keyhole wasps fully blocked them 93 times, the first within two weeks. Even the first bit of mud in a probe upsets the airspeed reading.

figure.caption: An X-ray of the tube's front. The mud nest (red) stops the ram air (gold arrows), and the needle rests at zero. The drain hole (the light-blue disc) is drawn larger so it shows.
figure.alt: An X-ray of the pitot tube's cone in gold with a red mud plug labelled Mud nest in its front opening, gold arrows of ram air stopped at the plug, light-blue outside air inside the tube, a glowing light-blue drain hole underneath and an airspeed indicator inset at zero.

article.heading: Ice on both holes makes an altimeter
paragraphs: In visible moisture, ice can seal the drain hole as well as the front. The air in the tube is then trapped, and speed changes no longer reach the needle.
Now climb. The static pressure in the case falls while the trapped pressure stays, so the diaphragm swells and the needle rises. Descend and it falls. It now works like an altimeter.
In the standard atmosphere, a 1,000 ft climb from 3,000 ft lowers the case pressure by about an inch of mercury. The trapped pressure stays put, and the diaphragm reads that extra inch as speed.

That 158 assumes a perfect seal and trapped air that keeps its temperature. Sealed at sea level, the same climb reads about 164, and from 6,000 ft about 152. Let the trapped air cool by 1 °C and it reads about 152.

The 172P POH's inadvertent icing checklist starts with pitot heat on (if installed), then turn back or change altitude. Heat keeps the tube working in possible icing conditions, but the POH prohibits flight into icing conditions.

figure.caption: Rime ice building over the tube's front opening in cloud.
figure.alt: A close view from below of the pitot tube's cone in grey cloud, with white rime ice built up over its front opening and a red label Ice pointing at it.

article.heading: Three mistakes a blocked tube punishes
paragraphs: Remove the pitot tube cover and check the tube's front opening and drain hole on every preflight. A cover keeps bugs out of a parked airplane's tube.

Check the static source opening too. A blocked static port makes the airspeed read low above the altitude where it blocked, and high below it. The altimeter freezes and the vertical speed indicator reads zero. Some 172Ps have an alternate static source valve below the throttle, and POH Section 5 gives its effect on airspeed.

Watch the airspeed rise as the takeoff roll begins. At rest, a blocked tube reads zero too. A needle still at zero on the roll is abnormal, and the Airplane Flying Handbook says abnormal situations can require rejecting the takeoff while still on the runway.

figure.caption: The pitot tube is the small tube under the left wing, ringed and magnified here. The pictures on this page are frames of the reel, not to scale. Reel credits: 3D model “Cessna172” by KOG_THORNS (sketchfab.com), CC BY 4.0, modified. Engine sound “1978 Cessna 172 Departure” by Wingspan Adventures & Flight (youtube.com), CC BY 3.0, modified.
figure.alt: A white Cessna 172P on the ramp, labelled CESSNA 172P, with the pitot tube under its left wing ringed in gold and labelled Pitot tube, and a magnified circle showing the tube.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. The airspeed stays at zero as your takeoff roll begins. Which blockage fits?
2. Sealed at 70 KIAS at 3,000 ft, what does the needle read after a 1,000 ft climb at the same speed?
3. You add power in level flight and the needle holds a normal-looking speed without moving. Which blockage fits?
4. Which openings do you check on the preflight so the airspeed indicator works?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. The tube's front opening, whether or not its drain hole is clear, because no ram air reaches the diaphragm.
2. About 158 KIAS, the red line, because the case pressure falls while the trapped pressure stays.
3. Both of the tube's openings. Trapped pressure ignores speed, and level flight holds the altitude too.
4. The tube's front opening and drain hole, with the cover off, and the static source opening.

posts.title: How the stall horn works
posts.headline: A slot in the left wing, a tube and a reed horn that runs on air.
posts.alt: An X-ray view of a white Cessna 172 with the stall warning tube, drawn in gold, running from the cabin along the left wing to the slot in its leading edge, where red arrows labelled AIR OUT leave it. Not to scale.
posts.related_text: The Cessna 172P's stall warning is pneumatic, with an inlet in the leading edge of the left wing, an air-operated horn near the upper left corner of the windshield, and the plumbing between them. At a low angle of attack the airflow virtually stops at a stagnation point close to the leading edge, where the stall warning inlet sits. As the airplane approaches a stall, the point where the air splits moves under the leading edge, the low pressure on the upper surface moves forward around the leading edge, and the differential pressure draws air through the warning horn. The horn sounds 5 to 10 knots above the stall in all flight conditions; it doesn't read airspeed, and stall warning devices alert the pilot when approaching the critical angle of attack, the angle at which a wing stalls regardless of airspeed. Power off at 2,400 lb with flaps up, the 172P stalls at about 44 KIAS wings level and about 62 KIAS in a level 60-degree bank (POH Figure 5-3, approximate values); in that bank the load factor is 2, and the stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor. On the preflight, check the stall warning opening for stoppage, then place a clean handkerchief over the opening and apply suction; a sound from the warning horn confirms the system works.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapters 4 and 5

posts.credits: 3D model: “Cessna172” by KOG_THORNS (sketchfab.com), CC BY 4.0, modified.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: The 172P's stall horn is pneumatic, and air drawn through it makes the sound. It reacts to angle of attack, the angle at which the wing meets the oncoming air, and it doesn't measure airspeed.
That is why it sounds 5 to 10 knots above the stall in all flight conditions, steep turns included. Test it on every walkaround with suction through a clean handkerchief over its opening.

article.heading: Where the inlet and the horn sit
paragraphs: Walk to the left wing and look at its leading edge, the rounded front edge that meets the air first. The small opening there is the stall warning inlet.
Plumbing runs from that inlet to an air-operated horn near the upper left corner of the windshield. The wing end senses the stall coming, and the horn makes the sound.

figure.caption: The stall warning inlet is the small slot in the left wing's leading edge, seen in the circle. The pictures on this page are frames of the reel, not to scale. 3D model: “Cessna172” by KOG_THORNS (sketchfab.com), CC BY 4.0, modified.
figure.alt: A white Cessna 172P seen from above over farmland, labelled CESSNA 172P and LEFT WING ONLY, with a magnified circle on the left wing's leading edge showing the dark inlet slot.

article.heading: What the air does at the inlet
paragraphs: At a low angle of attack the air meets the wing at a stagnation point. That is a spot close to the leading edge where the flow virtually stops. The inlet sits there, so the air just pushes in and the horn stays quiet.

Raise the nose and slow down. As the angle grows, the point where the air splits slides lower, under the leading edge. The low pressure on the upper surface moves forward around the leading edge, over the inlet.
The inlet now sits in lower pressure than the cabin air at the horn. That difference pulls cabin air in through the horn, along the tube and out of the slot. The reed sounds.

figure.caption: Nose up, the air now splits at the white dot, under the leading edge, and the blue dashes mark where it split at the slot in normal flight. The low pressure on top wraps forward over the gold slot. Not to scale.
figure.alt: A cross-section of the wing's leading edge at a high angle of attack, with dashed airflow lines curving around it and a red band labelled LOW PRESSURE wrapping forward over the gold slot.

article.heading: Why it still warns in a steep turn
paragraphs: For a given flap setting the 172P always stalls at the same angle of attack. Weight and bank angle don't change that angle.

The stall speed does change. Roll into a level 60-degree bank and the load factor, the load on the wing compared with straight-and-level flight, becomes 2. To hold altitude you add angle of attack, so the wing reaches its stall angle at a higher speed.

A load factor of 2 multiplies the stall speed by the square root of 2, about 1.41, a 41 percent rise. At 2,400 lb with flaps up and power off, that takes the stall from about 44 KIAS, knots of indicated airspeed, to about 62 KIAS.
The horn doesn't read airspeed. It answers the low pressure at the inlet, which follows the angle.

table.caption: Cessna 172P power-off stall speeds in KIAS (POH Figure 5-3) at 2,400 lb and the most rearward center of gravity, approximate as the POH gives them. At the most forward center of gravity the flaps 10° speeds are 2 to 3 knots higher.

article.heading: Three mistakes the horn invites
paragraphs: Check the stall warning opening for stoppage on every walkaround. It is item 3 of the left wing's leading edge check. Put a clean handkerchief over it before you apply suction, and a sound from the horn confirms the system works.

Ease the nose down when the horn sounds while you maneuver, whatever the airspeed indicator shows. In a steep turn it can sound at a speed that would feel comfortable wings level. Less angle of attack silences it. Then roll the wings level and add power. The POH notes that a stall recovery may lose as much as 230 feet.
Keep reading the wing's own cues when the horn stays quiet. A stall warning system can fail. Aerodynamic buffet, loss of roll authority or a descent you cannot stop still point to a stall.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. In a 172P at 2,400 lb, flaps up and power off, roughly what is the stall speed in a level 60-degree bank?
2. Why does a horn that doesn't read airspeed still sound before the stall in that steep turn?
3. You apply suction through a handkerchief over the stall warning opening and hear nothing. What has the check told you?
4. Which cue do you trust when the airframe buffets and the ailerons lose authority but the horn stays quiet?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. About 62 KIAS. A load factor of 2 multiplies the 44 KIAS wings-level stall by the square root of 2, about 1.41. The horn sounds 5 to 10 knots above that.
2. It reacts to the low pressure reaching the inlet, which follows angle of attack. The wing stalls at the same angle in the turn, only at a higher speed.
3. Nothing proves it works yet. Check the opening for stoppage, seal the handkerchief and try again. If it stays silent, the stall warning isn't working, so have it fixed before you fly.
4. Trust the buffet and the weak ailerons. A stall warning system can fail, and those cues still tell you a stall is close, so lower the angle of attack.

posts.title: Compass acceleration error
posts.headline: Speed up heading east and the compass shows a turn toward north.
posts.alt: Compass acceleration error: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Speed up heading east and the compass shows a turn toward north.
posts.related_text: On an easterly or westerly heading, accelerating makes the magnetic compass indicate a turn toward north, and decelerating a turn toward south; the memory aid is ANDS, Acceleration North, Deceleration South. The error comes from the magnetic dip and the inertia of the pendulous card: accelerating tips the aft end of the card up and decelerating tips it down, and the dip acts on the tilted card. On a north or south heading, diving, climbing or changing airspeed causes no compass error. The compass indicates correctly only while its card is horizontal, so the swing during a speed change on an east or west heading is an error, not a turn; read the compass again once the speed is steady. This is the Northern Hemisphere behaviour, where Earth's magnetic field dips down into the ground, more steeply nearer the Magnetic North Pole.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 8

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: On an east or west heading, the compass shows a turn toward north as you gain speed and toward south as you lose it. Pilots carry it as ANDS, Acceleration North, Deceleration South.
That swing is an error, so keep the wings level and take a fresh reading once the airspeed stops changing.

article.heading: How the compass card hangs
paragraphs: Inside the compass, two small magnets ride on a metal float, sealed in a bowl of clear fluid much like kerosene. The card is a scale wrapped around the float. You read it through a window against the lubber line, a fixed mark across the glass.
Its letters mark north, east, south and west, with a number every 30° between them and the last zero left off. So 3 means 30°, 6 means 60° and 33 means 330°.

The float hangs from a pivot with its center of gravity below it, like a pendulum. Earth's magnetic field runs level with the ground only at the Magnetic Equator, halfway between the magnetic poles. Everywhere else it tilts, and that tilt against the ground is called magnetic dip.

Because the float hangs low and is heavy, the field's downward pull is too weak to tip it, so the card stays level. This hanging, or pendulous, mounting is what lets one compass work at all latitudes away from the poles without a correction for dip.

article.heading: Why a speed change tips the card
paragraphs: You're eastbound, and you push the power up. The float has inertia, the tendency of a mass to resist a change in its motion, so it lags behind as the airplane gathers speed. That lag tips the aft end of the card up, so its front tips down. Slowing down tips it the other way.

Now the card is no longer level, and the compass reads correctly only while it is. On the tilted card, the field's downward pull drags the magnet's north end down, and that turns the card so the reading swings toward north.
That rotation of the card is acceleration error. The reading moves although your heading hasn't, and it stops once a steady speed lets the card hang level again.
Everything here is the Northern Hemisphere case. There the field dips downward toward the north, and the dip grows steeper as you near the Magnetic North Pole.

figure.caption: Speeding up eastbound, the card's front tips down, and the dip pulls it so the reading swings toward north.
figure.alt: A high-wing trainer seen from the side over farmland, below a compass card drawn as a tilted dark disc with labels Front down and Magnetic dip, magenta arrows sloping into the ground, Northern Hemisphere above, and a compass reading between E and 6 labelled Speeding up and Shows north.

article.heading: Which headings show the error
paragraphs: Point the nose north or south and a speed change brings no compass error. Climbing and diving on those headings bring none either.
East and west are where it shows. Eastbound, a false turn toward north makes the heading numbers fall, and westbound it makes them rise. Slowing down reverses both.

figure.caption: Heading north, the same speed change leaves the compass on N.
figure.alt: A trainer seen from above flying north along a road, labelled Speeding up, beside a compass reading N with the label No swing.

article.heading: Three easy mistakes with a power change
paragraphs: Hold the wings level and let the card swing. Turning to chase the reading back steers you off a heading you never left.

Set the heading indicator, the gyro instrument you line up with the compass, only in steady flight. Set it during a speed change and it copies the error. If the card still wobbles once you're steady, use the average of its swings.

Make power changes smoothly and read the compass only once the airspeed has settled, not when the throttle stops moving. Abrupt changes of speed or attitude send the card moving erratically and make it very hard to read.

figure.caption: Hold the wings level through the swing: the red airplane chased it and ended off its heading.
figure.alt: A trainer seen from above flying west along a road with the label Speed steady and a compass reading W, and a red airplane turned off the road below it, labelled Off heading, with its own compass.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. What has your heading done if, flying east, the reading creeps from E toward 6 while the speed builds after you add power?
2. Are you turning if, heading west with the wings level, the reading slides from W toward 24 as you slow down?
3. Should the compass swing when you're flying north and the airspeed rises after you add power?
4. Should you set the heading indicator to the compass while flying east with the speed still building?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. It hasn't changed. That swing is acceleration error, and 6 means 60°, on the north side of E.
2. No. 24 sits on the south side of W, which is exactly where slowing down drags the reading on a west heading.
3. No. North is one of the two headings where a change of airspeed brings no compass error.
4. No. Wait until the speed is steady, or you set the heading indicator to the false turn toward north.

posts.title: Magnetic compass errors
posts.headline: Turning toward north, roll out before the compass shows north.
posts.alt: Magnetic compass errors: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Turning toward north, roll out before the compass shows north.
posts.related_text: The magnetic compass reads correctly only while its card is horizontal; in a bank the card tilts with the airplane, and the dip of Earth's magnetic field then turns it. In the Northern Hemisphere, turning toward north the reading falls behind the real heading (the handbooks say the card leads), so stop the turn before the compass reaches north; turning toward south the reading runs ahead (the card lags), so let the compass pass south first. One rule of thumb is 15 degrees plus half the latitude, early toward north and late toward south: near 40 degrees north that is 15 + 20 = 35 degrees. On an easterly or westerly heading, accelerating shows a turn toward north and decelerating a turn toward south (ANDS); on a north or south heading, a change of airspeed causes no error. The float and card tilt freely to about 18 degrees of bank, and the compass reads erratically in a steeper bank; after a roll-out the card swings around the heading before it settles, so use the average of the swings.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 8

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Steering by the magnetic compass in the Northern Hemisphere, stop a turn to north before the compass reaches north. On a turn to south, let the compass pass south before you stop. Near 40 degrees north, one rule of thumb makes each allowance about 35 degrees.

article.heading: Why the card reads wrong in a bank
paragraphs: Magnets on a float line it up with Earth's field. A card on the float carries the headings, read at the lubber line.
Earth's magnetic field runs level with the ground only at the magnetic equator. Nearer the magnetic north pole it slopes down into the ground, and that angle is called dip.

The float sits on a pivot and is weighted below it, so it hangs like a pendulum, too heavy for dip to tip. In a coordinated bank it hangs toward the airplane's own floor, so the card tilts with the airplane, and dip starts to turn it.

Turning toward north, dip swings the tilted card the same way you turn, so the lubber line's number falls behind your real heading. Turning toward south, the card is held back and the number runs ahead. The handbooks say it from the card's side: the card leads toward north and lags toward south.

figure.caption: Banked left toward north, the card tilts with the airplane and dip drags it the same way you turn, so its reading falls behind.
figure.alt: Seen from behind, a high-wing trainer banks left over farmland below a tilted compass card drawn as a dark disc. Magenta arrows show Earth's field dipping into the ground, and labels read Northern Hemisphere, Magnetic dip, Tilted card, and 035 Falls behind.

article.heading: Sizing the roll-out for your latitude
paragraphs: The error grows nearer the magnetic poles, so the allowance depends on latitude. The FAA's Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge offers one rule of thumb: 15 degrees plus half your latitude.

The Instrument Flying Handbook gives a second method for compass turns at a 15 to 18 degree bank. Turning to north, start the roll-out about your latitude before north, plus the few degrees you normally allow for rolling out. Turning to south, start it once the compass has passed south by about your latitude, minus those few degrees. Its example, from east at 30 degrees north in a 15 degree bank, starts the roll-out at 037 for north and 203 for south.
The two give different numbers because both are rough. Whichever you use, roll out, let the card settle, then correct with small turns.

With the first rule, flying east near 40 degrees north, that is 15 + 20 = 35 degrees. Turning left to north, stop the turn when the compass reads 035, and the card settles on north. Turning right to south, let it pass south and stop the turn at 215.

figure.caption: Near 40 degrees north the rule of thumb gives 35 degrees both ways: stop the turn at 035 turning from east to north, and at 215 turning from east to south.
figure.alt: Two trainers seen from above, side by side. Under East to N, a compass reads 035 and the label says Early: 035. Under East to S, a compass reads 215 and the label says Late: 215. Below them: Undershoot N, overshoot S.

article.heading: False turns on the compass
paragraphs: Start a turn from a northerly heading and the reading at first falls behind, and may even show a turn the other way. Start one from a southerly heading and the reading runs ahead, showing more turn than you have made.
On an east or west heading, speed up and the compass swings toward north with your wings level. Slow down and it swings south. The memory aid is ANDS, Acceleration North, Deceleration South.
On a north or south heading, changing speed, climbing or diving causes no error.

article.heading: Three mistakes on a compass turn
paragraphs: Keep the bank under about 18 degrees in a compass turn. The float and card tilt freely only to about that angle, and in a steeper bank the readings turn erratic.
Read the average of the swings after you roll out, because the card swings around your heading before it settles.
Change attitude and airspeed smoothly, because abrupt changes set the card swinging erratically and make it very hard to read.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Flying east near 40 degrees north, you turn left toward north. At what compass reading do you stop the turn?
2. Using 15 plus half the latitude near 30 degrees north, how far past south should the compass go before you stop the turn?
3. Should you bank to correct the compass when it swings toward north as you speed up on a steady westerly heading?
4. Flying north, you roll into a right turn and the compass briefly shows a turn to the left. Is the compass faulty?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. At about 035, because 15 plus half of 40 is 35, and the card then settles on north.
2. By 30 degrees, because half of 30 is 15, and 15 plus 15 is 30.
3. No, keep the wings level. That swing is acceleration error, the A in ANDS, not a turn.
4. No. Starting a turn from a northerly heading, the reading falls behind at first and can briefly show a turn the other way.

posts.title: A microburst on final
posts.headline: Your headwind on entry becomes a tailwind on exit.
posts.alt: Cover slide titled Microbursts. A storm cell drops a heavy rain shaft beyond an airfield at dusk, with a Cessna 172 on final and the control tower at right. Text: Fly through one and a 45-knot headwind can become a 45-knot tailwind, a few hundred feet up.
caption: Fly through a microburst and a 45-knot headwind can become a 45-knot tailwind, a few hundred feet above the ground. Here's how to spot one, why a sudden airspeed jump is a warning, and why you can't count on getting one.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
posts.related_text: A microburst produces a headwind gain on entry followed by a downdraft and then a tailwind on exit. The initial airspeed increase is the warning, and reducing power to correct it removes the margin needed moments later.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: A microburst on final gives you a headwind that raises your airspeed, then a downdraft, then a tailwind that takes it away. That early gain is the warning. Don't reduce power to fix it, and be ready to go around. The margin you would trim off is the margin you need moments later.

article.heading: What a microburst does to the wind
paragraphs: A column of air drops out of a shower or thunderstorm and spreads outward in all directions when it reaches the ground. That is a microburst, the most severe kind of wind shear, meaning a sudden change in wind speed or direction over a small area.
Going in, the outflow, the air racing away from the center, meets you as a headwind. In the middle the air pushes you down, and coming out the outflow runs your way as a tailwind.

Vertical winds usually peak more than 500 ft above the ground. In the center of a strong microburst, the downdraft can exceed 3,000 fpm (feet per minute). How hard it hits you depends on your height and how near the center you pass.

table.caption: The size and strength of a typical microburst.

figure.caption: A microburst: a small, intense downdraft falls from the cloud and spreads out along the ground in every direction.
figure.alt: A dense rain column falls from a dark storm cloud onto farmland near an airfield and spreads outward at the ground. A blue arrow down the column is labelled downdraft, and arrows along the ground each way are labelled outflow.

article.heading: Why the airspeed gain is a trap
paragraphs: A rising headwind lifts your indicated airspeed and performance. The nose tends to pitch up as the airplane works back to its trim speed, leaving you fast and high.

Correcting that with less power and a lower nose sets up what comes next. The tailwind arrives and takes away airspeed and performance, and it finds you nose low with the power back. Recovery from there is harder, and the airplane can stall or land short of the runway.
So treat a rapid or large airspeed gain near convective weather, meaning showers and storms, as a possible sign of a coming loss. It may be reason enough to break off the approach.

figure.caption: The headwind's airspeed gain tempts you to take off power and lower the nose, so when the tailwind takes that airspeed away you sink below the approach path and land short of the runway.
figure.alt: The headwind's airspeed gain tempts you to take off power and lower the nose, so when the tailwind takes that airspeed away you sink below the approach path and land short of the runway.

article.heading: When the warning never comes
paragraphs: A microburst's outflow can be symmetric, the same on every side, but it is often asymmetric, stronger on some sides than others. Depending on your path, the gain going in may never appear, or may be much smaller than the loss coming out.

An intense rain shaft at the surface can mark a microburst. Sometimes the only visible clue is virga, rain streaks that never reach the ground, or a ring of blowing dust. If you've met or seen one, watch for another, since the same weather system can produce more than one.

figure.caption: Virga and a ring of blowing dust can be the only signs a microburst gives.
figure.alt: Grey streaks of virga hang from a dark cloud base over an airfield, fading before they reach the ground, and a ring of blowing dust spreads along the fields below. Both are labelled.

article.heading: Three easy mistakes in a microburst
paragraphs: Go around at the first sign of a microburst. Only 5 to 15 seconds may be available to recognize it and recover. At low altitude, recovery may be impossible.

Hold the nose at its normal pitch or higher as the airspeed falls, and accept the slower speed. The airplane's natural response to low airspeed is to pitch down, and letting it go there adds to the height you lose.
Fly a stabilized approach, holding one steady speed and path, so a bad trend stands out early. Feeding in power bit by bit may mask the first drop in airspeed.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. What should a sudden jump well above your target airspeed on final near a shower tell you?
2. Can you rule out a microburst near the airport if you see virga below the cloud base but no rain at the surface?
3. How should you handle pitch when the airspeed starts falling partway down final and the nose wants to drop?
4. If you fly into a microburst's outflow and feel no airspeed gain at all, can you expect a gentle exit?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. It may be a microburst's headwind, with a tailwind loss to follow. Keep the power in and be ready to go around.
2. No. Virga or a ring of blowing dust is sometimes the only visible sign of a microburst.
3. Hold pitch at normal or higher and accept the lower airspeed. Letting the nose drop to chase speed costs height you can't spare.
4. No. In an asymmetric microburst the gain going in may be small or missing, and the loss coming out much larger.

posts.title: Going around: power first
posts.headline: The moment you go around, power comes first.
posts.alt: Going around: power first: an illustrated diagram for pilots. The moment you go around, power comes first. The picture shows the house aircraft right of centre, nose raised a few degrees, climbing away from the runway; a ghost of the house aircraft below and slightly behind it, nose level, still descending toward the touchdown zone; two thin pale flight paths that part above the threshold, one bending up to the solid aircraft and one continuing down to the ghost; a blurred propeller disc on the solid aircraft. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Why does power come before attitude and configuration in a go-around?

Power goes in the instant you decide to go around, full and smooth, with no hesitation. Expect two reactions. The added power raises the nose and yaws the airplane left, so forward pressure and right rudder hold a safe attitude.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
posts.related_text: A go-around rests on three cardinal principles: power, attitude and configuration. Power is the first concern: the instant you decide to go around, apply full power smoothly and without hesitation. The added power raises the nose and yaws the airplane left, so expect forward pressure and right rudder to hold a safe attitude.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: A go-around, abandoning a landing to climb away, rests on three principles, which are power, attitude and configuration. The instant you decide, push in full power smoothly and without hesitation, and hold it until flying speed and control are back.

As the nose tries to rise and swing left, hold a safe attitude, its position against the horizon, with forward pressure and right rudder. The configuration, here the flaps, changes last, once the descent has stopped.

article.heading: Why the throttle moves before the yoke
paragraphs: A sinking airplane has inertia, a tendency to keep moving the way it already is, and it takes enough power to overcome it. Pitching up alone raises the angle of attack, the angle at which the wing meets the oncoming air, and bleeds off airspeed. The result is a faster sink, a stall close to the ground, or both.

Below stall speed an airplane cannot fly, and below minimum power required speed, where level flight takes the least power, it cannot climb. So resist pitching up for the climb until the airspeed is there, and in some cases lower the nose briefly to gain speed.

Full power here means full or maximum allowable takeoff power, put in positively. In some airplanes a jab at the throttle makes the engine falter, so keep the push smooth. If yours has carburetor heat, turn it off for maximum power.

article.heading: Holding the nose once the power is in
paragraphs: Expect to push hard to hold the nose level or in a safe climb attitude. Your trim, which takes the load off the controls, is still set for the slow approach. If the nose rises too early in a low go-around, the stall that follows could be unrecoverable.
The swing to the left comes from torque and P-factor, the left-turning effects of the engine and propeller under full power. Use as much right rudder as it takes to cancel them.
Once the speed is right and the climb pitch is set, give it a rough trim, a quick setting that eases the pressure. Fine-tune the trim when things have settled.

article.heading: Bringing the flaps up without losing lift
paragraphs: Fly the airplane before you reach for the flap handle. In airplanes with heavy control pressures at maximum power, reach for it with caution, because control comes first.

Bring the landing flaps partway up first, or to the takeoff setting, as the manufacturer recommends. Depending on height and speed, it is wise to raise them in small steps, giving the airplane time to speed up. Pulling them all up at once could take away lift and settle the airplane onto the ground.

figure.caption: What each of the three principles asks of your hands and feet, from the decision until the flaps are up.
figure.alt: What each of the three principles asks of your hands and feet, from the decision until the flaps are up.

article.heading: Two mistakes that spoil a go-around
paragraphs: Go around the moment the landing looks uncertain. The maneuver is not dangerous in itself, only when it is delayed unduly or flown badly. Delay normally comes from expecting the landing to work out, or from pride that treats going around as failure.

Don't trust the cushion of air you feel just above the runway. Near the ground the wing makes less induced drag, the drag that comes with making lift, and that is ground effect. That help is borrowed and repaid as you climb out. Climb too soon and you may not be able to climb, or even hold altitude, at full power.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. You decide to go around over the threshold with the airplane sinking. Why does power go in before you pull back?
2. Low and slow with full power just in, you feel the nose climbing by itself. How do you respond?
3. How should full flaps come up once the descent has stopped and your climb is set?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. It takes power to overcome the sinking airplane's inertia. Pulling back alone bleeds speed toward a faster sink, a low stall, or both.
2. Push firmly forward to hold the nose level or in a safe climb attitude, with right rudder to keep straight. Letting it rise early this low risks an unrecoverable stall.
3. Partway up or to the manufacturer's takeoff setting first, then in small steps as speed builds. All at once could cost lift and settle you onto the ground.

posts.title: What flight following does not do
posts.headline: With flight following on, the lookout is still yours.
posts.alt: What flight following does not do: an illustrated diagram for pilots. With flight following on, the lookout is still yours. The picture shows a small radar antenna on a far hilltop at the left edge with five or six thin pale lines fanning out to the right; the lowest radar line grazing the crest of a substantial ridge just right of centre; a lee valley on the ridge's right side in deep shadow, below the lowest radar line, with no line entering it; the solid house aircraft upper right of centre, nose right, wings level, inside the radar lines. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Does flight following mean ATC will call out every airplane near you?

Radar limits and a busy controller both cut the traffic calls you hear, as do heavy traffic and a crowded frequency. A quiet frequency is no proof of an empty sky. Seeing and avoiding other aircraft stays with you.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
posts.related_text: Radar traffic information can be limited by the radar itself, the volume of traffic, controller workload and frequency congestion. The service does not relieve the pilot of the responsibility to see and avoid other aircraft.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Flight following is radar traffic advice that ATC gives a VFR pilot who asks for it. The controller tells you about targets close enough to your position or route to deserve a look. Some targets may never get a call, for reasons you can't see from the cockpit. Keep watching for other aircraft and keep clear of them yourself, all flight, because the service never takes that over.

article.heading: Why a traffic call may never come
paragraphs: You cruise with flight following, and the frequency stays quiet for a long stretch. Nothing may be near you, or a call may have had no way to reach you.

Many things could stop a call. Among them are the radar's own limits, the volume of traffic, the controller's workload and a crowded frequency. A controller tied up with other airplanes, or a frequency with no gap to speak in, can leave your call unsaid.
The controller alone decides whether they can give the service, or keep giving it. They needn't tell you the reason, so the quiet doesn't tell you which case you're in.

Some traffic may not show on the screen at all. If part of the radar is out of service, ATC normally says so. Then the display shows only aircraft reporting through a transponder or ADS-B, and anything without them in use can't be called.

article.heading: Why the clock position can be off
paragraphs: A call tells you where to look, on the 12-hour clock around your airplane. A typical one is traffic 10 o'clock, 3 miles, westbound, with distance in nautical miles. Type and altitude follow only if known.

The controller sees only your track, the path over the ground, and never your heading, where the nose points. When you crab, angling the nose into the wind to hold your track, the two differ. Your clock turns with the nose, but the call's clock stays lined up with the track.
In the AIM's example, traffic called at 12 o'clock would appear at 2 o'clock to one pilot and 10 o'clock to another. A call of 2 o'clock would appear at 3 o'clock to a third.
A fourth pilot, needing no wind correction, would see the traffic right where it was called, at 11 o'clock. Turning just as a call comes in can throw it off the same way.
Altitude has its own gap. Radar gives none unless the other airplane has Mode C, the transponder feature that reports altitude, and the facility can display it.

figure.caption: The call is set to your track, so with the nose crabbed left, traffic called at 12 o'clock sits at 2 o'clock through the windshield.
figure.alt: The call is set to your track, so with the nose crabbed left, traffic called at 12 o'clock sits at 2 o'clock through the windscreen.

article.heading: Three mistakes with flight following
paragraphs: Keep scanning the whole sky after a call, well beyond the spot it named. A call covers one target the controller saw and had time to report, and others may be nearby with no call at all.
Treat a called altitude as a lead to confirm with your eyes. It may come from Mode C that nobody has checked against what that pilot reports.

Choose your own way to keep clear once you see the traffic. The service gives no vector, a heading to fly away from traffic, unless you ask for one. Even then, the controller gives it only as far as they can.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Can you treat the sky as clear when flight following on a busy frequency has gone a long stretch without a traffic call?
2. You're crabbing with the nose left of your track when ATC calls traffic at 12 o'clock. Where should you look first?
3. ATC calls traffic with an altitude taken from its Mode C. Can you count on that altitude being right?
4. Traffic the controller called is in sight and closing. Should you hold your heading until ATC turns you?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. No. A busy frequency is one of the things that can stop calls, and the controller needn't tell you why, so keep scanning.
2. Look right of the nose. The call's clock is set to your track, and your track runs right of where the nose points.
3. No. It may be unverified, so find the traffic and judge its height yourself.
4. No. Act to keep clear yourself as soon as you need to, because ATC won't turn you away from traffic on its own.

posts.title: Where Class G ends
posts.headline: Rising ground can lift Class E's floor above you.
posts.alt: A forested ridge under a blue Class E floor that follows the ground, 1,200 ft AGL above the crest. A Cessna holding 3,500 feet MSL is 1,000 ft AGL over the crest, below the floor, in Class G. Printed above is the subtraction 3,500 minus 2,500 equals 1,000 ft. Not to scale.
posts.related_text: Class G is the uncontrolled airspace not designated Class A, B, C, D or E, and it runs from the surface up to the base of the overlying Class E, which is 1,200 feet AGL unless the chart designates otherwise. A floor set in feet AGL rises and falls with the terrain; over a 1,500-foot MSL valley a 1,200-foot AGL floor lies at 2,700 feet MSL, and over a 2,500-foot MSL crest at 3,700 feet MSL, so an airplane holding 3,500 feet MSL passes from Class E into Class G where no Class B, C or D is designated. Under 14 CFR 91.155 an airplane in Class G at or below 1,200 feet above the surface needs 1 statute mile and clear of clouds by day; by night it needs 3 statute miles and 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds, as in Class E below 10,000 feet MSL; at night in a traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway it may instead fly clear of clouds with at least 1 statute mile. Class G more than 1,200 feet above the surface and below 10,000 feet MSL needs 1 statute mile by day and 3 statute miles by night, with 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds; under 14 CFR 91.155(e) an aircraft operating at the base altitude of a Class E area is considered to be within the airspace directly below it. Near airports with an approved instrument procedure, Class E transition areas, for aircraft transitioning to and from the terminal or en route environment, often begin at 700 feet AGL, marked by a magenta vignette, and they remain in effect continuously, regardless of airport operating hours or surface area status. A Class E surface area, drawn with a magenta dashed line, brings Class E down to the surface; a surface area operating less than continuously is indicated by a note on the sectional, the airport's Chart Supplement page gives its status, and a part-time surface area may become Class G while it is not in effect. A blue vignette marks floors other than 700 feet that border Class G, a 700-foot floor keeps its magenta vignette where it borders Class G, differing floors above 700 feet carry a symbol and a number, and some Class E begins at an MSL altitude that stays level; except where Class E is designated lower, it begins at 14,500 feet MSL and extends up to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL, so there Class G reaches up to 14,500 feet MSL; that Class E leaves out the air less than 1,500 feet above the surface.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 15
FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide (VFR Terms and Symbols), page 17
citations.note: how the FAA's charts draw each airspace

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Where no Class B, C or D is designated, uncontrolled Class G runs from the surface up to the base of controlled Class E. Unless the sectional shows otherwise, that base is 1,200 feet AGL, above ground level. So it rises and falls with the terrain. Check the class wherever the ground changes, and fly that class's weather minimums.

article.heading: Why the floor rises with the ground
paragraphs: A floor set in feet AGL is measured from the ground directly below it. Copy the ground's profile, raise it 1,200 feet, and you have the floor.
Start over a valley at 1,500 feet MSL, above mean sea level. The Class E floor sits at 2,700 feet MSL there, so an airplane level at 3,500 feet MSL is above it, in Class E.

Hold that altitude toward a ridge whose crest is 2,500 feet MSL. The floor climbs the slope with the ground and reaches 3,700 feet MSL over the crest. You are now 200 feet below it and, with no Class B, C or D designated, in Class G. Same altitude, new airspace.

figure.caption: A floor set at 1,200 feet AGL sits 1,200 feet above the valley, the slope and the crest alike, so it climbs where the ground climbs. Not to scale.
figure.alt: A valley and a ridge under a blue Class E floor that follows the terrain, with 1,200 ft AGL marked over the valley, the slope and the crest, under the title "AGL floors follow the terrain". Not to scale.

article.heading: What crossing the floor changes
paragraphs: Under visual flight rules (VFR), your minimums, the least visibility and cloud clearance allowed, depend on the airspace class and your altitude. Over the ridge you are 1,000 feet above the crest, so the table's first row applies by day.
The night row for low Class G matches Class E below 10,000 feet MSL, apart from one traffic-pattern exception. So over this ridge, the crossing changes your minimums only by day.

table.caption: Weather minimums for airplanes below 10,000 feet MSL. Class G is more than 1,200 feet above the ground only under a higher floor, such as where it reaches 14,500 feet MSL.
rows: Class G, 1,200 ft or less above the surface, day
Class G, 1,200 ft or less above the surface, night
500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
Class G, 1,200 ft or less above the surface, night, in a traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway
Class G, more than 1,200 ft above the surface and less than 10,000 ft MSL, day
500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
Class G, more than 1,200 ft above the surface and less than 10,000 ft MSL, night
500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
Class E, less than 10,000 ft MSL
500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal

article.heading: How the sectional marks each floor
paragraphs: Near an airport with an approved instrument procedure, Class E often comes down to 700 feet AGL. That lower layer is a transition area, for traffic moving between the airport and en route flight.

Class E's edges are drawn as vignettes, narrow shaded bands, or as a dashed magenta line. A magenta vignette marks a floor of 700 feet AGL, and a blue one marks any other floor where it borders Class G. The dashed magenta line encloses a Class E surface area, which starts at the ground.

Where a floor above 700 feet differs from the one beside it, a symbol and a number give its height. Some Class E begins at an MSL altitude printed on the chart, and that floor stays level whatever the ground does.

Where no lower Class E is designated at all, Class G reaches up to 14,500 feet MSL. Class E runs from there up to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL, leaving out the air less than 1,500 feet above the surface.

figure.caption: Near an airport with an instrument approach, the floor often comes down to 700 feet AGL, and the sectional marks it with a magenta vignette. Not to scale.
figure.alt: Farmland around an airport with a magenta layer labelled 700 ft AGL below the 1,200 ft AGL floor, and a round sectional inset showing the magenta vignette. Not to scale.

article.heading: Three mistakes about where Class G ends
paragraphs: Plan for Class E's minimums near an AGL floor. Over changing ground you can cross it without noticing. For weather minimums only, 14 CFR 91.155(e) counts an airplane exactly at the floor's altitude as in the airspace below.

Check the airport's page in the Chart Supplement before counting on a Class E surface area. Some run part-time, and the sectional marks those with a note. While one is off, its airspace can be Class G.
Expect a 700-foot transition area to be in force at any hour. Unlike a part-time surface area, it stays in effect whatever the airport's hours or the surface area's status.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. By day, 1,000 feet above a ridge under a 1,200-foot AGL floor, what visibility and cloud clearance does Class G require?
2. Holding 3,500 feet MSL over the 2,500-foot crest, how far below the Class E floor are you?
3. Back over the 1,500-foot valley at 3,500 feet MSL by day, what flight visibility do you need?
4. An airport in a magenta vignette has its part-time Class E surface area off. How high does Class G go over the airport?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. You need 1 statute mile of flight visibility and must stay clear of clouds. At 1,000 feet above the ridge you are 1,200 feet or less above the surface.
2. 200 feet. The floor there is 2,500 plus 1,200, or 3,700 feet MSL.
3. You need 3 statute miles. The floor there is 2,700 feet MSL, so at 3,500 feet you're in Class E, below 10,000 feet MSL.
4. To 700 feet AGL. The transition area the vignette marks stays in effect even while the surface area is off, so Class E still starts there.

posts.title: How fuel reaches the engine in a high-wing trainer
posts.headline: Gravity brings your fuel down from the wings.
posts.alt: How fuel reaches the engine in a high-wing trainer: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Gravity brings your fuel down from the wings. The picture shows two box-shaped tanks up at the wing line, the left tank's top cutaway showing fuel inside; the short curved vent tube opening from the outer left end of the left tank; the square selector valve plate with its round FUEL SELECTOR dial, centred below the tanks; the round strainer bowl with its mesh screen directly below the selector, beads of water and grit in its bottom. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Here's how fuel gets from the wing tanks to the carburetor in a high-wing trainer.

In a high-wing trainer the tanks are in the wings, and gravity carries the fuel to the engine. The vents keep each tank at atmospheric pressure. A strainer takes out moisture and sediment before the fuel reaches the carburetor.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
posts.related_text: On high-wing airplanes the fuel tanks are in the wings, and a gravity-feed system uses gravity to move the fuel from the tanks to the engine. The tanks are vented to the outside to keep atmospheric pressure inside them. Before the fuel reaches the carburetor it passes through a strainer that removes moisture and other sediment.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 7

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: In a high-wing trainer, gravity moves the fuel from the tanks in the wings down to the engine. Each tank has a vent open to the outside air. On the way down, a strainer cleans the fuel, and you drain that strainer before every flight.

article.heading: Why the fuel runs downhill
paragraphs: Stand under a high-wing trainer's wing and the fuel is over your head. The carburetor, which meters fuel into the air headed for the cylinders, sits below the tanks on the engine. Fuel leaving the tanks runs downhill to it, and that is a gravity-feed system.

A low-wing airplane shows why that height matters. Its tanks sit below the carburetor, so gravity can't deliver the fuel. It carries two pumps instead, one engine-driven and one electric for starting and backup.

In the high wing, both tank lines meet at the fuel selector valve, which picks the tank that feeds the engine. On a common type, LEFT or RIGHT feeds from one tank, BOTH from the pair, and the fourth position is OFF.

article.heading: Why each tank breathes outside air
paragraphs: The vent keeps the pressure inside the tank at atmospheric pressure, the pressure of the air around the airplane. As fuel runs out, outside air comes in to take its place.
The vent may be part of the filler cap, the lid over the filling hole on top of the wing. Or it may be a tube through the wing's surface.
Each tank also has an overflow drain, which lets fuel expand as it warms without damaging the tank. After a fill on a hot day, seeing fuel come out of it is not unusual.

article.heading: What the strainer catches
paragraphs: The strainer sits in the line below the selector valve, so all the fuel passes through it before the carburetor. It removes moisture and other sediment, the grit and dirt carried along in the fuel.
Gravity does a second job here. Water and sediment are heavier than the fuel, so they sink and gather at the bottom of the strainer. That low point is called a sump, and a fuel tank can have one too.
Your airplane may have a sump, a strainer and tank drains, with some sharing one spot. Systems vary, so learn where each drain is on the airplane you fly.

article.heading: Four fuel mistakes worth avoiding
paragraphs: Look at every fuel sample you drain for water and dirt. In cold weather, water left in the sump can freeze and block the fuel lines. In warm weather it can flow into the carburetor and stop the engine.
Keep draining when a sample shows water. Water in the sump means more is probably in the tanks, so drain them until none shows. Don't take off until the system is clear of water and sediment.

Set the fuel selector as its placard, the printed limits on tank use, tells you. On the selector the FAA handbook shows, LEFT and RIGHT each read 19 gal and LEVEL FLIGHT ONLY. BOTH reads 38 GAL with TAKEOFF, LANDING and ALL FLIGHT ATTITUDES.

Watch your fuel burn so no tank runs completely dry. Running a tank dry stops the engine, and the air it can let into the system makes a restart difficult. Long stretches on one tank also unbalance the fuel load.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Just after a hot-day fill, fuel runs from the overflow drain. What is happening?
2. What do you do before takeoff when your strainer sample shows water?
3. Your high-wing trainer's tanks feed by gravity. Why does a low-wing airplane carry fuel pumps?
4. Before takeoff the selector is on LEFT, under a placard reading LEVEL FLIGHT ONLY. Where do you set it?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Most likely it's fuel expanding as it warms, which the overflow drain lets out so the tank isn't damaged.
2. Drain the strainer and the tanks until no water shows, since water in the sump means more is probably in the tanks.
3. Its wing tanks sit below the carburetor, so gravity can't move the fuel to it. Pumps do that job instead.
4. Set it to BOTH, if the placard marks BOTH for takeoff and landing as the handbook's does. LEFT is for level flight only.

posts.title: When the radio goes quiet: light gun signals
posts.headline: Wait for steady green before you land.
posts.alt: Light gun signals with no radio contact, in the air: an illustrated card for pilots. Only steady green clears you to land. At dusk a control tower aims a steady green beam at a Cessna 172 on final approach. Below, the tower's six light signals and their meaning to an aircraft in flight: steady green, cleared to land; flashing green, return for landing, with steady green to follow at the proper time; steady red, give way to other aircraft and continue circling; flashing red, airport unsafe, do not land; flashing white, not applicable in flight; alternating red and green, exercise extreme caution. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Your radio has gone quiet and the tower is flashing green at you: what is it telling you?

It wants you back. Flashing green in the air means return for landing, and a steady green follows at the proper time to clear you to land. On the ground the same lights change jobs: flashing green clears you to taxi, steady green clears you for takeoff. All six signals are on the slides, air then ground.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
posts.related_text: In flight, steady green means cleared to land, and flashing green means return for landing, to be followed by steady green at the proper time. In flight, steady red means give way to other aircraft and continue circling, and flashing red means airport unsafe, do not land. On the ground, steady green means cleared for takeoff, flashing green cleared to taxi, steady red stop, and flashing red taxi clear of the runway in use. Flashing white, a ground-only signal, means return to starting point on the airport, and alternating red and green means exercise extreme caution everywhere. If the radio fails in flight under VFR in Class D airspace, you may land with at least basic VFR weather, the tower in sight, and a clearance to land. Acknowledge light signals by moving the ailerons or rudder in daylight and by blinking the landing or navigation lights at night. Departing a towered airport in Class D airspace requires two-way radio communication with the tower, and ATC can authorize a deviation.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Only a steady green clears you to land in the air or to take off on the ground.
Alternating red and green means exercise extreme caution everywhere. The other five signals change meaning between the ground and the air, and the table puts the two side by side.

table.caption: All six light gun signals, with their meaning on the ground and in flight.
rows: Return for landing (to be followed by steady green at the proper time)
Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
Taxi clear of the runway in use
Return to starting point on airport

article.heading: Three easy mistakes
paragraphs: Don't land on a flashing green. In the air it means return for landing, to be followed by steady green at the proper time.
Don't treat both reds the same. Steady red in flight means give way to other aircraft and continue circling, while flashing red means the airport is unsafe, so do not land there.
Don't expect white in the air: flashing white is a ground signal only, and it means return to starting point on the airport.

figure.caption: The same six lights, read for an aircraft on the ground.
figure.alt: Light gun signals with no radio contact, on the ground: an illustrated card for pilots. Wait for steady green before you take off. At dusk a control tower aims a steady green beam at a Cessna 172 waiting on a taxiway. Below, the same six signals and their meaning to an aircraft on the ground: steady green, cleared for takeoff; flashing green, cleared to taxi; steady red, stop; flashing red, taxi clear of the runway in use; flashing white, return to starting point on the airport; alternating red and green, exercise extreme caution. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.

article.heading: If your radio quits
paragraphs: If the radio fails after you leave the parking area, watch the tower for light signals and keep listening on the tower frequency.

In Class D airspace, a VFR pilot whose radio has failed may still land, on three conditions. The weather must be at or above basic VFR minimums, the tower must stay in sight, and a clearance to land must be received.
Departing a towered airport in Class D airspace, you must establish and maintain two-way radio communication with the tower. ATC can authorize a deviation from that.

article.heading: Answering the tower
paragraphs: Acknowledge each signal by moving the ailerons or rudder by day, or by blinking the landing or navigation lights at night.
At night you may need the tower's attention first. Turn on a landing light and taxi clear of the active runway, to a spot where the tower can see it. Keep the light on until a signal comes back.

figure.caption: Clear of the active runway, the airplane holds its landing light toward the tower until a signal comes back.
figure.alt: Clear of the active runway, the airplane holds its landing light toward the tower until a signal comes back.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. On final with a dead radio, the tower shows you a flashing green. Can you land?
2. Holding short with a dead radio, you get a flashing green. Can you take off?
3. Circling the field, you get a steady red and then a flashing red. What changed?
4. At night, with your radio dead, how do you get the tower to see you?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Not yet. It means return for landing, and the steady green that clears you to land follows at the proper time.
2. No. On the ground, flashing green clears you to taxi, and only a steady green clears you for takeoff.
3. Steady red meant give way to other aircraft and continue circling. Flashing red says the airport itself is unsafe, so do not land there.
4. Turn on a landing light and taxi clear of the active runway, to where the tower can see it. Keep the light on until a signal comes back.

posts.title: The stall that turns into a spin
posts.headline: Stop the yaw and the stall stays a stall.
posts.alt: The stall that turns into a spin: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Stop the yaw and the stall stays a stall. The picture shows the solid house aircraft right of centre, nose high and stalled, its nose on a thin dashed line of flight; the solid aircraft's rudder visibly deflected, with the green tag's leader line landing on it; a translucent ghost of the house aircraft to the left and lower, in the same nose-high attitude, with its nose swung clearly off the line of flight; the ghost's left wing dropping as it starts to roll toward it. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Why does a stall sometimes turn into a spin?
Poor yaw control during a stall makes a spin entry more likely. So your feet are part of the recovery. As you recover, cancel any yaw with the rudder so the stall doesn't progress into a spin.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
posts.related_text: Poor yaw control during a stall increases the likelihood of a spin entry. In a stall recovery, cancel any yaw with the rudder so the stall does not progress into a spin.
posts.intent: A stall turns into a spin when the airplane is yawing as the wing quits, which is why the rudder matters most at that moment.

article.heading: What turns a stall into a spin
paragraphs: You're slow, the nose is high, and the wing quits. That is a stall, and it comes from too much angle of attack, the angle between the wing and the air meeting it. If the nose stays pointed straight ahead, lowering that angle gets the wing flying again.
Now let the nose swing left or right just as the wing quits. That sideways swing is yaw. A spin starts when at least one wing is stalled while yaw acts on the airplane, at the stall or beyond it.

Once it starts, each wing is making different lift and drag. The airplane rotates around its vertical axis, the up-and-down line the nose swings about when it yaws. It descends, rolling, yawing and pitching along a corkscrew path.

A spin is an aggravated stall, one that can follow once a stall has happened. Poor yaw control during the stall makes a spin entry more likely. Since a spin needs both the stall and the yaw, keeping the yaw out leaves the stall as just a stall.

article.heading: Where the yaw comes from
paragraphs: Misused rudder is the obvious source of yaw, and it is only one of several. Moving the ailerons creates adverse yaw, a sideways swing of the nose that comes from the aileron deflection itself. The engine and propeller add yaw of their own.
Wind shear can yaw the airplane too, and so can wake turbulence from other aircraft. None of these come from your feet.
Yaw you cause with the wrong rudder has its own trap. You may not notice the wing has stalled until the airplane yaws out of control toward the dropping wing.
In a slipping or skidding turn, the rudder and ailerons are out of balance. A stall there can start a spin in the direction of the rudder you're holding, whichever wingtip is raised.
So the defense starts before any recovery does. Use the right amount of rudder to keep the nose from yawing and the wings from banking.

article.heading: Why the base-to-final turn is the trap
paragraphs: You're on base with a tailwind you haven't noticed. Your groundspeed is higher than you think, so you turn late or too shallow and overshoot the runway centerline.

The fix feels obvious. You steepen the bank, pull back, and push too much rudder toward the inside of the turn to swing the nose onto the runway. That inside push is called bottom rudder, and it makes the turn a skidding one.

Each input feeds the next. The difference in lift between the two wings grows, so the bank keeps steepening without you asking for it. The nose slices down through the horizon, and the natural reaction may be to pull back, raising the angle of attack toward the stall.

This is a skidding cross-control stall, and this turn is the most likely place for one. Cross-control means aileron pressure in one direction and rudder pressure in the other. If the wing stalls with those inputs held, the airplane may rapidly enter a spin.
The safest answer to an overshoot is a go-around. At that low height, be reluctant to bank past 30 degrees, and don't skid the turn as a correction.

article.heading: How the rudder fits into stall recovery
paragraphs: The handbook's stall recovery has six steps. A single-engine trainer without an autopilot would likely use only four of them. In that airplane, the actual first step is lowering the angle of attack until the stall warning goes away.

Nose-down trim may be needed if the elevator alone is not enough, though too much trim may make things worse. In a trainer that is less of a concern, because most pilots can overpower the trim and correct it on the way back.

Next, roll the wings level, but only after the angle of attack is down. Roll control is far better once the wing is flying again. This is where the rudder comes in, canceling any yaw so the stall does not progress into a spin.
Then add power as needed, promptly but smoothly, with rudder and elevator stopping any yaw or unwanted pitching. Power usually cuts the altitude you lose, but it does not end a stall.
Finally, fly back to your intended path. Keep the inputs smooth and coordinated, with rudder and ailerons working together, and watch for a secondary stall, the wing stalling again.

figure.caption: Canceling yaw is not a separate step, because the rudder works under all four of them.
figure.alt: Canceling yaw is not a separate step, because the rudder works under all four of them.

article.heading: What a spin costs once it starts
paragraphs: A spin has four phases, named entry, incipient, developed and recovery. The incipient phase, the early part, runs from the stall and the start of rotation until the spin is fully developed. In the developed phase, rotation, airspeed and descent rate have settled into a nearly vertical path.
For most airplanes the incipient phase can take two to four turns. Start recovery before 360 degrees of rotation.

In typical single-engine airplanes the rudder tends to be the most important recovery control. Apply it briskly. Slow, overly cautious rudder can let the airplane keep spinning even with recovery inputs in.

The first turn of a spin loses about 1,000 feet, and each turn after it loses about half that. Intentional spins should start high enough to finish recovering at or above 1,500 feet above ground level, or AGL. The turn from base to final is flown at a relatively low height.

table.caption: Every figure here comes from the handbook's spin section, in the order a spin unfolds.
rows: About half the first turn's loss

article.heading: Why recovery is no safety net
paragraphs: Modern airplanes tend to be more reluctant to spin than older designs, but they can still spin. Mishandled turns, stalls and slow flight with the controls out of balance can put even a reluctant airplane into an accidental spin. Continued stall practice helps you react promptly, and by instinct, when a spin is approaching.

Normal category single-engine airplanes certified under 14 CFR 23.221(a) only had to recover from a one-turn spin or a three-second spin, whichever takes longer. Recovery had to come within one more turn after the first recovery input. The other option was to meet that section's optional spin-resistant requirements.

So many of these airplanes were never required to recover from a fully developed spin. That rule still applies to airplanes certified under it, while section 23.2150 sets spin requirements going forward.

The pilot's operating handbook for your airplane gives its own spin recovery technique, and that takes precedence over general guidance. Some airplanes carry a placard prohibiting intentional spins. In those, there is no assurance that recovery from a fully developed spin is possible, so assume the airplane could become uncontrollable in one.

posts.title: Three different nights
posts.headline: Your night starts three times in one evening.
posts.alt: Three different nights: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Your night starts three times in one evening. The picture shows a sky that darkens from left to right, from a narrow pale rim of last light at the far left to full dark with stars on the right; three thin vertical lines rising from the horizon, in order from left to right: sunset, end of civil twilight, one hour after sunset; a runway running across the lower third with small pale edge lights; the house aircraft touching down just right of the third line, its small position lights lit. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: When does night start for your logbook, and when does it start for passengers?

Position lights go on at sunset. Night you can log starts later, when evening civil twilight ends. For carrying passengers, the three takeoffs and three full-stop landings you need within 90 days count only from one hour after sunset.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
posts.related_text: Night for logging runs from the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight. To carry passengers from one hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise, you need three takeoffs and three full-stop landings in that window within 90 days, as sole manipulator, in the same category, class and, if required, type. Position lights must be on from sunset to sunrise.
posts.intent: The rules use three different nights, so the time you log, the time passengers need your currency and the time your lights go on all start at different moments.

article.heading: Three rules switch on after sunset
paragraphs: You take off on an evening flight just before the sun goes down. As the light fades, three separate rules switch on, and each one picks its own moment.

Your position lights, the lights that show other pilots where you are, must be on from sunset. The night you log starts when evening civil twilight, the fading glow after sunset, has ended. Passenger currency, the recent night landings you need before flying people, starts one hour after sunset.
Each rule sits in a different part of the regulations and does a different job. So the word night can mean three different times on the clock, depending on which rule you're reading.

table.caption: Each night has its own start, its own end and its own job.
rows: Carrying persons, and which landings count

article.heading: Position lights go on at sunset
paragraphs: Taxi out at sunset and the lighting rule has already started. Under 14 CFR 91.209, your position lights must be lit whenever you operate an aircraft between sunset and sunrise. It's the first of the three rules to begin and the last to end.
The rule doesn't wait for the sky to look dark. Your aircraft is lit through all of evening twilight, before the logbook counts a single minute of night.

The same hours cover parking or moving in or near an airport's night flight operations area. There the aircraft must be clearly illuminated, show lit position lights, or sit in an area marked by obstruction lights.

Alaska uses a different trigger, tied to the light rather than to sunset. There it applies whenever the sun is over 6 degrees below the horizon, or a prominent unlighted object can't be seen from 3 statute miles.

article.heading: Logged night waits for twilight to end
paragraphs: Right after sunset the sky keeps a glow for a while. That stretch is evening civil twilight, and the definition of night in 14 CFR 1.1 leaves it out.

Night, as the regulations define it, runs from the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight. That is the night you log, so only flight time inside it counts as night time.
The times come from the Air Almanac, converted to local time. You look the moment up rather than judge it by how dark the cockpit feels.
The definition sets no fixed number of minutes after sunset. Read the published time for your date and place instead of adding a guess to sunset.

article.heading: Passenger currency starts an hour after sunset
paragraphs: Now put a friend in the right seat for a flight that runs late. From one hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise, 14 CFR 61.57(b) sets what you need, and its window does two jobs.
The first job is deciding when you need night currency. If you act as pilot in command, the pilot responsible for the flight, carrying anyone inside that window, you must be current.

The second job is deciding which landings count. In the 90 days before the flight, you need three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop, all inside that same window. Full stop means the aircraft comes to a complete stop, so a touch and go, where you add power and leave without stopping, doesn't count.
You must be the sole manipulator, the only person working the controls. The landings must also be in the same category of aircraft, meaning the broad grouping such as airplane.

They must be in the same class too, a group within a category such as single engine or multiengine, land or water. If a type rating, a rating for one specific model, is required, the type must match as well.

article.heading: Early landings log night but don't count
paragraphs: Say civil twilight ends well before the one-hour mark on the evening you fly. Between those two moments is a stretch where the logbook calls it night and the passenger window is still shut.
Fly three full-stop landings in that stretch and the time goes in your logbook as night. The landings still don't make you current for passengers, because they came before the window opened.

The same stretch matters if a passenger comes along. The night rule hasn't started yet. The general rule for carrying anyone still applies, with its three takeoffs and three landings in the preceding 90 days.
Once the clock passes the hour mark with that passenger still aboard, the night rule applies as well. If you might still be flying then, check your night currency before you leave.
Before an evening flight, note three times. Sunset is for the lights, the end of civil twilight is for the logbook, and sunset plus one hour is for passengers.

article.heading: At dawn the three windows close
paragraphs: The morning runs the same rules from the other side. The passenger window closes one hour before sunrise, so landings for currency have to be done by then.
Logged night ends when morning civil twilight begins, the first light before sunrise. Your position lights stay on longest, until sunrise itself.
You depart in full darkness before dawn with a passenger aboard, well inside the passenger window. You need night currency at takeoff, the logbook is counting night, and your lights are on.
As the sky brightens, those three conditions end one at a time. The lights always go last, because sunrise comes after both of the other closing times.

figure.caption: Over a whole night, the lights rule spans sunset to sunrise, and the other two windows open later and close earlier.
figure.alt: Over a whole night, the lights rule spans sunset to sunrise, and the other two windows open later and close earlier.

posts.title: An attitude indicator failing slowly
posts.headline: Your attitude indicator can be wrong without looking broken.
posts.alt: An attitude indicator failing slowly: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Your attitude indicator can be wrong without looking broken. The picture shows the vacuum system as Figure 8-20 draws it: heading indicator, attitude indicator, suction gauge, air filter, relief valve, pump and the hoses connecting them, the two gyro instruments side by side between the filter and the pump; the vacuum pump cold and still, nothing flowing in any hose; the suction gauge needle resting well below the short green arc that marks its normal range; the attitude indicator intact and convincing but showing a left bank as the FAA draws one: horizon and bank scale turned together, the orange miniature airplane level. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Would you spot an attitude indicator drifting slowly after a vacuum failure?

After a vacuum pump failure the gyros slow down, and the attitude indicator can wander and show a wrong picture while still looking normal. Cross-check it against every other instrument. An electric turn coordinator still shows direction and rate of turn. Many small aircraft have no vacuum warning, so watch the suction gauge for a reading below its normal range.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
posts.related_text: After a vacuum pump failure the attitude and heading indicators can fail progressively: as their gyros slow down they may wander, so the attitude indicator can show a wrong picture without looking broken and lead an unsuspecting pilot into an unusual attitude. Where the vacuum system drives the attitude and heading indicators and the electrical system drives the turn coordinator, the turn coordinator keeps showing the direction and rate of turn while the attitude indicator wanders. It does not display a specific angle of bank.
